We all have the firm idea that reality somehow “enters” our consciousness. What we tend to forget is that our consciousness is itself part of reality.

Suppose, for example, that we are talking about the solar system. We must remember that this conversation is not taking place outside space and time. It is taking place **inside the solar system itself**.

We can therefore say that, in the conversations we have about it, the solar system itself is in a sense “revealing” itself to itself.

If, for whatever reason, the temperature of the Sun suddenly rose or fell dramatically, humanity would disappear. And with humanity would disappear every theory, every opinion, and every conversation about the Sun.

These theories and discussions therefore depend in some way on the Sun itself. In a certain sense, they are consequences of its activity just as much as the evaporation of seas and oceans is.

If that is so, then we have to say that, through humanity and through human discourse, the solar system itself in a sense “reveals” itself to itself.

It becomes an astronomical “truth” when the meaning of the **discourse** produced within it coincides with what the solar system **actually is**.

There is nothing “mystical” about this. On the contrary, it is a “realist,” or if one prefers “materialist,” conception of truth—one that shows truth itself to be something **real**.

We can now understand why the only guarantee that an opinion is true is its **realization**, whether through technology or through politics.

An opinion can become knowledge—that is, can coincide with truth—if and only if, through work and struggle, it itself becomes in some way a real part of the world. It thereby becomes part of the reality that “reveals” itself to itself.<sup>122</sup>

From the “realist,” or “materialist,” standpoint established by Phenomenology, **truth** is therefore reality itself as disclosed in coherent discourse.

**Knowledge** is the opinion that coincides with truth: coherent discourse whose meaning has become real.

Truth and knowledge are two sides of one and the same thing.

Truth is the **objective** side of knowledge: the reality that is “disclosed” in the discourse constituting that knowledge.

Knowledge is the **subjective** side of truth: the content of human consciousness, or of opinion, that corresponds to this truth.

It follows from this definition that **truth** can exist only where there is a **reality** corresponding to the meaning of the discourse that expresses that truth.

And it follows in turn that **knowledge** exists only where the meaning of the corresponding opinion has been **realized**.

So if Phenomenology is supposed to **make** true philosophical knowledge possible—and if this first of all requires it to **show** the philosopher that such knowledge is possible—then Phenomenology must investigate the boundaries and limits of both reality and realization.

When it comes to reality itself—that is, to *nature*—the problem is relatively simple. We can say that nature has, in a sense, exhausted all its real possibilities from all eternity and remains eternally unchanged. In other words, the *natural* side of *truth* has existed since the “beginning of time.” What develops is only our *knowledge* of it: human ideas about nature gradually come closer to the truth.

This happens by putting those ideas into practice through technology. So, with regard to the natural world, the task of Phenomenology is to establish the limits of this *realization*. It must show that while natural *reality* already exists in its entirety, the process of *realizing* our ideas about nature is not yet complete. Human beings therefore do not yet possess, and cannot yet possess, complete *knowledge* of the natural world. Complete knowledge would exist when reality as it is independently of our ideas fully coincided with the practical realization of those ideas.

We can see this process of realization in the distinctive “technical world” that human beings have created within the natural world—a world made by us and for us on the basis of our knowledge of nature. And we can see that this process remains incomplete because the natural world and the technical world do not yet fully coincide: nature can still disrupt the internal order of the world we have created.<sup>123</sup>

The situation is much more complicated when we turn to the human world. Here, *reality itself* has not yet reached its completion. Human beings have not yet, in our time, exhausted all their real possibilities. One of the central tasks of Phenomenology is therefore to show that human reality is unfinished.

In the case of humanity, or the historical world, it is not only *knowledge* that is incomplete. *Truth itself* is incomplete as well. There is not yet any fully true knowledge of humanity, and there cannot yet be. This is not merely because such knowledge is still developing, but because human beings themselves are still in the process of realizing what they can become. There is not yet a final truth about humanity because humanity itself is not yet, so to speak, fully “true.”

This difference between natural *reality* or *truth* and human *reality* or *truth* means that *realizing* ideas about nature is not the same as *realizing* ideas about human beings. Developing and changing our ideas about nature does not change nature itself. But changing the ideas human beings have about themselves is part of the very process by which they realize themselves, and partly determines that process. So, in the human world, establishing the limits of what human beings can think about themselves is in part the same thing as establishing the limits of what human beings themselves can become.<sup>124</sup>

But the two are not completely identical. True knowledge cannot go beyond truth itself, and human beings can *be known* only to the extent that they have *realized themselves*.<sup>125</sup> Yet they do not immediately become conscious of what they have already become. A “new” kind of human being often continues to hold old ideas about humanity—and therefore about itself.<sup>126</sup>

Phenomenology must take this into account. It must draw the philosopher’s attention to the possible gap between humanity’s actual *realization* and the way that realization is reflected in human *consciousness*.

And even that is not enough. We must also distinguish between what is *familiar* to human beings and what they actually *know* or understand.

The situation is similar to our knowledge of the natural world. Someone may simply *not know* that the Earth travels around the Sun in an ellipse. But someone may also *know* this without *understanding* why it is so. The same is true of changes that have taken place in humanity. A change may be familiar to us, yet we may either fail to *understand* it altogether or understand it more or less *incorrectly*.

Phenomenology must therefore establish not only how far humanity has actually *realized* itself and how much of that realization has become *familiar* to human beings, but also how much of it they genuinely understand. And then, as we will see, it will repeatedly turn out that the “new” human being understands the “old” better than the old human being understood himself.<sup>127</sup>

In any case, Phenomenology must show that perfect knowledge—knowledge that is absolutely true—is *possible* only when truth itself is complete, which means when reality has fully realized all of its possibilities. It must show that such knowledge will actually exist when human beings not only grasp reality in its entirety but know it completely. Phenomenology must therefore show the philosopher that none of these three processes has yet reached its end at the time he is writing it.

Everything we have said so far about Phenomenology follows from its purpose: to prepare the possibility of philosophical knowledge. The first essential feature of such knowledge is its *self-awareness*. We can now turn to its *second* essential feature: its *concreteness*.

Philosophy seeks knowledge of actual reality—of what really or “concretely” exists—not of an “abstraction” that exists only in human consciousness, that is, in the “imagination.” As we already know, only reality *as a whole* exists concretely, not its separate parts. What concretely exists, for example, is “this table at a particular moment in time and in a particular place within the real universe.” What does not concretely exist is an isolated table located nowhere in particular and at no particular time.

And, as we already know, the real universe includes human beings themselves and everything they actually do, whether they are actively changing the world or passively observing it. The concrete solar system, for example, includes not only its planets and their natural, material movements. It also includes the Earth and its human world—and therefore, among other things, human knowledge of the solar system, whether true or false, right down to this very sentence I am writing now.

Phenomenology must teach the philosopher to take this aspect of concreteness seriously. When speaking about reality, the philosopher must also include the *consciousness* to which, within which, and through which that reality “reveals itself” in coherent discourse.

There can be discourse about the world only where human beings live, and human beings can speak about the world only because they live *within* it. So we cannot *speak* about concrete reality by concentrating either on the world alone or on humanity alone. What concretely exists is a world that includes human beings—or, which amounts to the same thing, human beings who exist within a world.

Knowledge of *concrete* reality therefore cannot be reduced either to knowledge of the world taken by itself or to knowledge of humanity taken by itself. It must be knowledge of both together, understood through their actual interaction.<sup>128</sup>

A philosopher who has passed through the school of Phenomenology will therefore differ from the ordinary person—the so-called “naive realist”—who can speak, for example, about the Sun while completely forgetting that he is *speaking* about it and that *he* is the one speaking.

The “naive” person thinks he is talking about *concrete* reality when in fact he is talking only about the “ob-ject” of his consciousness: something present within consciousness as referring to something outside it. It then turns out that he is not only failing to speak about *concrete* reality; strictly speaking, he is failing to speak about reality at all. If he is speaking about anything, it is merely his own subjective impression. A person speaking “naively” about the Sun would therefore have to describe it as a disc about the size of a plate, and so on.

But the philosopher also differs from the critical “scientist” who corrects the naive person’s mistakes. The scientist does introduce consciousness into the picture, since he distinguishes subjective illusion from objective reality. In trying to discover what reality is “really” like, he studies the way reality enters human consciousness.

But he does so only in order to *eliminate* everything purely subjective afterward—and, along with it, consciousness itself.

Admittedly, science, especially the theory of relativity and quantum mechanics, has recently understood that consciousness cannot simply be eliminated. Without it, nothing can be known about reality, since actual consciousness of reality modifies reality itself.<sup>129</sup> Yet when science introduces the subject into its account, it reduces the subject to an extreme simplification. It is interested only in sensory perception, and even that only in a schematic form.

In the end, science takes account only of the fact that human beings must actually *see* reality in order to know something about it. It completely ignores the further fact that they must also *think* about reality and in some way *speak* about it—that is, express it, for example, in mathematical formulas.

Science therefore never deals with *concrete* reality either. It is always content with knowing abstractions that have no actual existence in space and time.

A complete “scientific” knowledge of the natural world—say, a complete physics—does not even set itself the task of explaining why this very *scientific knowledge* of the natural world exists within that world, together with the discourse in which the knowledge is expressed.

When the “scientist” speaks about the world, he forgets, more or less consciously, that he is *speaking* about it and that *he* is the one doing the speaking. Yet he can only speak about the world that he actually speaks about, and that world really includes both this human being and his discourse. So the scientist, precisely insofar as he remains a “scientist,” does not speak about the concrete world. He speaks about an abstraction that exists as such only within the scientist’s consciousness.

The philosopher, by contrast, seeks knowledge of concrete reality. He must therefore study a world that includes knowledge of that very world—or, which amounts to the same thing, study a consciousness that contains knowledge of the real world in which that consciousness itself actually exists.

Finally, Phenomenology must also help the philosopher avoid falling into religious—or, more precisely, theological—error.

As we will see later, when human beings speak about “gods,” they are not simply telling “fables.” Without realizing it, they are really speaking about themselves: they give their “gods” characteristics they have first discovered in themselves.

The theologian thinks he is talking about God. The phenomenologist shows that he is in fact talking about himself.

One of the central tasks of Phenomenology is therefore not only to show that true knowledge of humanity is incompatible with belief in the existence of God, but also to uncover the human meaning behind different theologies.

Phenomenology shows that human beings fall into theological error because, in their knowledge, they adopt the “naive” or “scientific” standpoint. In other words, they forget to include within their knowledge of *reality* that very *knowledge* of reality itself. As a result, they are not dealing with concrete reality but with an abstraction just as “nonexistent” as their “God.”

The “naive” person, like the “scientist,” is accustomed to projecting the contents of consciousness beyond consciousness and treating them as realities that exist independently of him. He therefore tends to do the same with contents of consciousness that actually refer to himself. He treats them as some “objective” reality that is human-like or “anthropomorphic,” yet supposedly exists outside or independently of humanity. It therefore appears to him as “divine” or “theomorphic.”<sup>130</sup>

But once we try to have *concrete* knowledge of “God”—that is, once our knowledge of God includes the fact that it is a human being who knows God and speaks about God—it becomes clear that no such concrete reality exists or could exist, because the idea contains an internal contradiction.

It turns out that if human beings can *speak*, this is only because there is no God.

We can therefore say that, in teaching the philosopher to seek concrete knowledge of himself, Phenomenology also tends to teach him to be an atheist.

All of this will become clearer and more convincing from the text of the *Phenomenology* itself. For now, however, if we are to explain its purpose, we must examine what follows from the third and final feature of the philosophical knowledge that Phenomenology is meant to prepare. We must ask, in other words, what follows from its *power to convince*.

Only Phenomenology can, *strictly speaking*, give a complete answer to the question: “What is philosophy?” The nature of philosophy will become fully clear only at the end of Phenomenology, on the basis of its development as a whole. Only then will it become fully clear what the specifically philosophical “power to convince” must consist in.

To clarify the issue, we need to distinguish “opinion” from “knowledge,” and “ideology” from “truth.”

An “opinion” can happen to be correct. Its meaning may correspond to something that exists independently of it. But simply *as an opinion*, it can never *guarantee* that it is correct. Nothing therefore prevents us from accepting another opinion that differs fundamentally from the first or even directly contradicts it. Opinion, as such, is not “convincing” at all.

“Knowledge,” by contrast, is not contingent but *necessary*. To understand its meaning is at the same time to understand that this meaning is true and that its opposite is false. It is therefore precisely *as knowledge* that knowledge is “convincing.” And it is not convincing merely “today” or merely “for me.” It is convincing always and for *everyone*—at least for everyone who understands it.<sup>131</sup>

“Ideology,” meanwhile, is true only *in appearance*, and appears true only to those whose interests it serves. “Truth,” by contrast, does not depend on particular “interests”—or, if one prefers, it corresponds to the permanent interests of *everyone*.

We can also say that an “ideology” correctly reflects not the reality expressed by its explicit meaning, but the conditions that produced that meaning—namely, “class interests.” “Truth,” by contrast, is nothing other than the disclosure, through meaning, of the reality that meaning expresses.

Phenomenology must therefore show the philosopher that genuine knowledge, properly understood, is possible.

First of all, it must expose the inadequacy of both the rationalist and the empiricist accounts of knowledge.

The dialectic of rationalism shows:

1. first, that mere “consistency”—the absence of internal contradiction—is not enough to make something genuinely convincing;
2. second, that if we examine only the consistency of different forms of discourse, we have no way to determine which is true and which is false. This also means that there are no so-called “self-evident truths” or “axioms requiring no proof”;
3. third, that the content of any discourse must, as a rule, originate in something that exists outside and independently of that discourse.

But the dialectic that accepts this final point from empiricism also reveals the inadequacy of empiricism itself. It shows that knowledge cannot be made convincing simply by comparing, *within knowledge itself and using knowledge alone*, the meaning of what we say with the reality that this meaning is supposed to express.

The dialectic of empiricism therefore leads onward to “experimentalism.” Experimentalism understands that knowledge can acquire convincing force only through practical verification: knowledge of nature must be tested “technically,” through work, while knowledge of the human world must be tested “revolutionarily,” through struggle.

Yet the internal dialectic of “experimentalism” shows that only perfect “knowledge”—that is, *omni*science—can be definitively convincing. Technical and revolutionary verification can ultimately apply only to knowledge of a *concrete* being, and a concrete being cannot be separated from reality *as a whole*.

So, in the end, showing that “convincing” knowledge is *possible* means showing that omniscience is possible—that perfect knowledge, knowledge that can no longer change, or “wisdom,” can be reached.

And it is the *entire* content of Phenomenology—the *complete* dialectic it describes—that reveals this possibility.

By explaining the origin, or “genesis,” of human knowledge and the regular pattern of its development—its “evolution” or “progress”—Phenomenology shows that the idea of *completed* knowledge is not utopian. In other words, it shows that this development can reach the absolute limits of knowledge—or, more precisely, that it can exhaust all the discursive or “logical” possibilities of knowledge. This is not a fiction.

On the contrary, it is precisely Phenomenology’s description of the past and present development of knowledge that allows us to discover its future possibilities.

But to show that knowledge can continue to develop is also to show that present knowledge remains imperfect.

Phenomenology therefore does more than reveal to the philosopher that perfect knowledge is *possible*. It also shows how imperfect the knowledge available at the time of Phenomenology still is—an imperfection revealed by the fact that this knowledge is not yet fully convincing.

But showing this is not enough if knowledge is to be completed in a “real” rather than merely “utopian” way.

Phenomenology must not merely show the philosopher the “abstract” possibility of perfect knowledge. It must also reveal the *real conditions* under which existing knowledge can be brought closer to perfection.

It does this by showing where new historical conditions have emerged: new social, political, and technical conditions that did not exist when the knowledge we already possess was first produced. By understanding these new conditions, the philosopher gains the possibility of improving that knowledge.

Why?

Because these new conditions are preparing the conditions under which perfect knowledge itself will become possible—that is, they are preparing communist society.

But Phenomenology does not merely show the philosopher that existing knowledge is imperfect or unconvincing, or point to the “real” possibility of improving it. It must also identify, within the existing mass of “unconvincing” knowledge, those elements that *are* convincing: the elements that can become part of a convincing omniscience.

And because this partial convincing force can arise only through technical and revolutionary verification, Phenomenology accomplishes this by describing the dialectical process of human work and revolutionary struggle.

Whatever survives this process of mutual and dialectical destruction can be retained by the philosopher as true knowledge and incorporated into systematic philosophy. In this sense, Phenomenology gives the philosopher the material from which he will construct the edifice of his philo-sophy.

But because Phenomenology also teaches the philosopher the *origin* of this knowledge, it teaches him its limits as well.

He will know that his knowledge is partial and fragmentary, which means unfinished and imperfect, and therefore not yet fully “convincing.” From this standpoint, he will seek, on the one hand, to have his knowledge verified—and Phenomenology will show him that this can only take the form of public recognition by the society that has created the real conditions making his new philosophy possible.

On the other hand, he will also know that his knowledge as a whole must be revised whenever real conditions change. And he will finally know that this process of revision will come to a definitive end only when the final forms of social and political life have been realized—that is, with communism.

To sum up: the purpose of Phenomenology is to prepare real or concrete philosophy—or at least to make it possible. In other words, it is meant to prepare a *true* description of reality.

To do this, it must enable both its author and its reader to move from “opinion” to “knowledge,” from “ideology” to “truth,” or—which amounts to the same thing—from unconsciousness or partial consciousness to full *self-awareness*.

It does this by describing and examining all the “opinions” and “ideologies” available to us—that is, all the possible forms of humanity’s “unconscious” existence.<sup>132</sup>

But it is easy to see that this purpose contains a very serious internal difficulty.

On the one hand, Phenomenology is supposed to make true knowledge *possible*—to *prepare* it. On the other hand, Phenomenology itself claims to *be* true knowledge. So in a sense it already *presupposes* the possibility of the very thing it is meant to prepare.

Phenomenology may deal with opinions and ideologies—that is, ultimately, with errors and falsehoods. But its description of those opinions, ideologies, and errors is, in principle, *true*. Its own content is therefore not itself an opinion or an ideology, not an error or a falsehood, but genuine *knowledge*.<sup>133</sup>

The content of Phenomenology is therefore, *as a whole*, an essential part of *philosophy* in the broad sense.

As philosophy’s first, dialectical or introductory part, Phenomenology prepares its second part: the “dogmatic” or “systematic” part, which we can call “philosophy” in the narrower sense in order to distinguish it from “Phenomenology.”

But the first part is just as true as the second, and both are equally necessary. The complete *System* of true knowledge contains Phenomenology and systematic Philosophy on the same footing and gives equal status to both.

And yet Phenomenology is supposed to prepare this true knowledge—to make it *really* possible.

We will see at the *end* of Phenomenology that the standpoint it studies finally coincides with Phenomenology’s own standpoint—that is, with the standpoint from which Phenomenology conducts its study.

To show the inner order of the process that leads to this coincidence—to show the *necessity* of this *final* coincidence between the standpoint being studied and the standpoint of the one studying it—is to justify the latter standpoint. It is to *prove* its *truth*, and therefore the truth of the content that depends on it.

But that content is not only the systematic Philosophy that must be written from this standpoint. It is also Phenomenology itself, taken as a whole.

From Phenomenology’s own point of view, its standpoint remains unchanged from beginning to end. What changes are only the false standpoints that it studies, not the true standpoint from which it studies them.

At the beginning of Phenomenology, these standpoints are very far apart. As the work progresses, they gradually converge, until at the *end* they coincide.

Yet the standpoint reached at the end of Phenomenology is the same standpoint from which Phenomenology began.

It therefore seems as though Phenomenology presupposes and anticipates its own conclusion from the very start—even though, from its own point of view, that conclusion can be reached only by passing through *everything* that lies between beginning and end.

In other words, the phenomenologist becomes a philosopher only after he has written—or thought through—Phenomenology from beginning to end. But at the same time, unless he is already a philosopher, unless he already knows what philosophy is and what its task consists in, he cannot write or think a Phenomenology in the first place. He cannot even begin one—that is, undertake the task and conceive its “project.”

The very purpose Phenomenology sets itself therefore leads necessarily to what logic calls a “vicious circle” (*vitiosus circulus*). It presupposes from the outset what it hopes to prove at the end, and it can prove it only because it has already presupposed it.

There is no doubt that this “circle” exists. And we can state explicitly that it is absolutely unavoidable in philosophy[^E033], so long as philosophy seeks to be genuinely philosophical knowledge: knowledge that is absolutely true, fully concrete, and therefore complete.

Every other field of knowledge either deals with abstractions or is not concerned with truth.

Pure mathematics, for example, is concerned only with what makes deductions from wholly arbitrary premises—its “axioms” or “postulates”—logically valid. These premises are not in themselves true or false. All they need to be is “consistent,” meaning free of internal contradiction.

The so-called “real” sciences, such as physics and biology, deal only with a *part* of concrete reality, or with one partial *aspect* of it. They must therefore always begin with certain propositions that they simply accept “on faith” and never prove, because those propositions lie beyond the part or aspect of reality that the science itself studies.

All the real sciences, for example, accept “without proof” that a reality exists independently of our consciousness and that this reality can “reveal itself” through our discourse, provided that discourse obeys certain logical laws.

For philosophy, by contrast, reality, consciousness, discourse, the laws governing discourse, and so on are not simply “facts” or “axioms.” They are questions whose answers must themselves be proved.

But in attempting to prove these things, the philosopher necessarily has to use at least discourse itself and its logical laws. So when he tries to prove their truth, he necessarily falls into a “vicious circle.”

Because philosophy seeks *concrete* knowledge, it seeks *omni*science: knowledge of *everything* that can in any way be known. And because it seeks *knowledge*, it accepts nothing merely “on faith.” It tries to “show” or “prove” the truth of everything it claims.

It therefore seeks rigorous proof of everything.

Yet whenever it offers a proof, it is clear that it must already presuppose some part of what it is trying to prove.

With Hegel, philosophy became fully aware of the necessity of this logical circle.

But instead of treating the circle as “vicious,” Hegelian philosophy sees its “circularity” as the distinctive sign of perfect knowledge—of its *completeness* or *wholeness*.

By returning, at the end of its regular internal or dialectical development, to its own beginning, philosophy shows that it has exhausted *all* of its possibilities. It can therefore neither be expanded nor altered.

And this means that it is absolutely and definitively true: complete or perfect as knowledge.

From the standpoint of “formal logic”—that is, of the laws governing discourse—the circularity of philosophy means only that it is not its *isolated propositions* that are individually “true” or “proved.” What is true is philosophy *as a whole*, philosophy *in its entirety*.

Only the truth of the *whole* guarantees or “proves” the truth of its parts, even though the whole obviously could not exist without those parts.

Each individual element of the philosophical system may not be convincing by itself. But if the system as a whole is convincing, and if that system can stand only through the elements that actually make it up, then those elements ultimately prove convincing as well—precisely because the system *presupposes* them from the beginning.<sup>134</sup>

That this philosophical “circularity” is perfectly compatible with truth becomes clear once we notice that the same kind of “circularity” exists in reality itself—and can therefore also exist in the way reality is “revealed” through discourse, which is to say, in truth.

Philosophy presupposes what it proves in the same sense that any whole presupposes its parts, while those parts in turn presuppose the whole.

Take a geometrical ellipse.

Obviously, an ellipse presupposes its parts—its segments—because without them it could not exist. But those parts, insofar as they are parts of an *ellipse*, also presuppose the ellipse itself. Without the ellipse, they could not exist as what they are.

We might suppose that the ellipse is made up of geometrical points that “exist” independently of it. But this is not really so.

At every point on an ellipse, we can draw a tangent—that is, a straight line. The point in question therefore belongs at once to a point, a straight line, and an ellipse. At each of its points, then, the ellipse can coincide with a straight line.

So where is the ellipse actually elliptical—that is, curved?

Clearly, the components or elements of an ellipse, *as an ellipse*, are not points but segments, however tiny those segments may be—“differentials.” And these segments cannot exist *as segments of the ellipse* without the ellipse itself.

They exist *only within it*.

Take an even simpler example.

A dog is obviously made up of parts—a head, legs, a tail, and so on—and could not exist without them. In that sense, the dog’s existence “presupposes” its parts.

But equally, the dog is not made up of a head, legs, and a tail “in general.” It is made up of a *dog’s* head, a *dog’s* legs, and so on.

The parts of a dog therefore presuppose, so to speak, the dog itself. They cannot exist without it or apart from it. Or take the classic problem of the chicken and the egg. The chicken presupposes the chicken egg from which it hatched, while the egg in turn presupposes the chicken that laid it.

Of course, we usually bring up this problem precisely to show that we do not really understand where the chicken ultimately came from. So one might raise the same objection against circular philosophy. Even if such a philosophy is possible—that is, even if it contains no contradiction—its origin still seems impossible to understand. We might grant that, in a system that had somehow “fallen from the sky,” the whole could prove the truth of the parts that make it up. But we would still have no idea how that whole could ever have been constructed in the first place. How, in other words, can someone who reaches the philosophical point of view only at the end of Phenomenology write the Phenomenology at all, when he apparently has to possess that point of view from the very beginning?

In reality, there is nothing incredible or impossible about this. The same thing happens whenever we arrive at genuine knowledge: there is a kind of circular dependence between a “hypothesis” and the technical or revolutionary test that verifies it.

Take an example we have already used: the invention of the first airplane. The airplane could fly only if the design was correct. But the design became demonstrably correct only when the airplane actually flew.

Exactly the same applies to the philosopher. He constructs his systematic Philosophy on the basis of a project that he assumes to be true. He then **establishes** or “proves” its truth through the “success” of the completed system. In this sense, the philosopher’s “work”—the actual completion of the philosophical system—is itself, so to speak, an experimental or technical test of the system’s truth, and therefore of the truth of the elements it initially had to presuppose. To this technical test through work is then added a “revolutionary” test: the public recognition that the philosopher’s system receives.<sup>135</sup>

What is true of the system as a whole is also true of its parts, and especially of Phenomenology.

Until the phenomenologist has finished his work, he cannot be certain that his starting point was correct or that the conclusions he reached along the way were true. Only the completed work, by displaying the convincing force of the whole, can finally convince him that he began in the right place and never strayed from the right path.

If we like, we can say that when the phenomenologist—and the philosopher—begins his work, he takes a “risk,” and that his success is therefore “contingent.” But this risk is smaller, say, than the one taken by the engineer who built the first airplane, and his success is correspondingly less contingent.

We can call this unavoidable element of “contingency” ability, talent, or even genius, depending on the scale of the risk involved—that is, on the possibility of failure. But even where the risk is enormous, success is neither incredible nor miraculous.

It would be miraculous only if the phenomenologist genuinely began “from the beginning,” with no help from the work of his predecessors. It would have been miraculous, for example, if Hegel’s *Phenomenology* had appeared in the Athens of Pericles or in the hut of an Australian “Aborigine.” It would have been equally miraculous for a workable design for an airplane to have appeared there.

But we do not have to travel the whole road again every time. We need only travel a small new section of it—indeed, a very small section in comparison with the whole—which extends a path that others have already cleared.

Of course, while travelling this new but short stretch of road, one may discover that from the point now reached it would be better to take a different route. In other words, someone who reaches that point may open up a new and very long path. Yet even then, he can do so only because the road leading to that point had already been cleared.

We must not forget that every phenomenon that “breaks with the series” still presupposes the series from which it breaks away. The scale of the “risk” Hegel took may justify calling the “contingency” that enabled him to write his *Phenomenology* an act of genius. But we should remember that he owed no less to his philosophical predecessors than, say, the Wright brothers owed to theirs in pure and applied mechanics.<sup>136</sup>

In any case, the “circularity” remains. If we like, we can call it a kind of “circular guarantee” within Phenomenology.

For its author, this has a practical meaning: he could not write it correctly “in one go.” He had to write it, so to speak, circularly. Having reached the end, he had to go back and correct the beginning. Starting again from that corrected beginning, he then had to revise the end and the path leading to it, and so on, until the work formed a whole that was genuinely convincing.

For the reader, the same circularity means that Phenomenology can be fully understood in all its parts only after it has been read in its entirety. Yet the whole obviously cannot be understood unless its parts have been understood. Reading it must therefore also be “circular.” Strictly speaking, only a second reading can be fully convincing.

And this means that Phenomenology can properly be criticized only as a whole, not by tearing isolated passages out of it.<sup>137</sup>

### 2. The theme and object of a Phenomenology

Having established the aim—or aims—of a Phenomenology, we must now determine its **theme**. That means identifying its **object**: what it studies, and what kind of true knowledge it claims to provide.

But we must not make it seem as though the phenomenologist simply chooses his subject at random. We need to show that the introductory first part of the philosophical system could not have any object other than the one chosen by Hegel’s *Phenomenology*—and by mine.

So we must connect the theme of Phenomenology with its purpose. In defining its object, we have to show that once Phenomenology sets itself the goals described above, it is necessarily led to this particular object and no other.

We should not forget, however, that only Phenomenology itself can ultimately justify the phenomenologist’s choice of these goals.

As we have seen, the purpose of Phenomenology is to prepare us for **philosophical knowledge**: true knowledge of **concrete reality**.

Strictly speaking, philosophical knowledge is philosophical precisely because it is concrete, unlike “scientific” knowledge in the narrower sense, which deals with abstractions.

But if we use the word *science* more broadly and contrast scientific knowledge—as convincing and secure, that is, necessary and universal—with the contingent information possessed by ordinary people, then philosophical knowledge must first of all also be **scientific** knowledge.

It is scientific precisely because it is **knowledge** (*epistēmē*) rather than **opinion** (*doxa*).

And what distinguishes knowledge from opinion is the presence of **self-consciousness**, or conscious awareness of what one knows.

A person who merely holds an opinion cannot, on the basis of that opinion itself, know that it is only an opinion. For no clear reason, he may simply take it to be genuine knowledge.

Knowledge is different. Genuine knowledge itself shows the person who possesses it that he possesses knowledge—and why what he possesses really is knowledge.

That is to say, it shows itself to be true knowledge: knowledge of truth, or of reality itself as reality reveals its own essence to human beings through the meaningful content of coherent, intelligible human speech.

Someone who possesses knowledge **knows that he possesses it**. Conversely, only someone who knows that what he possesses really is knowledge can truly be said to possess knowledge.

But we can know that we possess knowledge only if we know **what knowledge is**.

Knowledge of what knowledge is therefore a necessary condition for possessing knowledge at all—and, as we will see, it is also a sufficient condition.<sup>138</sup>

Now, the aim of Phenomenology is to make philosophical knowledge possible, and Phenomenology itself claims to be a necessary preliminary condition for possessing that knowledge. We must therefore say that Phenomenology is nothing other than **knowledge of what knowledge is**.

In other words, if its **aim** is to create the real possibility of actually possessing knowledge, then knowledge itself must necessarily become the **theme** of its investigation.

The **object** of Phenomenology is therefore knowledge as such.

It studies knowledge in order to acquire knowledge **of knowledge as knowledge**. In this sense, it is a “discourse on knowledge”—an *epistemo-logy*: a science of knowledge, or a **theory of knowledge**.

And since the possession of knowledge, together with the process by which it is acquired, is called cognition (*gnōsis*), Phenomenology can also be defined as a “discourse on cognition”—a *gnoseo-logy*: a science or **theory of cognition**.

The theme of Phenomenology therefore coincides with the theme of Kant’s three famous *Critiques*. Their object—both Kant’s *Critiques* and Phenomenology—is human knowledge and the process of cognition that makes this knowledge possible. They make cognition their theme because their goal is to prepare the way for philosophical knowledge.

Kant was the first to formulate clearly the principle that philosophical knowledge is impossible without some prior knowledge of **what knowledge is** and of the process of cognition that leads to it.

Kant’s reasoning was roughly this. In order to possess a truth—that is, a true **content** of knowledge—we must first understand the **form** taken by that content: knowledge and cognition as such.

Or, to put it another way, cognition is the **instrument** by which we reach truth, which is the content of knowledge. So we can hope to reach truth only if we first turn our attention to this instrument and study it.

On the one hand, once the *Critiques* have taught us what cognition is, we can determine the **limits** of cognition and therefore establish what can and cannot become the content of true knowledge—that is, what can count as truth.

On the other hand, once we understand the instrument itself, we can take account of the changes or distortions caused by its use. We will then stop attributing to the objective content of knowledge—that is, to truth—features that in fact belong only to its subjective form: to human knowledge and the process of human cognition.

This formulation of the theme of a “theory of cognition” appears explicitly for the first time in Kant.

But the idea that knowledge of human knowing must in some sense come before the content of philosophical knowledge is as old as philosophy itself.

In one sense, the distinction between knowledge and opinion was already the theme of all Plato’s *Dialogues*. The works attributed to Aristotle and collected under the title *Organon*—works that served throughout the Middle Ages as an “introduction to philosophy”—are devoted to the study of knowledge and cognition as a means of reaching truth.

Likewise, at the beginning of modern philosophy, Descartes devoted two of his earliest philosophical works to the study of knowledge and cognition: the *Discourse on Method* and the *Meditations on First Philosophy*.

More generally, one can find “gnoseological” investigations in every major philosopher. In that sense, the theme of Phenomenology is a traditional philosophical theme.

Still, we must emphasize again that Kant was the first to understand clearly the full significance and fundamental necessity of this preliminary investigation into cognition. He showed not merely that such an investigation conditions the **possibility** of philosophical knowledge, but that it in some sense determines the whole character of that knowledge.

In this respect, the true “father” of Phenomenology is Kant.

Yet although the themes of Phenomenology—whether Hegel’s or mine—and of Kant’s *Critiques* are identical, we must not overlook a fundamental difference between them.

They study the same **object**—human knowledge and cognition—but they differ radically in how they define, understand, and interpret that object.

Hegel accused Kant of having an “idealist” understanding of cognition and knowledge.

Kant himself objected to being counted among the “idealists.” And it is true that he never went so far as idealism in the strict sense: the absurd claim that only consciousness and the processes occurring within it exist, while outside consciousness and independently of it there is no reality at all.<sup>139</sup>

Still, Hegel was right in the sense that Kant’s thought undeniably contains idealist tendencies and distortions. It is certainly no accident that the neo-Kantians who were so widespread at the end of the nineteenth century and the beginning of the twentieth were hardened “idealists.”<sup>140</sup>

For the purposes of his investigation, Kant was entirely right to distinguish between the **form** and **content** of truth—that is, between knowledge and cognition on the one hand and the reality they express on the other.

But he seems to have forgotten that, in actual fact, the two are inseparable, and that when we study them separately we are dealing only with **abstractions**.

Kant nowhere says that subjective knowledge can exist independently of objective reality or outside it. Yet in his account the subject who knows begins to resemble a kind of “consciousness in general,” composed of intuition, understanding, and reason, whose relation to reality remains obscure.

This consciousness starts to look suspiciously like the “mind,” “soul,” or “world-reason” of the rationalist philosophers: something that derives the whole content of its consciousness from itself, *a priori*, rather than from the reality that exists outside it.

In any case, Kant treats it as possible to study consciousness, knowledge, and cognition as such, independently of the reality revealed in and through them.

So although he allows part of the content of knowledge to come somehow from reality, he still locates another part—the *a priori* or “immanent” content—within consciousness independently of reality.

Conversely, while Kant rightly maintains that reality exists independently of consciousness and cognition, he forgets that the reality we are actually talking about includes, as a matter of fact, our consciousness and cognition of that reality.

For this reason he wrongly contrasts the reality actually known by human beings with some “true” reality—the “thing in itself”—that supposedly remains inaccessible to cognition.

What we know, on this account, is not that “true” reality itself, but a product arising from the interaction between it and the consciousness that knows it: a “phenomenon.”

Truth therefore ceases to mean **reality itself revealing itself** through human consciousness and our knowledge of reality. Instead, truth becomes **knowledge itself**, possessing a certain content.

Kant himself understands this content as the product of an interaction between consciousness and a reality that, in its pure form, cannot be known.

But because the nature of this interaction remains obscure, and because we cannot separate what comes from reality from what depends only on consciousness, the criterion of truth can no longer be found by empirically comparing knowledge with reality. It has to be sought, in a purely rationalist way, through an examination—or “critique”—of knowledge itself.

It is hardly surprising that Kant’s immediate successors, especially Fichte, discarded what seemed to them an unnecessary concept: the concept of reality, or the “thing in itself.” The result was pure idealism.<sup>141</sup>

The source of the whole problem is easy to see. It lies in separating form from content and treating cognition as an instrument fundamentally different from, and independent of, the material on which it operates.

If cognition is an instrument made of something different from reality, then using it must indeed distort reality.

And if reality exists entirely without knowledge, then there is nothing surprising about its being inaccessible to knowledge.

So if we retain a realist concept of reality, we are driven toward a sceptical or agnostic rejection of truth, and therefore toward a denial of knowledge.

If, on the other hand, we want to preserve the idea of true knowledge, we are driven toward an idealist denial of reality and a rationalist search for the criterion of truth within knowledge itself.

But we have already seen that examining knowledge by itself gives us no way to distinguish true knowledge from false knowledge. So this route also ends, in practice, in scepticism.

If Phenomenology understood its **object** in the same way Kant did—if it studied knowledge independently of reality—it could hardly achieve its **purpose**. Instead of preparing the way for true knowledge, it would demonstrate that true knowledge is impossible.

Hegelian Phenomenology understands its object quite differently.

It begins from a genuinely realist—or “materialist”—conception of truth as **reality revealing itself to itself through human consciousness, cognition, and knowledge**.

It knows that rationalist attempts to find the criterion of truth within knowledge alone are just as hopeless as empiricist attempts to compare the content of consciousness with reality while remaining entirely **inside consciousness**.

Phenomenology therefore turns toward what we might call **experimentalism**. It finds the criterion of truth in technical verification through work and revolutionary verification through struggle—tests that take place in **reality itself**.

The products of these “techniques”—work and revolution—combine knowledge and reality so closely that the two become virtually inseparable. An airplane or a State, for example, can equally well be understood as a product of knowledge about reality or as the realization of knowledge in reality.

Phenomenology therefore understands that knowledge cannot be separated from reality and studied independently of it.

If truth is reality revealing itself through knowledge, and if Phenomenology aims to prepare the possibility of true knowledge, then Phenomenology cannot study some vague “consciousness in general,” some cognition or knowledge “as such” existing nowhere in particular and made of no one knows what.

It must study **real knowledge that reveals reality itself through its meaningful content**.<sup>142</sup>

We can now see that Phenomenology arrives at the definition of its **object** directly from the **goal** it has set itself.

It wants to prepare philosophical knowledge: concrete knowledge, or knowledge of concrete reality.

Reality “in general” may of course exist without human beings knowing it. But once human beings exist and actually speak about reality, concrete reality genuinely includes this speech about itself.

Concrete reality is therefore inseparable from concrete knowledge, and concrete knowledge is likewise inseparable from reality.

What concretely exists is **reality revealed in knowledge**—or, what amounts to the same thing, **knowledge revealing reality**.

And because Phenomenology studies concrete knowledge, it must study precisely this kind of knowledge, not some abstraction called “knowledge in general.”

For Phenomenology, then, knowledge and cognition are not instruments that somehow exist outside reality and independently of it and are then applied to reality from outside, with no explanation of where they came from.

If they are indeed instruments that reveal reality, they are nevertheless **real instruments, forged by reality itself and, so to speak, for its own use**.

They therefore cannot distort reality simply by being applied to it.

If we like, we can say that the instrument of cognition changes reality when applied to it, just as any instrument changes the material on which it works. But these changes must not be treated as distortions.

The instrument, its use, and the changes produced by that use are just as real as the supposedly “untouched” reality that existed beforehand.

Indeed, only reality **as modified through cognition** exists concretely and actually. “Untouched” reality is itself merely an abstraction or fiction, just as unreal as an instrument of knowledge imagined apart from the reality to which it is applied.

From the standpoint of “naive” realism—the standpoint of rationalists and empiricists, and one shared more or less consciously by all the “sciences” in the narrower sense—cognition can be compared to the scaffolding used to construct a building.

Once the building is finished, the scaffolding is removed, and the building itself—the “true” reality—would supposedly stand revealed to the observer.

But to **what observer**? That remains a mystery.

Phenomenology knows two things.

First, this building could not be revealed to **human beings** without knowledge, because reality without cognition would remain inaccessible to them.

Second, even if we imagined some “divine” observer contemplating the building after the scaffolding had been removed, what this observer saw would not be reality itself. It would merely be an abstraction that exists as such only in human consciousness.

Rationalism—and idealism—makes the opposite mistake. It imagines that if we abstract from reality, we can discover “true” consciousness and knowledge in their “pure form.”

Phenomenology knows instead that knowledge is nothing other than the **revelation of reality**.

Remove reality, and nothing remains to be revealed. What remains is therefore **nothing**.

By proceeding in this way we reveal nothing at all, and knowledge itself collapses into nothingness.

From the standpoint of Phenomenology, then, knowledge and reality are inseparable.

Phenomenology can therefore study not knowledge “in itself,” but knowledge that reveals reality. Yet if it does so, it necessarily also deals with **reality as revealed in and through knowledge**.

Even so, its theme remains the study of **knowledge**, not reality. Knowledge, rather than reality, is its object.

Reality revealing itself in knowledge, on the one hand, and knowledge revealing reality, on the other, are two inseparable and complementary aspects of one and the same thing: **known reality or realized knowledge—that is, truth**.

Knowledge and reality form an inseparable whole, like the red and green sides of the same apple.

Yet we can look at an apple from either side, and it is equally correct to say that it is red on one side and green on the other.

The same is true of truth.

We can regard truth either as **reality revealed in knowledge** or as **knowledge that reveals reality**.

Phenomenology takes it in the second sense.

So despite everything, Phenomenology is not a discourse on reality—an onto-logy or “metaphysics.” It is a discourse on knowledge—a gnoseo-logy, a theory of cognition.

But it is a discourse on **concrete**, and therefore philosophical, knowledge: a **philosophical or concrete theory of cognition**.

In truth itself, the ontological and gnoseological—or logical—aspects of discourse coincide completely.

For this reason, in the systematic exposition of truth—that is, in systematic Philosophy—a discourse on reality, or Ontology, is inseparable from a discourse on knowledge, or Gnoseology; and both are inseparable from a discourse on the “concept,” that is, Logic.<sup>143</sup>

Phenomenology, however, does not yet deal with truth itself. Its task is to prepare the possibility of true knowledge.

Put very briefly, it deals not with true knowledge but with **“false” knowledge**.

And false knowledge that reveals reality does **not** coincide with the reality revealed within that consciousness.

Phenomenology can therefore separate these two aspects and legitimately study only one of them.<sup>144</sup>

Yet although Phenomenology restricts itself to the study of **knowledge**, it does not study “consciousness in general,” cognition “as such,” knowledge “in itself,” or some kind of “pure” knowledge.

It studies consciousness, cognition, and knowledge **of reality**.

For this reason, it may sometimes seem that Phenomenology is speaking about **reality** from beginning to end.

But what appears there is not reality itself. It is only reality as reflected in “false” knowledge—that is, reality as the **content** of this knowledge.

Of course, even false knowledge is real in the sense that it actually occurs within reality. It therefore reveals reality in some way.

And we will see that such knowledge is “false” only because it presents itself as universal or complete while in fact remaining **one-sided**.

If we examine false knowledge, we can isolate the aspect of reality that it does reveal. If we then combine all these aspects, we obtain full or true knowledge of reality.

But carrying out that analysis of the reality revealed through cognition is simply **not the task of Phenomenology itself**.<sup>145</sup>

Thus, although Phenomenology studies only **knowledge**, it does not separate the “form” of knowledge from its “content.” It studies **knowledge of reality**.

And the reality embraced by Phenomenology in the fullest sense is **concrete reality**.

What exists concretely is not “reality in general,” but the real material world: the natural world of mountains, rivers, and forests, as well as the technical world of houses, roads, and cars.

And this real world genuinely includes the real subject who knows it, together with that subject’s historical, social, and political world.

So when Phenomenology studies knowledge of **concrete reality**, it studies knowledge of both the natural and the human world.

Let us say it once more: it studies **knowledge of this real world**, not the world itself in its reality.

But knowledge of this world is itself **real**, and Phenomenology studies not only knowledge of concrete reality but also the **concrete reality of knowledge**.

Real, concrete knowledge exists in the real world in the person of **human beings**.

Phenomenology therefore studies not “consciousness in general” or some kind of “world-reason,” but **human consciousness and human reason**.

In other words, it studies concrete human knowledge of the concrete world. It studies not the world in its reality, but the world as it is **revealed** or **manifested** to human beings—that is, if we like, the **appearance** of the world to humanity, its **phenomenon**.

This is where the name comes from: *phenomeno-logy*, a discourse or science of **appearance** and **appearances**.

Now, the real world includes humanity itself.

So when the world “manifests” itself to human beings, the world is in one sense appearing **to itself**.

Phenomenology therefore studies not only the ways in which the world appears to human beings, but also the ways in which human beings appear to themselves.

It studies not reality itself but **knowledge of reality**. And this concrete knowledge is itself nothing other than a human being.

So the “appearance” of the world reveals not so much the world as the human being to whom that world appears.

In this sense, Phenomenology can be described not as a discourse or science of the world—not as a cosmo-logy—but as a discourse or science of **human beings**: an **anthropology**.

Yet it studies human beings not simply in their reality, but insofar as they **manifest themselves** within the world—insofar as they are a “phenomenon.”

The object of Phenomenology is therefore not simply **the human being**, but **the appearance of the human being to the human being**.

So although we can call Phenomenology an anthropology, we must now add that it is a **phenomenological anthropology**.

Since for human beings the appearance of humanity to itself amounts to an experience of oneself—to becoming aware of oneself or becoming self-conscious—we can define Phenomenology still more precisely as the **science of human self-consciousness**.

And because self-consciousness reveals to human beings a human being **within the world**, Phenomenology studies not only the appearances of humanity to itself, but also appearances of the world.

It is therefore phenomenology in the **full sense of the word**.

And because the experience of oneself involves both cognition and knowledge, Phenomenology, in studying self-consciousness, studies both and is therefore also a gnoseology.

At the same time, because it does not separate form from content, and because the content of self-consciousness is knowledge of humanity, it is also—while remaining a gnoseology—a phenomenological anthropology.

So we can call it, with equal justification, a **phenomenological gnoseology**, a **phenomenological anthropology**, an **anthropological gnoseology**, or a **gnoseological anthropology**.

But Phenomenology does not study human cognition and “appearances” simply out of curiosity. Its specific purpose is to make **true knowledge** possible.

Self-consciousness interests it only insofar as self-consciousness contains this knowledge, or the real possibility from which Phenomenology itself can arise.

And we know that the only criterion of the truth of knowledge is technical and revolutionary verification.

But revolutionary verification takes place **in time**. It marks the **transition** from one form of knowledge, consciousness, and self-consciousness to another.

Phenomenology therefore studies the appearance of human beings to themselves not only at some particular moment, but throughout its **temporal—that is, historical—development**.

In other words, it studies the **becoming**, evolution, development, or history of the way human beings—and the world—appear to human beings.

That means the becoming, development, or history of self-experience, and therefore of consciousness, cognition, and knowledge in general.

For this reason, Phenomenology can also be defined as a **historical gnoseology** or a **historical anthropology**.

But whatever name we give to Phenomenology—that is, to the book placed before the reader—we must always remember that it is first and foremost precisely a **phenomeno-logy**: a doctrine of “appearances.”

As such, it differs fundamentally both from gnoseology in the usual sense and from ordinary anthropology.

It differs from ordinary, “Kantian” gnoseology because it does not study some abstraction existing no one knows where—a consciousness and cognition supposedly existing in themselves. It studies a **concrete consciousness: the consciousness of a human being**.<sup>146</sup>

For this reason, it would actually be more accurate to call the present work a **phenomenological anthropology**, because those words identify its object and the character of its theme quite precisely.

The object of Phenomenology is the human being; its theme is the phenomenological investigation of the human being.

But if this definition is to become fully intelligible—and if we are to avoid misunderstandings while reading the text—we must explain more precisely how the phenomenological study of human beings differs from the ordinary “scientific” study of them.

The word *anthropo-logy*, meaning the “science of humanity,” is highly ambiguous and has been used to mean many different things.

Most often, I imagine, it refers to the science that studies human races, both historical and non-historical, and more generally the characteristics of the **human body**.

Phenomenological anthropology has absolutely nothing to do with this science.<sup>147</sup>

It is interested in knowledge and therefore, ultimately, in **speech**. It examines human beings only insofar as this is necessary for understanding what they say.

And since we presuppose that only human beings—not animals—can speak coherently, that is, can reveal reality through the meaningful content of discourse, we may say that Phenomenology is interested in human beings only insofar as they are **different from animals**.

Since there is nothing specifically human in the human body itself, Phenomenology excludes the body from its investigation, together with everything **immediately** connected with it.<sup>148</sup>

If we want to compare Phenomenology with a general “science” of human beings, therefore, we should compare it not with human anatomy or physiology, but with **psychology**.

The Greek word *psycho-logy* means a discourse or science of the “soul” (*psychē*).

One of the fundamental tasks of Phenomenology is certainly to show that there is no “soul” in the human being.

But if by “soul” we simply mean the **aspect** of real human existence that distinguishes specifically human existence from merely animal existence, then we could also call Phenomenology a kind of *psycho-logy*—or, more exactly, that general part of psychology concerned with specifically human “psychic” phenomena.

Still, it is better not to use the word, because—as we will see—Phenomenology has nothing in common with what is ordinarily called psychology, even when psychology understands that the “soul” is not an independent reality or “substance,” but only an aspect of the real human being that can in practice be distinguished from our animal and bodily existence.

Finally, the word “anthropology” is also used for the scientific study of the life of “primitive” peoples: their forms of culture, the basic elements of their worldview, and so on.

Phenomenological anthropology resembles “anthropology” in this sense more closely than it resembles any of the others.

It is true that Phenomenology does not restrict itself to the study of “primitive” humanity. But there is nothing in this concept of anthropology that logically requires us to apply it only to “savages.”<sup>149</sup>

In this sense, “anthropo-logy” is really nothing more than a **history of “primitive” peoples in the broadest sense**: not merely their political and military—that is, social—history, but also their economic, technical, religious, aesthetic history, and so on.

Because the historical life of “primitive” peoples is relatively simple, we usually study it as a whole. The history of civilized peoples, by contrast, is normally divided into a number of supposedly “independent” histories.

In principle, however, everyone recognizes that dividing a single real process in this way is artificial and undesirable.

These separate “histories” nevertheless form a single whole. So there can be no principled separation between the study of properly historical periods and the study of “prehistoric,” “non-historical,” or “primitive” periods.

If the history of humanity as a whole, embracing every historical and therefore specifically human phenomenon, is called “anthropology,” then Phenomenology most closely resembles anthropology in this sense.

In other words, Phenomenology could be called the **complete history of humanity as a whole**.

But it is better not to use this name, because Phenomenology differs just as much from what is ordinarily called “scientific” history as it does from what is ordinarily called “scientific” psychology.

Phenomenology is therefore very close in its **object** to what we ordinarily call history and psychology,<sup>150</sup> while differing sharply from both in the way it treats its **theme**.

And since anyone who looks for ordinary psychology or ordinary history in Phenomenology is likely to misunderstand it, we need to complete our definition of its object and theme by comparing it with history and psychology and setting it against them.

In one sense, we can say that psychology and history differ from Phenomenology precisely because they present themselves as separate and supposedly independent “sciences.”

Psychology studies what a human being **is** at a particular moment rather than what human beings **were** and **will become**.

More exactly, it tacitly assumes that human “psychic” qualities are eternal and unchanging, and can therefore be studied independently of time—and therefore of history.

Whether it intends to or not, psychology thus recognizes precisely the existence of a “soul”: some thing or “substance” possessing fixed and unchanging qualities or characteristics—“attributes.”

It therefore posits something that remains “eternally” identical to itself in its qualities, much as, say, an oxygen atom, granite, a pine tree, or a tiger does.<sup>151</sup>

A more cautious psychology may avoid making such claims or assumptions. It may say only that it studies those “psychic” qualities that are independent of time and history.

Phenomenology has no objection to this.

It too recognizes that human beings possess certain “eternal” qualities,<sup>152</sup> and it fully accepts that these can be studied—and may well be worth studying—from a scientific psychological point of view.

But Phenomenology holds that these qualities are not **specifically human**, and therefore do not belong to the theme of **its** investigation of human beings.

At first sight, then, it seems very easy in principle to draw a boundary between the respective objects of Psychology and Phenomenology.

In practice, of course, there will inevitably be arguments about which qualities are genuinely unchanging and which depend on historical development.

But what matters here is that the objects can, in principle, be distinguished. Possible mistakes in drawing the boundary are not our concern.<sup>153</sup>

Still, this distinction is not enough.

It is true that Phenomenology does not study the unchanging qualities of human beings. But psychology cannot possibly avoid studying, alongside unchanging qualities, some qualities that **do** change with history and therefore also belong to Phenomenology.

Even when psychology knows that such qualities are “historical,” however, it will still study them independently of history and time.

Psychology takes, so to speak, a **cross-section** through the historical development of humanity at some particular historical moment, whether present or past.

Phenomenology can then point out that this psychology is not studying the consciousness of humanity “in general,” but, say, the consciousness of the liberal-bourgeois age, or “pagan” or “ancient” consciousness, and so on.<sup>154</sup>

But even if psychology admits this, it does not thereby become Phenomenology.

A phenomenological study of “pagan” consciousness will still differ from a psychological study of the same consciousness.

The difference lies precisely in the fact that psychology abstracts from time, whereas Phenomenology must include time in its investigation.

Psychology is not interested in the **origin or genesis** of the psychological qualities it studies. Phenomenology describes them as the **result of a historical process**.

Phenomenology therefore differs from psychology as **dynamics** differs from **statics**.

Psychology studies the result of the development of a quality independently of the development that produced it—that is, it does not study the quality **as a result**.

Phenomenology studies a quality in its **becoming**, its development, and as the **result of that becoming**.

In short, Phenomenology differs from **psychology** because psychology **is not historical**.

As for **history**, we can say the reverse: it differs from Phenomenology because it **is not psychological**.

Since psychology abstracts from time and history, it cannot, without Phenomenology, know in principle that it is examining the “soul” of a particular historical age. It will therefore tend to assume that it is studying the eternal and unchanging qualities of humanity “in general.”

History, by contrast, consciously studies human beings belonging to a **particular age** and assumes that it is studying only those people.

When it speaks about the Greeks of the age of Pericles, for example, it deliberately puts aside the French of the revolutionary period, and vice versa.

In other words, history is not interested in what belongs to humanity “in general,” and therefore has little interest in human “psychology.”

Of course, the historian talks about what a historical individual—or even a crowd, a class, or an entire people—“wants,” “feels,” “thinks,” “says,” “experiences,” and is “conscious of.” The historian also describes their “self-consciousness.”

But in doing so, the historian studies only **what** the people in question think, want, say, and so forth—not what an “opinion,” an “action,” or the “capacity for speech” is as such.

Phenomenology, by contrast, reminds the historian that there is such a thing as **historical inheritance**.

A new historical age does not “fall from the sky.” It is conditioned by the age that preceded it, and therefore ultimately by all previous ages.

Once this has been recognized, Phenomenology can point out that what a person of a particular historical age thinks and does is, in a certain sense, also characteristic of humanity “in general.”

By examining the desires, thoughts, and so forth of a particular historical age, we can also discover what “desire as such,” “thought as such,” and so forth are.

Properly **human** qualities—the very qualities history studies—are certainly not unchanging. They are historical, which means that under different historical conditions they would be different.

But precisely because they are historical, they do not simply disappear. Once they have emerged, they remain present in humanity.

“Christian” consciousness may be different from “pagan” consciousness. But because Christian consciousness is historically the **heir** of pagan consciousness, it still contains what pagan consciousness produced—even if in modified form, even if as a **negation**, or even if only as a **memory**.

In this sense, the “psychic” qualities of the pagan also belong to humanity in general.

But this “humanity in general” is itself **historical**.

Its “psychology” therefore cannot be fully understood without studying its “history.” We cannot forget that human qualities did not all belong to humanity “from the beginning.” They emerge during the historical process and change along with it.

To understand them, we need to know **when, how, and why** they emerged and changed.

By studying history, we **can** understand this “psychology.”

But to do that, we have to study history very differently from the way the “scientific” historian does.

The scientific historian is quite properly not interested in this psychology. He therefore excludes whatever belongs to it, or at least does not consciously draw the conclusions that would give us knowledge of it.

History differs from Phenomenology, then, because it does not try to derive a “psychological” knowledge of humanity from knowledge of human history. Phenomenology, by contrast, treats history as the material from which such knowledge can be obtained.

Phenomenology is therefore, so to speak, a **union or synthesis of history and psychology**.

Phenomenological psychology differs from scientific psychology because it is historical. Phenomenological history differs from scientific history because it makes use of psychology.

So we could equally call Phenomenology **phenomenological psychology** or **phenomenological history**. We could also define it as a **historical psychology** or a **psychological history** of humanity.

But even these descriptions can cause serious misunderstanding.

Psychology and history are not separated from one another by accident.

The psychologist cannot simply add history to psychological research: there is, so to speak, no room for it within psychology as normally conceived.

Likewise, ordinary historical research has no need to add psychology in the sense intended here.

To produce this “synthesis” of psychology and history, we therefore have to change both of them fundamentally. We must treat the human “psyche” and history very differently from the way scientific psychologists and historians do.

If we define Phenomenology as “historical psychology” or “psychological history,” then, we must immediately add that it differs fundamentally from both history and psychology in their ordinary senses.

For that reason it is better not to use these expressions at all.

So what, exactly, distinguishes Phenomenology from psychology and history? And why does it differ from them?

Ultimately, it differs because it is precisely **Phenomenology**.

If it is in some sense a “history,” it is the history proper to Phenomenology—and therefore, in some sense, also a “psychology.”

And if it is in some sense a psychology, it is a psychology proper to Phenomenology—and therefore, in some sense, also a “history.”

To understand this, however, we must return again to the question: in what sense is Phenomenology actually **Phenomenology**—that is, a discourse or science of “phenomena,” which, as we already know, are in a certain sense both historical and psychological?

To understand more clearly the distinctive *sui generis* character of the object and theme of Phenomenology, it is useful to compare them with the object and theme of the systematic Philosophy for which Phenomenology prepares us and to which it serves as an introduction.

We have seen that Philosophy must, in principle, answer **every** question a human being can ask.

But among the enormous number of possible questions, we need to distinguish those that are specifically philosophical—in the broad sense, whether phenomenological or systematic—from those that a non-philosopher can in principle answer, whether an ordinary “naive” person or a scientist.

The distinctive feature of these non-philosophical questions is that, in the minds of the people asking them, they concern “reality itself”—what contemporary philosophers call “objective” reality.

If an ordinary person or a scientist is talking about a birch tree, for example, they talk precisely about the birch tree and nothing else. Everything else is, so to speak, forgotten.

The birch is separated from all the other objects in the world. At most, the world remains an undefined “background” that apparently need not be examined any further.

For the person talking about the birch, neither the “ideal” world of words, judgments, mathematical formulas, fictional characters, and so forth, nor the human, technical, social, and political world exists.

Indeed, even the person who is talking seems, in his own eyes, to have disappeared.

More generally, a non-philosophical answer responds only to what the question immediately asks about. It deals only with the **object** of the question and leaves aside everything “outside” that object,<sup>155</sup> including, in particular, the **question itself** and the **person asking it**.

Of course, the object of a non-philosophical question can in principle be almost anything.

It might be an isolated thing in the real natural world. It might even be the natural world as a whole. But in that case the real human world and the “ideal” world are excluded.

The ideal world can also become the object of non-philosophical questions. But then the answer will contain nothing concerning the real world. A mathematician studying a mathematical object, for example, effectively forgets that mathematics is created by a **real human being** living in the **natural world**.
