Finally, the theme of a non-philosophical investigation can even be a human being or the real human world.

But then, say, the natural world—or, as always, the person carrying out the investigation—is put to one side.

When an ordinary person writes an autobiography, or when a scientist conducts psychological “introspection,” the object of study is indeed himself.

Yet even leaving aside the fact that while reflecting on himself he partly forgets the surrounding world, he also leaves behind one part of himself: precisely the part that is **doing the reflecting**.

In other words, he observes himself, so to speak, “from the outside,” just as an ordinary person observes a pine tree or a scientist observes Julius Caesar or a parabola.

The ordinary person or botanist looking at a birch tree forgets himself entirely.

The scientific psychologist then observes this observer, who might even be the psychologist himself. But in doing so, the psychologist not only forgets the birch as something existing outside the observer. He also forgets **himself**, just as completely as the observer of the birch did.

His theme is only the study of the “object itself.”

For the observer of the birch, that object is the birch. The observation itself, and the observer himself, remain outside the field of observation.

In short, as we have already said several times, the ordinary person and the scientist deal with **abstractions**, not with concrete reality.

A human being can speak only about the reality **of which he is speaking**.

Concrete reality therefore includes not only the ideal or real, natural or human **object** of discourse, but also the discourse itself and the human being who produces it.

The ordinary person abstracts from these things and speaks only about the object. He therefore speaks about an **abstraction**.

The philosopher knows this.

He therefore calls this abstraction—the object of the ordinary person or scientist—a **phenomenon** or **appearance**.

Now, ordinary people and scientists can in principle speak about virtually **anything**. And because whatever they speak about is, for the philosopher, a phenomenon or appearance, it follows that literally anything can function as a “phenomenon.”

A phenomenon might be an isolated thing in the real natural world, or the natural world as a whole.

It might be an individual human being, a particular aspect of human life or activity, whether practical or theoretical, or the historical world as a whole.

It might be an isolated ideal entity or the entire “ideal world.”

Ordinary language does not use the word *phenomenon* quite so broadly.

We may speak, for example, of a volcanic eruption as a “natural phenomenon,” but we do not normally call a birch tree a phenomenon. We speak of Greek tragedy as a “literary phenomenon,” but not usually of Euclidean geometry as a “mathematical phenomenon,” and so on.

These boundaries in ordinary language are obviously contingent and have no fundamental importance. There is no serious objection to extending the word *phenomenon* more widely.

The real issue is that the everyday and philosophical meanings of the term do not fully coincide.

When an ordinary person or scientist speaks of a “natural phenomenon,” the emphasis falls on the word **nature**.

Nature itself is supposed to manifest itself in a volcanic eruption, and if we knew **all** natural phenomena, we would supposedly know what nature itself is.

When the philosopher uses the same expression, however, the emphasis falls on **phenomenon**.

For the philosopher, a volcanic eruption is not primarily a phenomenon **of nature**. It is an **appearance of nature to human beings**.

The philosopher therefore takes the word *phenomenon* literally.

In ordinary language, the phenomenon is effectively treated as “the thing itself.”

In philosophical language, by contrast, the phenomenon is precisely the **appearance of the thing**, not the thing apart from its manifestation.

Every phenomenon is certainly the phenomenon **of something**—a real natural thing, a human being, an ideal entity.

But it is also always the **appearance** of that thing, and therefore the appearance of that thing **to someone**.

As I have already said, what appears can be absolutely anything. Its phenomenon can therefore also be anything.

And it can appear to, so to speak, “anyone.”

But since by *phenomenon* we mean the appearance of something **to a person**, that “someone” can only be a human being.

A **phenomenon**, then, is anything that appears to a human being, regardless of what appears or, so to speak, to whom it appears.<sup>156</sup>

Literally anything can “appear.”

Everything that exists **really** can appear: the natural world and the human world—the historical, technical, social, and political world—in every aspect, from every angle, and in every possible combination.

But things that do **not** exist in reality can also appear: √2, Chichikov, God, the dative case, a dragon, and so on.

Even what does not **exist at all** can appear in a certain sense.

What I call “nothingness” or “non-being,” for example, in some sense “appears” to me precisely as what cannot be spoken of, what cannot be known, and so on—even though it does not exist.

Return to our example of the birch.

The birch I am actually looking at now “appears” to me. But so does the birch I looked at ten years ago.

So too does the “birch in general,” which no one could ever literally **look at**, but which the botanist describes.

Even the **word** “birch,” considered as such by a philologist, can be said to “appear.”

The phenomenon of the birch can therefore take the form of sensory perception, memory, spoken discourse about it, and so forth.

And anything that appears to a human being can appear in any number of ways: in sensory perception, memory, imagination, human discourse, a mathematical formula, a painting, a musical work, and so on.

A birch manifests itself to human beings not only when an ordinary person **sees** it, but when a scientist talks about it—whether a botanist, biologist, chemist, physicist, mathematician, or someone else—or when an artist or poet depicts it.

Finally, anything can “appear” in any way to anyone: to ordinary people and scientists, to the mad and the “sane,” to children and old people, to people of our own age and people of the Stone Age, and so on.

An **appearance** or **phenomenon** is therefore anything that “manifests itself” in some way to some person.

Every phenomenon is consequently always an appearance **to a particular person**.

But what we call the “phenomenon” is not the person to whom it appears, nor the means through which it appears. It is simply **what appears**.

Suppose a birch appears to an ordinary person through an actual sensory perception.

In this case, the phenomenon is neither the person nor his perception. It is the birch.

But is it the birch “in itself”?

No. It is precisely **the birch as it appears to this particular person in this particular sensory perception**.

The ordinary person thinks he is dealing with the birch itself.

The philosopher knows that he is dealing with a birch **as it appears to him through his perception**.

So although the ordinary person—and the scientist—speaks about the birch, he completely forgets that it is appearing in a certain way to a certain person.

The philosopher, speaking about the same tree, continually remembers this.

For that reason the philosopher does not simply speak of the “birch,” but of the **phenomenon** or **appearance of the birch**.

He knows that this tree appears in a certain way to a certain person.

So even if, for the moment, he sets aside the question “to whom does it appear, and how?”, he still remembers that his account of the phenomenon “birch” is incomplete and must eventually be supplemented by an account of **how** it appears and **to whom**.<sup>157</sup>

**Phenomenology** is the philosophical discourse or science that studies phenomena **as phenomena**.

That is, it is a discourse that remembers not only that phenomena make **something** appear, but also that they make it appear **in a particular way** and **to a particular person**.

It is “philosophy” in the broad sense because it describes and studies its object—the phenomenon—without abstracting from anything.

But to understand what is distinctive about Phenomenology, we must remember that it is not the only philosophical science.

Alongside it there is “philosophy” in the narrower sense: **systematic Philosophy**.

If we can study the phenomenon as phenomenon, we can also move, so to speak, **beyond its limits** and ask what lies “behind” it.

More precisely, we can ask:

**What must reality itself be like for this phenomenon or appearance to be possible?**

Or again: if we use the word *world* (*cosmos*) for everything that exists in any way—naturally, historically and really, or ideally—what must the world be like for it to appear to a human being living within it **exactly as it actually appears**?

Using Kant’s language, we can define this properly philosophical theme as the question of the **“condition of possibility of phenomena”** (*Bedingung der Möglichkeit der Erscheinungen*).

To understand what is meant here, we can use an analogy from science, especially chemistry and physics.

An ordinary person—or a botanist—may say that a cornflower is dark blue and be satisfied with that.

The physicist and chemist ask a different question:

**What must this cornflower be like “in reality” for it to appear blue?**

The chemist may answer that it appears blue because it contains certain pigments: chemical bodies composed of supposedly elementary constituents or “atoms.”

The physicist goes further. He argues that the chemical atoms must possess a particular physical structure allowing them to emit or reflect “blue light”—that is, in reality, electromagnetic oscillations of a certain frequency—for the cornflower to **appear** blue.

Both the chemist and the physicist therefore move beyond what is revealed to the ordinary person’s “naked eye,” and the physicist goes beyond what is available to the chemist’s observation as well.

If the ordinary person is looking at the scenery on the stage of a theatre, the chemist is inspecting the backstage area, while the physicist is examining the machinery that makes the backstage effects possible.

Like the chemist and physicist, the systematic philosopher also goes, so to speak, behind the stage observed by the phenomenologist.

The phenomenologist sees the **appearances**. The philosopher asks about their “causes.”

But we must remember that this is only an analogy.

Physics and chemistry are no more philosophical than naive perception—or botanical perception.

So the “cause” sought by the philosopher has nothing in common with the cause sought by the physicist or chemist.

The philosopher seeks the cause of a **phenomenon as phenomenon**.

The scientist seeks the cause of the “thing itself,” independently of how it appears and of the person to whom it appears.

The physicist, for example, does not ask how electromagnetic vibrations themselves “appear,” or to whom they appear.

The philosopher knows that they too must appear in some particular way to some particular person.<sup>158</sup>

For the philosopher, therefore, the chemical and physical causes used to explain the blue colour of the flower are themselves just as much **appearances or phenomena** as the cornflower.

So when the philosopher searches for the “cause” of phenomena, he cannot find it in any science, because science itself is only one phenomenon among others.

Science explains some phenomena by means of other phenomena while forgetting that it is itself dealing only with phenomena.

The philosopher’s **world** or **cosmos**, by contrast—the world that must serve as the “cause” or “condition of possibility” of phenomena—must explain phenomena **precisely as phenomena**.

It must be such that not only **what** appears is possible, but also **how** it appears and **to whom** it appears.

Through a discourse or “science of the world”—a cosmo-logy—the philosopher must show what the existing world must be like not only in order to **exist**, but in order to **appear to human beings exactly as it actually appears**.

This philosophical “world” therefore includes not only whatever underlies **nature**, but whatever underlies **human beings and their cognition of nature**.

A philosophical description of the world—Cosmology—must therefore be just as concrete, complete, and non-abstract as the philosophical description of all possible phenomena of that world—that is, as Phenomenology.

The “world” of philosophy includes not only nature but also humanity, together with everything human beings have created throughout history through both practical historical activity and theoretical activity.

It therefore includes not only the real technical world, but also the “ideal” world of discourse.

So the theme or object of Cosmology is not a world separated from humanity, but **a world containing humanity**—or, what amounts to the same thing, **human beings in the world**.

Phenomenology, by contrast, studies **the world in the human being**: the way the world in the cosmological sense—that is, the human being in the world—“manifests” itself to human beings.

In other words, it studies how “the human being in the world” reveals both the world and itself **to itself**.

If we like, the cosmological world is itself also a “phenomenon,” since it too “manifests” itself in some way to someone.

But it manifests itself **only philosophically**, and **only to the philosopher as philosopher**.

A phenomenon in the narrower sense, by contrast, can manifest itself in any way to anyone—including to the philosopher insofar as the philosopher is not merely a philosopher but also an ordinary human being.

It is therefore better not to extend the word *phenomenon* to the world of Cosmology, especially because this world already **includes both the way in which it appears and the person to whom it appears**—that is, philosophy and the philosopher.

Cosmology therefore differs fundamentally from Phenomenology in both theme and object.

Phenomenology studies **phenomena**. Cosmology asks what the **world** must be like in order to appear as it does—to human beings and therefore, ultimately, to itself, since the world contains human beings.

But philosophical questioning is not exhausted by this cosmological question.

Just as we can ask about the “cause” of phenomena, we can ask about the “cause” of that cause—the “cause” of the world or cosmos.

And because this world **actually exists**, the question conceals another question: the question of the “cause” of existence or actuality itself.

This “cause” is called **being itself** (*on, ontos*).

We can say that actuality or the existence of the world is a form, appearance, or **mode of being** of Being.

Likewise, a phenomenon or appearance is the form, aspect, or mode in which real and ideal actuality exists.

If actuality—natural, human, and ideal—is the “condition of possibility of phenomena,” then **Being as Being** (*ontos on*) is the “condition of possibility of actuality or existence.”

A discourse or science of the existing, actual world—Cosmology—must therefore be supplemented by a discourse or science of Being: an **onto-logy**.<sup>159</sup>

In other words, we must also ask what Being itself must be like in order to exist as it actually does—that is, in order to be this world or cosmos that manifests itself in the way it actually manifests itself to human beings and therefore, ultimately, to itself.

We can return once more to our analogy and say that Ontology stands in relation to Cosmology and Phenomenology somewhat as physics stands in relation to chemistry and to the ordinary content of nature that anyone can observe.

But here it is even clearer that this is only an analogy.

Ontology has nothing in common with physics or, more generally, with any non-philosophical science.

In the case of Cosmology, some misunderstanding is still possible because many sciences deal with the world. We therefore have to distinguish “scientific” Cosmology from philosophical Cosmology by pointing out that science studies the world very differently from philosophy: abstractly rather than concretely.

Ontology is different. Only philosophical Ontology speaks of **Being as Being**, so there is no comparable danger of confusion.

This is not the place to define in detail the object and theme of Ontology or Cosmology.<sup>160</sup> We need only examine their relation to Phenomenology.

Because Ontology and Cosmology both deal not with phenomena but with their “causes,” they together form a single whole distinct from Phenomenology.

We call this whole **systematic Philosophy**, or Philosophy in the narrower sense.

If we move out of Phenomenology, then Cosmology must come first **after** it.

But if we present things **systematically**, Ontology comes first and Cosmology second. From that systematic point of view, Phenomenology ought to come only after Cosmology.

We would first show in Ontology what Being is and explain why—that is, how—it exists. We would then describe this existence in Cosmology and explain why it “appears” in the way it actually appears. From there it would be natural to describe this appearance itself, and so arrive at Phenomenology.

Yet, as we already know and will see again, Phenomenology is an **introduction** to Philosophy. It is therefore simultaneously an introduction to Ontology and Cosmology.

Within the overall system it comes **before** Philosophy in the narrower sense.

Philosophy in the broad sense thus divides first into **Phenomenology** and **systematic Philosophy**, while systematic Philosophy in turn divides into **Ontology** and **Cosmology**.

Phenomenology studies only phenomena.

But it studies them with Cosmology and Ontology already in view. It describes phenomena in such a way that we can move directly from their phenomenological description to a cosmological and ontological investigation of the world that appears and of the Being that exists in that world.

The phenomenologist therefore knows from the beginning what philosophy is, because he describes “phenomena” from the philosophical point of view.

In that sense, he is already a philosopher.

But at the same time, he knows that he becomes a philosopher only **at the end of Phenomenology and through Phenomenology**.

Only at the end will he truly know what philosophy is, because the philosophical point of view—his own point of view—emerges only there.<sup>161</sup>

Phenomenology is therefore the **last “phenomenon” described by the phenomenologist**.

Yet from the very beginning he describes every phenomenon—not just Phenomenology itself—from a phenomenological and therefore philosophical point of view.

In this sense, the whole of Phenomenology is a **philosophical science**: the philosophical science of phenomena.

That is why it can be treated as a part of Philosophy in the broad sense—the first and introductory part—on the same level as the Ontology and Cosmology that make up systematic Philosophy.

As I have already said, Phenomenology is a philosophical science because it describes its object—the phenomenon—**completely**, without abstracting from anything.

For this reason, its description also makes it possible to move beyond phenomena and understand their “cause.”

From the beginning, Phenomenology looks at phenomena, so to speak, from the outside.

It can therefore, on the one hand, describe **each phenomenon completely** and, on the other, look at what lies **behind it**.

The ordinary person and the scientist describe only a **part** of the phenomenon, without knowing that what they describe is only one part of a whole and that this whole is precisely the **phenomenon**.

They therefore cannot even formulate the cosmological and ontological question about the cause of the phenomenon **as such**.

When they look for the cause of one **part** of a phenomenon, they simply encounter another **part** of a phenomenon—that is, another phenomenon.

They discover only something that appears to a particular person in a particular way, without relating it to the person to whom it appears or to the way it appears.

Phenomenology, by contrast, begins by considering the phenomenon **as a whole**: not only **what** appears, but also **how** it appears and **to whom**.

For this reason, Phenomenology prepares us to ask about the cosmological world that appears as it appears to the person to whom it appears.

That is, it prepares us to ask about the world that serves as the “cause” of each phenomenon taken **as a whole**, and of **all possible phenomena in general**.

It is the world—and, through the world, Being—that “manifests itself,” not “appearance” itself.

The appearance is certainly given in some sense to the phenomenologist, since he speaks about it.

But the “phenomenon” does not itself “appear” to the phenomenologist any more than the “cosmos” appears to the cosmologist or “Being” appears to the ontologist.

The reason is the same in every case.

On the one hand, the “phenomenon”—considered as **phenomenon**, rather than as what appears within it; the **appearing** of the birch rather than the “birch that appears”—is not given to just anyone in just any way. It is given only to the philosopher, the phenomenologist, and only in a philosophical or phenomenological way.

On the other hand, this philosophical or phenomenological “given” already includes **the way in which it is given and the person to whom it is given**.

Phenomenology describes not only the phenomena themselves but also the way in which they are given. In that sense, it describes **itself as Phenomenology**.

And it also describes the person to whom they are given—that is, **its own author**.

The author of a Phenomenology is a **living human being**, and the *Phenomenology* itself is a **book**—thought through, written, and published.

So Phenomenology itself also becomes a “phenomenon”: something that can “manifest itself” to someone in all sorts of ways.

To a child or to a “savage,” for example, it might appear merely as sheets of paper and a chemical body, as difficult or completely incomprehensible speech, as the subject of an obscure scholarly investigation, and so forth.

Phenomenology itself, then, is described **within Phenomenology** as its final phenomenon.

But precisely because Phenomenology includes itself as a phenomenon, it is **not merely a phenomenon**.

Its author and its reader—at least a reader who has understood it—know that Phenomenology, as book or discourse, **appears to them**. They know **how** it appears to them. And they know **who they themselves are**, the people to whom it appears.

In this sense, once they have completed the *Phenomenology*—whether by writing it or reading it—it is no longer merely a phenomenon for them.

And for the same reason, the appearance described within it is no longer merely “phenomenal.”

This means that through *Phenomenology* its author and reader have **become philosophers**.

They now deal no longer merely with “appearances” but with the actuality that **appears**—to anyone and in any way, but in particular to them and in a phenomenological way.

In other words, they now deal with the **cosmos** studied by the cosmologist.

The only difference is that the phenomenologist describes this cosmos **as phenomenon**, whereas the cosmologist studies the world as the **cause of that phenomenon**.

If we like, Phenomenology is an **appearance appearing to itself**.

But an appearance that appears to itself is no longer merely an appearance. It is the **world appearing to itself**.

Phenomenology speaks about the **appearing of this world**. Cosmology speaks about the **world that appears**.

In this sense, the cosmologist returns, so to speak, to the perspective of the ordinary person or scientist.

Like them, he speaks not about the **appearing of the world** but about **the world**.

The difference is that the ordinary person and scientist do not know that this world “appears,” to whom it appears, or how it appears.

The cosmologist, by contrast, speaks of the world **as the cause of its own appearing**.

For that reason he does not speak about abstractions but about **concrete reality**.

And he can speak in this way only because Phenomenology has already spoken about **concrete appearing**, shown him what it is, and thereby made it possible for him to ask about its cause.

We can therefore state the point once more.

The ordinary person and the scientist speak about the “objects” that “appear” to them. But they forget that those objects **appear**, and consequently speak about them without asking **how** they appear or **to whom**.

The phenomenologist speaks about the **appearance itself**[^E034].

That means he speaks not only about the **object** that appears, but also about the **way** it appears and the **person to whom** it appears.

This “object”—an object appearing in a particular way to a particular person—is called a **phenomenon** or **appearance** (*Erscheinung*).[^E035]

In our example, the phenomenon is therefore not simply “the birch.” It is **the birch as perceived in a certain way by a certain person**.

The **way** in which this object appears is called its **cognition** or **experience** (*Erfahrung*).[^E036]

So in our example, this cognition is not simply “sensory perception in general,” but **the sensory perception of this particular birch by this particular person**.

Finally, the one **to whom** the object appears is called **consciousness** (*Bewusstsein*).

In our example, consciousness is not “the human being in general,” but **this particular human being insofar as he sensorially perceives this particular birch**.

It is therefore precisely the **consciousness of the birch**, not the complete human being taken as a whole.

Whenever Phenomenology speaks of a “phenomenon” or “appearance”—that is, of an appearing object—it therefore always relates that phenomenon, on the one hand, to its **cognition or experience**, through which the object appears, and, on the other hand, to the **consciousness** to which the object appears.

Taken **together as a single whole**, phenomenon, cognition, and consciousness are no longer merely an “appearance.” Together they constitute **reality itself**.

Yet this consciousness is consciousness only **of the phenomenon** through cognition; cognition is cognition only **of the phenomenon** through consciousness; and the phenomenon is the **appearance of reality** to a consciousness through cognition.

So the phenomenologist considers this reality precisely in its character as **appearance or phenomenon**.

He describes the way a reality **appears to itself** through cognition to a consciousness, and therefore appears as a phenomenon.

But once he has described this phenomenon, the phenomenologist naturally asks what this reality is that “makes itself appear” in this way to a consciousness through cognition.

He asks what this cognition is through which reality appears in this way to consciousness.

And he asks what this consciousness is to which reality appears in this way through cognition.

In other words, he searches for the **cause** of the phenomenon.

And he finds it in the **human being in the world** studied by the cosmologist.

But once he begins speaking about the **human being** who, through cognition and within consciousness, makes both the world and himself appear, and about the **world** that appears through humanity, the phenomenologist ceases to be merely a phenomenologist.

He becomes a **cosmologist—that is, a philosopher**.

Phenomenology therefore presents itself from the outset as a **philosophical science**. For that reason, it has nothing to do with what we ordinarily call “science.” In particular, it differs fundamentally and radically from scientific psychology and scientific history.

As a **philosophical** science, Phenomenology is not “abstract” but “concrete.” When the phenomenologist studies an “object,” he does not set aside the questions of **how** and **through what means** that object is given to him, or **who he himself is**—in other words, who this person is to whom the object is given in this particular way.

Taken as a whole, then, the text of the *Phenomenology*—its entire subject matter—does more than give a complete description of its “object.” It also explains how its own particular way of knowing that object is possible, and it answers the question of who its author is: who is this phenomenological “consciousness” to which a phenomenological object becomes “given” through a phenomenological form of cognition?

More simply, Phenomenology includes within its description of **what** it describes an account of **how** it describes it and of **who** is doing the describing. Alongside its object, its subject matter therefore includes both itself and its author.

Ordinary “science,” by contrast—and psychology and history in particular—limits itself to describing its “objects.” Its subject matter coincides with its object, or more exactly, consists only in a description of that object. The question of how the object is given, and to whom, lies outside the field of inquiry.

Yet an object must in fact be given to some particular person in some particular way if it is ever to become the subject of a description. “Science” forgets this and therefore imagines that it is describing the “object” simply as it exists “in reality.”

But precisely because it thinks this way, while forgetting that the object is given in a particular way to a particular person, science actually describes only **how that object appears to it**.

Science thinks it is dealing with “reality itself”—in effect, mistakenly taking itself for a kind of Cosmology. But what it actually deals with are “phenomena,” and these are what it describes. A “phenomenon,” however—and the unconscious, scientific description of it—is determined not only by the object that appears, but also by the way it appears and by the person to whom it appears.

A particular science therefore describes, on the one hand, only a particular **aspect** of its object: specifically, the aspect revealed by the particular form of cognition characteristic of that science.<sup>162</sup> On the other hand, it describes only the aspect given to a particular observer—to the consciousness of the person who created that science.

And this consciousness is determined not only by what is given to it, but also by the kind of **human being** who embodies it—that is, by that person’s individual interests and class interests. In this sense, “science” itself appears as a social ideology: a class **opinion**, rather than knowledge in the full sense of the word.

So “science,” without realizing it, describes isolated ideological aspects of reality—or of the cosmos, meaning the world in the broadest sense.

Phenomenology is different. Because it takes account both of **how** reality is given and of **the person to whom it is given**, it deals, in principle, with reality itself rather than with isolated ideological aspects of reality.

As the development of Phenomenology will show, its object is not given to it through one isolated form of cognition. Phenomenology makes use of cognition **as a whole**—that is, of all possible forms of cognition taken together. It is therefore given not one isolated aspect of its object, but **all** its aspects: the object itself, viewed from every side.

And because Phenomenology also includes an account of its author’s consciousness—while showing that this consciousness is not confined by one particular set of historical conditions—it describes not merely what is given to **this particular author**, or to his class or nation according to private, class, or national interests. It describes what is given to **consciousness as such**.

Phenomenology therefore presents not an “ideology,” not a private, social, or national opinion, but knowledge in the strict sense: something that **reveals reality itself**.<sup>163</sup>

In other words, Phenomenology differs from science because it actually achieves what science ultimately claims to achieve without being entitled to that claim.

Phenomenology is not an ideological **opinion** about some isolated **aspect** of an object. It is genuine **knowledge** of the object **itself, taken as a whole**. This is what makes Phenomenology a **philosophical science**, as distinct from every “science” in the ordinary sense—including psychology and history.

In its philosophical approach or point of view, Phenomenology does not differ from the other two philosophical sciences, Cosmology and Ontology, which together make up systematic Philosophy, or Philosophy in the narrow sense. Like them, Phenomenology is true knowledge of its object **itself, taken as a whole**.

What distinguishes Phenomenology from them is the nature of its object.

The object of Phenomenology is the totality of all possible “phenomena”: all the natural and human **appearances of reality as it appears to human beings**.

Cosmology, by contrast, studies “reality as it exists in itself,” whether natural or human, as the “cause” of these appearances. Ontology studies **being itself**, both real and ideal, which lies “beneath” existing reality and which “makes itself appear” to human beings.

The special nature of the phenomenological object therefore distinguishes Phenomenology not only from systematic Philosophy but also from ordinary “science,” whether natural science or the human sciences—psychology and history in the broad sense.

Consider nature first: the natural world.

A natural “science” such as physics mistakenly thinks that it is dealing with the world itself. In fact, only philosophical Cosmology deals with the natural world as such; indeed, the first part of Cosmology is devoted to it.

Science, for its part, describes **the world as it appears to science**, without realizing that what it is describing is precisely an appearing world.

Phenomenology consciously does something else. It does not describe the natural world as such. It describes the world’s **appearance to human beings**—the natural world **as a phenomenon**.

And if it describes the “phenomenon” of the natural world, it must speak not only about that world but also about **how** it appears and **to whom** it appears. It therefore describes not only the appearance or phenomenon of the natural world, but also the cognition through which the world appears and the consciousness to which it appears through that cognition.

But **whose** cognition is this, and **whose** consciousness?

Clearly, not the phenomenologist’s own.

Phenomenology is a philosophical science and therefore possesses true and complete knowledge of its object. If the natural world itself were its object, Phenomenology would possess true and complete knowledge of the natural world itself. But in that case it would not be Phenomenology at all. It would be Cosmology.

So the natural world whose “appearance” Phenomenology describes is **not** given to Phenomenology itself—not through phenomenological cognition, not to phenomenological consciousness, and therefore not to the author of a Phenomenology.

What is phenomenologically given to the phenomenologist is **the appearance of the natural world**, not the natural world itself.

Phenomenology does, of course, describe its own phenomenological knowledge of this appearance and the consciousness that possesses that knowledge. But this must not be confused with the consciousness and cognition to which the **world itself** appears.

We can put the distinction this way. The “appearance of the world” described by Phenomenology does not itself “appear” to phenomenological consciousness through phenomenological cognition. Rather, it is phenomenologically **given** to phenomenological **knowledge** through that knowledge itself.

It is the natural world that “appears” to a non-phenomenological consciousness, through a non-phenomenological form of cognition.

So to whom does the world appear, and how?

Clearly, it appears to **human consciousness**, through a **human way of knowing**. And we have already seen that this consciousness and cognition cannot themselves be phenomenological or philosophical.

The natural world therefore “appears” to the consciousness of any non-phenomenologist or non-philosopher who knows it in some way: to an ordinary person “in love with nature,” for example, or to a scientist studying nature, such as a physicist, and so on.

Unlike Cosmology, then, Phenomenology does not describe the natural world itself. And unlike the scientist or layperson, it does not mistakenly imagine that it is doing so.

Instead, it consciously describes **how the natural world appears** to a particular consciousness—whether that of an ordinary person, a physicist, or someone else—through sensory perception, physical science, or some other form of cognition.

And it also describes how this appearance of the world is given to a non-phenomenological consciousness through non-phenomenological cognition; how that consciousness and cognition are in turn given to the phenomenologist’s knowledge; and how phenomenological knowledge itself, together with the phenomenologist who possesses it, is also given within that same knowledge.

Phenomenology therefore differs from natural science in its **object**. It studies not nature itself but **nature as it appears to human beings**.

Phenomenology is consequently not a science of **nature**, but a science of **human beings**—human beings to whom, among other things, the natural world appears.

Because Phenomenology leaves nature itself aside, it cannot tell us how true what human beings say about nature actually is—that is, how closely their account corresponds to reality. From Phenomenology we do not learn **what nature is**. We learn only **what human beings are**, insofar as one of their defining features is that they come to know the natural world in particular ways.<sup>164</sup>

So, as we have already said, Phenomenology is ultimately a kind of **anthropology**: a science of human beings.

And since anthropology can be divided into psychology and history, in the broad sense of both terms, Phenomenology can also be called both psychology and history.

Yet although Phenomenology is indeed a science of **human beings** rather than of **nature**, it is still not a “science” of human beings in the ordinary sense. It is not the same thing as conventional psychology or conventional history.

As **phenomenological**, or philosophical, anthropology, it differs from both scientific psychology and scientific history.

We can now ask exactly what this means.

Phenomenology differs from psychology and history because Philosophy, in the broad sense, differs from “science” in two ways. Its **approach** is different: unlike the psychologist or historian, the phenomenologist includes himself within the investigation of his own object.<sup>165</sup> But the **object itself** is also different.

Let us begin with psychology.

We have just seen that, because Phenomenology does not deal with the natural world itself, it speaks not about the world as such but about the **appearance of the world to human beings**. In the end, then, it speaks about human beings—or more precisely, about human consciousness and human cognition of the world.

But consciousness and cognition are precisely what psychology studies.

Even so, Phenomenology also speaks about the world’s **appearance itself**—about the world **insofar as it appears to human beings**. It therefore speaks not only about consciousness and cognition, but also about the **content of cognition**.

And in this respect its object differs fundamentally from the object of psychology.

Suppose psychology wants to study a person’s consciousness and the sensory cognition contained in it—for example, the perception of a birch tree. Psychology does not, however, describe the **birch tree as sensibly known**.

Phenomenology, by contrast, is therefore as much a “history of natural science” as it is a psychology of natural science. It describes all the different ways in which the natural world can appear to human beings: what it “seems” to be to the layperson, the scientist, and others under different historical conditions.

There is another difference.

In our terminology, psychology studies not cognition **together with the consciousness that possesses it**, but cognition taken on its own. It does not describe the **human being** who possesses the cognition it studies.

Psychology therefore loses sight of the fact that cognition itself is conditioned by the historical—especially social and political—conditions of human life.

And everything we have just said remains true when the object of human cognition is no longer the **natural** world but **human beings themselves** and the historical world they have created.

Psychology abstracts so completely from the “phenomenon” itself—from the “content of consciousness,” or more exactly from the content of cognition—that the very distinction between knowing the natural world and knowing the human world becomes irrelevant to it. Psychology speaks about cognition in general, regardless of **what is being known**.

Phenomenology does the opposite. It describes not only cognition but its content, including the human world insofar as that world “appears” to human consciousness through cognition.

It describes not only human cognition of the world and of humanity, but the world and humanity themselves **insofar as they appear to human beings**.

And because human beings also “appear” to the psychologist, Phenomenology will describe the psychologist’s consciousness as psychologist and the psychologist’s cognition—that is, psychology itself.

The objects of psychology and Phenomenology therefore differ so radically that psychology itself becomes an object—or more precisely, one of the objects—of Phenomenology, while psychology as such scarcely suspects that Phenomenology exists, or even that human cognition can be studied **phenomenologically** rather than psychologically.

To put it differently: unlike Cosmology, which really does study cognition itself as part of reality, and unlike psychology, which merely claims to do so, Phenomenology studies the **appearance of cognition to human beings**—more exactly, to non-philosophers or non-phenomenologists, including the psychologist.

It therefore describes not only what cognition “seems to be” to different non-phenomenologists under different historical conditions, but also **how** and **why** it seems that way to them.

And finally, it describes the people **to whom** it seems that way, insofar as it seems that way to them.

So when Phenomenology discusses “psychological laws,” for example, it does not merely describe those laws as a particular way in which cognition appears to human beings. It also investigates **how psychology comes to know those laws** and **who this psychologist is**—or more exactly, what kind of “psychological consciousness” discovers them.

By excluding the **content** of the cognition it studies and excluding the **consciousness** that possesses that cognition, psychology necessarily becomes profoundly **unhistorical**.

As we will see, the driving force of historical development is not the “abstract” cognition or consciousness described by psychologists. It is the concrete **human being**, acting through work and struggle.

The psychologist’s “consciousness in general” obviously cannot work or struggle.

Psychology as such is therefore completely incapable of explaining how history can exist. For this reason, it tends in effect to deny history by treating the consciousness it studies as “eternal and unchanging,” even as independent of historical conditions—social, political, technical, and economic.

In one sense, psychology is right.

The **abstract** consciousness it studies really is “eternal and unchanging.” If one likes, one can say that consciousness itself does not change; only its **content** does.

Sensory perception and reason, considered simply as such, are the same in the ordinary person and the scientist, in a Stone Age human being and a medieval Christian, in an Australian “savage” and a contemporary French person.

Only differences in **content**, whether sensory or rational, allow us to distinguish the “consciousness of the layperson” from that of the “scientist,” the consciousness of the “primitive” from that of the “medieval person,” or the consciousness of the “bourgeois” from that of the “proletarian.”

Because psychology abstracts from the content of consciousness, it deals with abstractions—with a kind of consciousness that has never actually existed anywhere.

It therefore fails to notice that **concrete consciousness**, which is what Phenomenology studies, is necessarily the consciousness of a particular historical form of life: “primitive,” “medieval,” “proletarian,” and so on.

In this sense, as we have already seen, Phenomenology can also be said to differ from scientific psychology through its **historical character**.

But Phenomenology is historical only because its **object** is historical.

And its object is historical because it is not an abstract “consciousness.” It consists of an **appearance or phenomenon**—the content of a cognition or consciousness—**plus** the cognition through which that aspect of reality appears, **plus** the consciousness that possesses that cognition.<sup>166</sup>

The structure of its object therefore makes Phenomenology historical and distinguishes it from psychology.

Yet precisely the same structure also distinguishes Phenomenology from history.

So if we call Phenomenology a kind of “historical psychology,” this is only to distinguish it from traditional scientific psychology, not to bring it closer to ordinary scientific history.

Its object is just as far removed from the object of scientific history as it is from that of scientific psychology.

To emphasize this other difference, we could equally well call it a kind of **“psychological history.”**

Using our terminology, we can say that psychology ordinarily forgets both the “phenomenon” and the “consciousness” when it speaks about “cognition”—or at least forgets the consciousness.

History does the opposite. When it speaks about the “phenomenon,” it usually forgets both the “cognition” and the “consciousness”—or at least the cognition.

In other words, history leaves out precisely what psychology treats as its exclusive, or at least primary, subject matter; and psychology does the same in reverse with the primary subject matter of history.

In this limited sense, then, Phenomenology can be said to differ from history through its **“psychologism.”**

An example will make this clearer.

Suppose a modern historian—say, a bourgeois historian—is studying the Roman Empire under Marcus Aurelius.

We can leave aside the fact that, like every “scientist,” the historian forgets that the Empire “appears” to him in a particular way. We need not dwell on the fact that he imagines he is speaking **not** about how the Empire appears to him but about the Empire itself, as though he were a cosmologist—though without including his own account of the Empire within the Empire, as a genuine cosmologist would, and as a phenomenologist would include both himself and his cognition.

The historian does not merely forget that the Empire appears to **him** in a particular way.

More generally, he forgets that what he is dealing with is an **appearance or phenomenon** at all: that the Empire appears in a particular way **to a particular person**.

If a phenomenologist begins to discuss the same Empire, by contrast, he will discuss it only **as a phenomenon**.

He will not describe the Empire as it is given to **him as phenomenologist**—or more exactly, as philosopher, which would be the task of Cosmology. He will describe it only as it “appears” to non-phenomenologists, including the historian in question.

So here again, as in the case of psychology, the object of Phenomenology is not the **object studied by history**, but **history itself**.

Yet Phenomenology does not stop there.

Unlike the historian, it remembers that the Roman Empire appears not only to this particular historian, but also to historians from different periods, different social classes, and different nations.

It also remembers that the Empire appears not only to historians but to ordinary people who know it in one way or another—and even to the people who once actually lived within it.

When the phenomenologist speaks of the Empire, then, he speaks not of the Empire itself but of **its appearance**: both of **how it appears** and of **the person to whom it appears**.

The historian, of course, also deals with the people who lived in the Roman Empire. But he describes them as **they appear to him**, not as they **appeared to themselves**, and usually not as the Empire to which they belonged **appeared to them**.

In other words, he leaves aside their consciousness of themselves—their **self-consciousness**.

In any case, he does not discuss the **cognition through which they experienced and understood their own Empire**.<sup>167</sup>

History in the narrow sense—the history of social and political **reality**—therefore leaves aside both consciousness and cognition.

What about the so-called history of **ideas**: the history of worldviews, religions, sciences, or even philosophy?

Here the historian does introduce “consciousness,” but he still leaves aside “cognition”—precisely what primarily concerns psychology.

Suppose a historian studies the Catholic worldview of the thirteenth century and the physics of the seventeenth.

He will describe not only their “appearance”—while naturally imagining that he is describing the things themselves—not only the content of that worldview and that physics, but also the “consciousness” of the thirteenth- and seventeenth-century people who created them.

Even so, he will not discuss their **cognition** in the sense of asking **how**, and through what “psychological means,” they produced these forms of thought.

The same applies to the historian of philosophy.

When discussing Plato, for example, the historian will speak about the content of Plato’s philosophy and about Plato himself, but not about Plato’s “cognition”—the psychological means through which Plato developed his philosophy.<sup>168</sup>

The phenomenologist, like the psychologist, is primarily interested in precisely this **cognition**.

His aim, after all, is to make genuine philosophical knowledge possible.

History matters to Phenomenology only insofar as it is the history of this knowledge: the history of human cognition that eventually led to phenomenological knowledge and, through phenomenological knowledge, to philosophical knowledge—that is, ultimately, to perfect knowledge, wisdom, or omniscience.

In this sense, as I have already said, Phenomenology is above all a **theory of knowledge**: a science or theory of **cognition**. If one wishes, it can therefore also be called a kind of psychology.

But unlike ordinary theories of knowledge and ordinary psychology, Phenomenology studies **concrete cognition**. This cognition is inseparably connected not only with its content—the appearances or phenomena—but also with the real consciousness in which that content occurs: with the actual **human being**.

For this reason, it is better to call Phenomenology an **anthropology**.

And because concrete human cognition is essentially **historical**, phenomenological anthropology—or phenomenological theory of knowledge—is historical too.

Still, if we want to distinguish Phenomenology from history, it is better to call this phenomenological anthropology or theory of knowledge **dialectical** rather than merely “historical.”

For, as we will see again, the development and existence of concrete cognition and concrete consciousness—that is, of human beings—is not only historical in the ordinary sense. It is **dialectical**.

In terms of its subject matter or object, then, Phenomenology can be defined as a **“dialectical anthropology.”**

Calling it an “anthropology” emphasizes that it is first and foremost a theory of knowledge or psychology. But it also tells us how this theory of knowledge and psychology differs from its ordinary scientific forms: it deals not with abstract cognition or “consciousness in general,” but with the concrete cognition and consciousness of a **human being**.

The word “dialectical,” meanwhile, emphasizes its historical character. The cognition and consciousness of the human being studied by Phenomenology are not eternal and unchanging. They develop through time according to definite laws.

We therefore call phenomenological anthropology **dialectical** rather than merely historical, partly to distinguish it from ordinary scholarly history and partly to indicate that the laws governing the development of human consciousness are dialectical.

But in defining Phenomenology as a “dialectical anthropology,” we must not forget that it is first and foremost **Phenomenology**: a philosophical science of phenomena or “appearances.”<sup>169</sup>

In other words, unlike the dialectical anthropology that forms part of Cosmology, Phenomenology does not describe the **real existence of human beings themselves** within the natural world—their specifically human existence together with their material or bodily existence.

It describes the human being **as phenomenon or appearance**: the human being as he **appears to himself** throughout the historical development of humanity.

And because a human being appears to himself through a cognition **of himself**, while a consciousness that knows itself is **self-consciousness**, we can give Phenomenology a still more precise definition.

As *phenomeno*-logy, it is a philosophical **description of the development of self-consciousness**—or, if one prefers, the dialectical **history of self-consciousness**.

This is obviously true when Phenomenology describes the “appearance” of a human being and of the human world to a human being.

But it remains true even when Phenomenology deals with the natural world.

For it does not discuss the natural world itself. It discusses its “appearance”: the content of a human consciousness directed toward the natural world.

And human consciousness is always also **self-consciousness**. A human being is conscious not only of **what** he is conscious of, but also of the fact **that he is conscious**, and that **he himself** is the one who is conscious.

Ultimately, therefore, what the phenomenologist describes is self-consciousness.

But we must again remember that this is **concrete** self-consciousness: human self-consciousness, which means **historical** self-consciousness.

Phenomenology studies the **history of self-consciousness**, or self-consciousness in its historical development.

Phenomenology is therefore the philosophical and dialectical **history of self-consciousness**: “history,” as against psychology and the ordinary theory of knowledge; “of self-consciousness,” as against ordinary history.

It describes the historical—and therefore dialectical—development or becoming of human self-consciousness.

It begins with the “birth” of self-consciousness, with its “simplest” form: the moment when a human being first said **“I”**—when a human being first began to speak about himself, to refer to himself, and therefore to know himself and become conscious of himself.

It ends with the appearance of **complete self-consciousness**: a form that is therefore the “last” one, because its development can go no further.

This complete self-consciousness is that of the philosopher—or more exactly, the sage.<sup>170</sup>

And because philosophical self-consciousness is also, for that very reason, the self-consciousness of the phenomenologist, we can say that the phenomenologist brings the history of self-consciousness to an end by describing **his own self-consciousness**.

As we will see, this self-consciousness is phenomenological—which means philosophical, and therefore complete, final, and definitive—because it is, so to speak, the **sum of all the forms of self-consciousness described in Phenomenology**, all of which appear as possible types of self-consciousness in general.<sup>171</sup>

The phenomenologist can continue describing the historical development of self-consciousness only so long as his own self-consciousness is **broader** than the forms he describes—only so long as his description allows him to see that those earlier forms are still incomplete and that their development has therefore not yet finished.

But if the phenomenologist’s own self-consciousness is complete, this means that he “appears” to himself exactly as he really is.

At that point he no longer appears to himself **as a phenomenologist**. He is given to himself **as a philosopher**.

And once he becomes a philosopher, he can move beyond describing “appearances.” He can describe **existing reality itself**, including himself as something that really exists, and the being that underlies reality—including, of course, his own existence.

Phenomenology therefore ends, so to speak, where “appearances” and the forms of cognition and consciousness corresponding to them come to an end.

Phenomenology ends where **knowledge of the things themselves** begins.

In other words, Phenomenology describes all the incomplete forms of “consciousness” that have some cognition of “phenomena” without understanding that they are phenomena—that is, without understanding **how** their cognition takes place and **who** is doing the cognizing.

In this sense Phenomenology is genuinely a **complete phenomenology**: a universal description that exhausts every possible form of “appearance”<sup>172</sup>, together with every corresponding form of cognition and consciousness—that is, ultimately, every form of self-consciousness.

Phenomenology therefore gives an exhaustive description of **all phenomena that have existed or do exist**: all the ways in which the world and humanity appear to human beings.

In doing so, it describes every type of human **self-consciousness**.

And because it describes self-consciousness phenomenologically—that is, philosophically and therefore **concretely**—it also describes every type of human existence, insofar as that existence is conscious.

More exactly, it describes every type of human existence **insofar as human beings become conscious of it**: insofar as that existence “appears” through a corresponding form of cognition, through the “experience” of the consciousness of the human beings who actually embody that type of existence.

Phenomenology continues doing this for as long as there remains a **difference** between an existence itself and its “appearance”—for as long as the self-consciousness of that existence remains incomplete.

Or, what amounts to the same thing, it continues for as long as the phenomenologist can see **more** in a form of existence than the corresponding consciousness can say about itself.

Those consciousnesses believe they are saying **everything that can be said** about their existence. They therefore forget that what they are describing is an “appearance,” not existence itself.

Phenomenology passes through all these forms of human existence until it finally reaches **philosophical**, and therefore phenomenological, existence—the existence of its own author, who will also become the author of the future philosophical system.

At that point Phenomenology fully comprehends its author’s self-consciousness, and his existence therefore ceases to be merely an “appearance.”

So Phenomenology describes every type of human existence insofar as it appears as a **phenomenon**.

And because these forms of existence are conscious, while consciousness includes a kind of “cognitive experience,”[^E037] Phenomenology describes every type of human experience—experience both of oneself and of the world—from the “first” and “simplest” form all the way to phenomenological, and therefore philosophical, experience.

In this sense, it describes the **course of education** or formation (*Erfahrung*) undergone by human consciousness: the path along which consciousness and cognition have travelled before reaching the experience expressed in a Phenomenology that describes precisely the path that led to itself.

The “cognitive experience” described in Phenomenology makes different **aspects** of existence—the world and humanity—“appear” to human consciousness.

A later consciousness “remembers” the earlier experience and adds a new one to it. The aspect of existence that appears therefore becomes progressively broader and deeper.

The “last” experience gathers up all the earlier ones. By bringing together **all** the aspects of existence, it arrives at a **complete cognition of reality** and thereby turns into **perfect knowledge**.

The consciousness possessing this knowledge has become philosophical.

But this “summing up” of experiences and of the aspects revealed through them is nothing other than the whole of the *Phenomenology* that describes them.

We can therefore say that consciousness becomes philosophical—that is, capable of omniscience and of rising to Cosmology and Ontology—precisely because it has first become **phenomenological consciousness**.

And it becomes phenomenological only after it has described every form of experience and every form of consciousness—that is, all non-phenomenological or pre-phenomenological forms of self-consciousness.

Once the phenomenologist has described **all** the appearances of the world and humanity to human beings, while also counting himself among those appearances, he cannot continue describing appearances because no new ones remain.

If he wants to go further, he must stop describing “appearance” and begin describing **existence itself**, together with the being that underlies it—the existence that has now become “given” to him through his phenomenological description of every appearance.

In short, he must write a **systematic Philosophy**.

Phenomenology therefore does more than make philosophy genuinely possible. In principle, it also **proves philosophy to be true**.

It does so by showing that the philosopher’s self-consciousness is **complete**: his experience of his object includes not only the object but also his experience of cognition itself and of himself as philosopher.

His cognition therefore ceases to be an “opinion” and becomes genuine “knowledge.” It becomes experience not merely of the “appearances” or isolated “aspects” of existence, but knowledge of **existence itself taken as a whole**—that is, taken concretely.<sup>173</sup>

Of course, everything just said is true only if Phenomenology really does describe **all** the types of “experience” or “self-consciousness” that are possible in principle—or, where they are not final types, all those that have actually existed by the time Phenomenology itself emerges.

In other words, it must describe every type of conscious human existence.

The only thing that can guarantee this completeness is knowledge of the law governing the development of human existence and determining the stages—or types—through which it passes.

As we will see, and as we already know, this law is called **dialectic**. This is why it matters that Phenomenology is a **dialectical science**.<sup>174</sup>

By knowing and demonstrating this dialectic, Phenomenology can begin with the “simplest” consciousness or self-consciousness—the simplest form of conscious existence—and show **how and why it must eventually pass into the next form**, then the next, and so on.<sup>175</sup>

Phenomenology can therefore be certain that it has omitted no stage and no type of human existence.

It can also be certain that it has exhausted them all.

That is why it finally arrives at **itself** and can obviously go no further.

On the one hand, it arrives at the self-consciousness—or form of existence—of its own author, whose existence culminates in writing the *Phenomenology*. On the other hand, it then describes that very existence.

At this point Phenomenology would simply have to repeat itself, since the phenomenologist’s form of existence consists in writing the *Phenomenology* itself.

Phenomenology therefore knows that it has described **all** the types of self-consciousness or conscious human existence that are either possible in general or historically realized by the time it appears.

And this knowledge allows it to **select** from the material supplied by history.

It knows, on the one hand, **what the successive stages or types are**, and on the other, **why they succeed one another in precisely this order**.<sup>176</sup>

First, this allows Phenomenology to divide history correctly into periods—to identify the moment when a genuinely new historical stage emerges.

The duration of these stages—the time between the emergence of historical type A and the emergence of type B that follows it—can vary enormously, from a few years to several centuries.

But Phenomenology will treat each stage as a single whole. More exactly, it will select from each stage its most typical and defining element.

For this reason, the phenomenological or dialectical description of history can at first look astonishingly arbitrary. Phenomenology leaves out vast numbers of “historical facts” and seems simply to “jump” from one historical situation to another.

But once its method is understood, we see that these omissions and jumps are grounded in the dialectic itself.

Second, dialectical knowledge of the “causes” and “effects” belonging to each stage allows Phenomenology to describe only what is genuinely **new** at that stage and what is already quietly **preparing the next one**.

Phenomenology therefore not only leaves out most “historical facts.” It also reduces the facts it does discuss to an extreme schematic form, producing what looks, from the historian’s point of view, like a very incomplete picture.

But this “schematization” is justified in several ways, which will become clear from the text of the *Phenomenology* itself.

Finally, knowing the “essence” of these stages or types of conscious existence allows Phenomenology to **idealize** historical facts.

A type of conscious existence described by Phenomenology—the “slave,” the “skeptic,” the “bourgeois,” and so on—may never have existed anywhere in what we might call a **chemically pure form**.<sup>177</sup>

It is entirely possible that no flesh-and-blood human being ever lived **completely** in the way demanded by a particular type of existence, or ever understood that form of existence as fully as it **could have been understood**.

In this respect—and, strictly speaking, always—the phenomenologist “invents” a person who perfectly and completely embodies the type in question, usually by combining different traits found among people of the same historical period.

To the scholarly historian, phenomenological “history” may therefore look not merely fragmentary and schematic but positively arbitrary and “fantastical.”<sup>178</sup>

But once the historian has understood, through Phenomenology, the dialectical law governing the development of human existence, he will also understand the necessity and legitimacy not only of its **periodization** and **schematization** of history, but also of its **idealization** of historical forms.

We can end our preliminary account of the object and subject matter of Phenomenology here.

Before moving on, however, I want to emphasize once again—or revisit—the fact that Phenomenology, insofar as it is a “dialectical anthropology,” also appears as the phenomenologist’s own **“dialectical autobiography.”**

In other words, it is an autobiography of its own author.

We have seen that the phenomenologist must necessarily end his Phenomenology by describing **his own self-consciousness**—that is, by giving a true description of himself, insofar as his self-consciousness really is complete and his Phenomenology really is “finished.”

This necessity follows from the very purpose of Phenomenology.

Phenomenology is supposed to make philosophy genuinely possible. It must therefore make its author—and its reader—into a philosopher.

But the philosopher is precisely the human being who possesses complete knowledge of himself: knowledge that fully exhausts his self-consciousness.

Phenomenology must therefore end with the emergence of its author’s own complete self-consciousness.

The same conclusion follows from the nature of its **object and subject matter**.

If Phenomenology describes **all** appearances, it must also describe itself as an “appearance.”

And if the description of any appearance must be completed by a description of the corresponding cognition and consciousness, then the phenomenologist must also describe **himself**, insofar as his consciousness contains the experience whose content is the *Phenomenology* he has written.

Phenomenology therefore necessarily contains the self-consciousness of its own author.

But this self-consciousness appears within Phenomenology as the **result** of the entire historical development described before it.

That development thereby becomes, so to speak, the **history of this self-consciousness**, and the whole of Phenomenology becomes an **auto-biography**: the account of the history of a life.

Yet the “history” in question consists of the stages in the development of one human being’s **self-consciousness**, as described by Phenomenology—or the stages of that human being’s appearance to himself—rather than the historical development of the flesh-and-blood individual as such.

Phenomenology therefore gives us the “history” of the phenomenologist’s **consciousness**, not the biography of the phenomenologist as a concrete biological individual.

Its “autobiography” is not an autobiography in the ordinary sense. It is a **philosophical**, or more exactly **phenomenological**, autobiography.

It describes its author only insofar as he is **its author**, leaving aside everything in his life that belongs merely to him as an ordinary person.<sup>179</sup>

Taken as a whole—at its end—the *Phenomenology* allows its author, if one wishes, to answer completely the philosophical question about himself:

**“Who am I, and why am I doing what I am doing?”**

But that answer can be complete only if I do not consider myself simply as a living individual—**I, Alexandre Vladimirovich Kojevnikov**—but instead as an “anonymous” phenomenologist and future philosopher.

That is, I must reduce my relevant activity to the writing of the *Phenomenology* in preparation for writing a philosophical system.

At that point the philosophical problem becomes a phenomenological one, and I can answer it completely.

Who am I?

I am the person writing—or who has written—this *Phenomenology*.

What am I doing—or what have I done?

I am writing—or have written—this *Phenomenology*.

What does it contain?

Read the whole thing and you will see. Only the *Phenomenology* itself can answer that question.

Why am I writing it—or why did I write it?

Because I hoped that through it I could become a philosopher.

What is a philosopher?

That too is explained in the *Phenomenology* itself, especially in its “Introduction.”

But why **did I hope** that writing the *Phenomenology* could make me a philosopher?

The *Phenomenology* itself answers this question, but I can already give the answer in a few words.

My *Phenomenology*—or, more exactly, Hegel’s *Phenomenology*, which I first read and which is incorporated into my own—shows me, first:

1. that concrete or philosophical knowledge—that is, perfect knowledge or omniscience—is in principle **possible**, but must be preceded by phenomenological knowledge;
2. that such knowledge has **not yet actually been achieved**, not even by Hegel;
3. that Hegel’s philosophy has come **closer to it than anything else**;
4. that after the appearance of Hegel’s philosophy, and in connection with it, **Marx, Lenin, and Stalin created new historical conditions**—that is, a new type of conscious human existence, specifically a socialist type—which both requires and makes possible a critical revision and extension of Hegel’s philosophy, together with the Phenomenology contained within it;
5. and finally, that according to my own *Phenomenology*, nothing produced since Hegel can yet be regarded as this corrected and completed philosophy suited to the new historical conditions, or as a Phenomenology corresponding to such a philosophy.<sup>180</sup>

So this philosophy is **possible**, but it does not yet **exist**.

That is precisely why I can **hope** to create it.

But why is it specifically **I** who hopes to do so?

Here it is easy to see that the *Phenomenology* cannot provide an answer.

The fact that **I** am its author will become known only when—and because—I have actually written a Philosophy.

Phenomenology can, however, state the conditions that **any** author of a Phenomenology must satisfy.

Such a person must write—or think through—a *Phenomenology* that essentially coincides with the one I am writing or have written.

This means a Phenomenology that, on the one hand, incorporates everything in Hegel’s *Phenomenology* that has **passed the test of dialectical verification** through the historical development that continued after Hegel, and that, on the other hand, gives an additional and correct phenomenological account of that later development.

All of this means that I can hope to become a philosopher and go beyond Hegel’s philosophy only if I possess phenomenological knowledge of **everything that has happened on Earth up to and including Hegel, and everything that happened after him up to the moment when I decided to become a philosopher**.

And this is perfectly understandable.

Philosophy in general, like every new philosophy, does not “fall from the sky.”

It describes what **exists**.

A new form of historical existence must therefore first come into being.

And that new existence is conditioned by everything that came before it.

World history as a whole is therefore the **objective condition** that makes this new philosophy possible.

The **subjective condition**—the condition that allows a particular individual to hope that **he** might be the philosopher who produces it—must obviously be **knowledge of this history**, insofar as history is the objective condition of the philosophy in question.

More precisely, the subjective condition is **phenomenological knowledge of history**.

A new philosophy becomes **objectively** possible when world history creates a new historical stage.

But **subjectively**—that is, **for me**—it becomes possible only when this stage begins to “exist **for me**”: when I become conscious of it and understand it, rather than merely participating in it “physically.”

Only then does an objective historical stage become a subjective stage as well.

The phenomenological description of the dialectical historical process that created the **objective conditions** making a new philosophy possible is therefore the necessary **subjective condition** that allows the author of that description to hope that he can turn this objective possibility into reality.

He does so by actually creating a new philosophy which, once embodied in a real **book**, separates itself, so to speak, from its author and becomes a real, objective part of the new historical period—at least if that period “recognizes” the book.

In this sense, the *Phenomenology* really is my **philosophical autobiography**.

It describes my philosophy through my own “activity”—through the philosophical **formation** or education I must undergo in order to become a philosopher, or at least to acquire the subjective possibility of becoming one.

And if this formation could—or can—turn **me** into a philosopher, then in principle it can do the same for anyone else who undergoes it: every reader who genuinely understands my *Phenomenology*.

We can therefore say that, by being a **dialectical anthropology**, the *Phenomenology* necessarily becomes a **philosophical autobiography**.

And by becoming a philosophical autobiography, it also serves as an **Introduction to Philosophy**.

It “introduces” both its author and its reader to philosophy because, by bringing them to full consciousness, it creates the **subjective possibility** for the author to **produce** the content of the complete self-consciousness called philosophy, and for the reader to **reproduce** that content—that is, to **understand** the philosophy.

And in doing so, Phenomenology guarantees to both author and reader the truth of that philosophy by showing its historical, dialectical **necessity**—and therefore its claim to universal, objective recognition.<sup>181</sup>

We can stop here with our preliminary definition of the object and subject matter of Phenomenology. But one further point is worth noting. The idea of a “philosophical autobiography” that serves as an “introduction to Philosophy” is as old as philosophy itself.

We find it at the very beginning of Philosophy, in Plato’s “Socratic” *Dialogues*. Plato is not, of course, talking about himself but about Socrates. Yet since Plato presents Socrates, rather than himself, as the philosopher, we can say that the philosophical biography of Socrates contained in the *Dialogues* is effectively the philosopher’s autobiography. By showing how Socrates came to philosophy, it also helps anyone who understands the *Dialogues* to reach philosophy themselves. And these *Dialogues* must also establish the truth—that is, the necessity and universality—of the philosophy Plato sets out in his “Dogmatics,” namely his lost book *On the Good*.

The same thing happens at the beginning of Christian, medieval, theological philosophy. It begins with Augustine’s *Confessions*, which describe how and why Augustine arrived at Christianity. By showing the necessity of this “conversion,” the book is also meant to lead its readers to the same destination.

Then, at the dawn of “modern” philosophy, Descartes writes the *Discourse on Method* and the *Meditations*, and plans to write *The History of My Mind*.<sup>182</sup> These works are all philosophical autobiographies: accounts of a path already travelled. By describing the path that led him to his philosophy, Descartes tries to establish the validity of that path by showing that it is necessary and universal. In other words, he tries to show that his autobiography is true while also making it accessible and understandable to everyone.

But only Hegel fully understood and explained why a philosophical autobiography is a necessary introduction to philosophy and a guarantee of its truth. In his *Phenomenology*, he showed what form such an autobiography must take if it is to achieve this goal.

## II. The method of Phenomenology

Once we had established the *aims* of Phenomenology, we were able to identify its *subject matter* and so define its *object*. We must now ask *how* Phenomenology is to deal with that subject matter and investigate that object if it is to reach its goal. In other words, we must determine the *method* used in Phenomenology.

First, we need to examine the dialectical character of Phenomenology. We must show that its *method* is “dialectical” only because its object is dialectical—that is, because the phenomena it describes are themselves dialectical.
