The realization of freedom therefore seems to split the human being in two.

By negating himself as something “given,” he *opposes himself to himself*. He thereby exists *for himself*—in other words, he exists **consciously**.

So if we say that “the human being is human—that is, different from an animal—simply because he possesses self-consciousness,” we must now add that this self-consciousness necessarily presupposes **self-negation**: creative action, the realization of freedom, and therefore a certain **revolutionary character**.

It is only *after* a revolution, through the revolution and because of it, that we can fully understand what the “old regime” was and relate to it with full *consciousness*.

And what is true of political life is equally true of every other domain of human life.

The human being is human—that is, free and self-conscious—only because his existence includes the “moment” of **antithesis**.

But he can no more be *only* antithesis than he can be *only* thesis.

More precisely, if he were only thesis, he would certainly exist, but not as a human being. He would simply be an animal.

If, on the other hand, his existence were reduced entirely to antithesis, he would annihilate himself. He would turn, so to speak, into “pure” negation—that is, into **nothing**.

If the human being “were” nothing but negation, he would not be at all.

So insofar as he *exists*, and exists specifically as a *human being*, he must be simultaneously both thesis and antithesis.

And this means that he must be not merely thesis, and not merely antithesis, but a third thing as well:

**synthesis**.

We must therefore ask what the human being is **as synthesis**.

What is his synthetic aspect? What is the “moment” in which, as we already know, the category of **totality** predominates?

We know that synthesis appears as the *result* of antithesis, which itself presupposes thesis.

And we also know that antithesis reaches a positive or synthetic result because its negation is **concrete**: it is determined by the specific character of what it negates.

Non-A becomes some determinate B because it contains A within itself, preserves A, and is defined by it.

And this is exactly what happens in every “conversion.”

What a converted person becomes is determined by what he was before the conversion.

When a member of the thirteenth-century “gilded youth”—Francis of Assisi—is converted, the result is very different from what happens when the same thing occurs to a sixteenth-century Spanish soldier such as Ignatius of Loyola.

And when a minor French nobleman of the eighteenth century becomes a revolutionary—for example, Robespierre—the result is different from what happens when a minor Russian nobleman of the nineteenth century becomes one.

In the first case, the outcome includes “the sacred right of property”; in the second, its abolition.

And so on.

More generally, the result of every revolution is in some way determined by the “old regime” it overthrows.

That old regime is therefore, in a certain sense, **preserved within the revolution**, although obviously in a transformed form.

And what is true of humanity as a whole is also true of every individual human being.

When a person *negates himself*, it is *himself* that he negates.

For that very reason, he remains identical with himself.

Even in his negation, he is determined by what he was before it.

This is why the result of a free action—that is, an antithetical or negating action—is always **synthetic**.

The past that is negated can be said to survive insofar as a person *remembers* it. The synthetic side of human existence therefore corresponds to *memory* (*Erinnerung*). Memory is what gives a personality its unity. If someone who had undergone a “conversion” completely forgot who they had been before, we could hardly say that we were dealing with one and the same person; we would really be dealing with two different individuals. And there is no doubt that the memory of the past enters into every revolution and helps determine its character. More generally, a real human being is never an “Ivan the Amnesiac”[^E054]. Memories of the past—including the past one rejects—form an essential part of conscious, and therefore human, life. We simply have to understand “memory” here in a broad sense. Ordinary conscious recollection makes up only a small part of it. The past therefore often continues to operate in a person’s present without that person being aware of it.

We can also say that memory brings inside us what at first existed only outside us. The past exists only “inside” a consciousness that remembers it, not in the objective reality “outside” us.<sup>210</sup> So when a person retains the memory of a thesis after having negated it in the antithesis, they internalize and make their own something that had previously been, in a certain sense, “dead” and external to them. What had existed “in itself” now exists “for them”: as *their* past, the past they *know*. Through memory, in this broad sense, a human being seems to absorb the past. The past lives in the human being just as the human being lives in the past. And in this sense the human being is genuinely total, because they contain *everything* that came before them.<sup>211</sup>

But memory and knowledge of the past are nothing other than *history*. And any being that incorporates its past into its present existence, and can be defined by that past, is *historical*. We can therefore say that a human being is synthetic—that is, genuinely human—to the extent that they are historical.

But we must not forget that a person’s historical past, precisely because it is dialectical and human, necessarily contains an antithesis as well: a *negation* of what that past was and of what the person themselves once was. Human beings differ from animals, and are “more” than animals, only because they negate themselves—or at least can negate themselves. Yet they remain genuinely *human*, rather than becoming sheer nothingness, only because they remember what they have negated. It is only through this memory that they remain the *same* person who is being negated and the same person who performs the negation.

Or, as Hegel puts it:

> Human consciousness *sublates* [*aufhebt*] in such a way that it *keeps* [*aufbewahrt*] and *preserves* [*erhält*], and therefore survives [*überlebt*] its being sublated [*Aufgehobenwerden*].[^E055]

(p. 145)

In its synthetic aspect, then, the human being unites the other two aspects: thesis and antithesis. Through memory, in the broad sense, a person remains *connected* to what has been given to them—to both the natural and the human or sociopolitical world. In this respect they remain connected to the thesis. But they are also *free* from this given reality insofar as they negate it in the antithesis.

The thesis becomes genuinely *human* only in the synthesis, because it becomes human only by passing through self-negation. The antithesis, by contrast, does not exist at all outside the synthesis, because the synthesis is the *realization* of the antithesis. An action becomes real in what it produces, and what it produces then becomes part of what already exists—that is, part of the thesis. So an action that has entered into reality in this way is itself a synthesis.

A revolution is revolutionary only because it *negates* the “*old* regime.” But it becomes *real* only by creating a “new *regime*.” And this new regime is synthetic or historical only because it contains both the “old regime,” in an essentially transformed form, and the revolutionary negation of that regime—which is itself essentially transformed in the process of becoming real.

Once a synthesis is complete and established, however, it has already become a thesis. It is not a thesis while it is still being created, and certainly not for the people who are creating it. It becomes a thesis only for those who encounter it as something “given”: something they did not “make,” something that was already fully formed before they arrived. It can then serve as the starting point for a new dialectical triad.

Still, we should repeat that a real human being is *always* synthetic, whether we happen to describe them as a “thesis” or as an “antithesis.”

As long as we are dealing with a *human being*, what is “given” to them always includes the memory of their *historical* past. And that historical past necessarily presupposes the negation of something that had once been given. At the same time, insofar as a human being *exists*, they are always something given as well. If they negated absolutely *everything* that was given, they would simply annihilate themselves.

Human existence is therefore always “dialectically sublated.” Most of its content consists of “memories” of the past: a past that has been *abolished* through negation, yet *preserved* within that negation, and in this way raised—once it has become conscious and free—to a “higher level.”

In other words, human existence is always “mediated.” Between a human being and what is given to them, whether natural or historical, there always stands the real or merely possible *negation* of that given reality. So even the decision to preserve what is given is, from one point of view, always “free,” because it presupposes choosing *not* to exercise a possible negation. To that extent, the given is “freely accepted,” and the person becomes “responsible” for it.

So when we say that a human being—or a society, or humanity as a whole—exists at some particular moment as a thesis, we mean only that what is *given* predominates. In particular, the “animal” side predominates. The person accepts this given reality more or less “unfreely” or “unconsciously,” because they do not even “see” the possibility of negating it.

A human being exists as an antithesis, by contrast, when the *negation* of what is given predominates—that is, when freedom or free action predominates. Such a person lives and maintains themselves within the existing world only in order to “overcome” it.

Finally, a human being exists as a synthesis when “totality” or “historicity” predominates: when they freely and consciously accept a given reality which, as they know and remember, was itself created through the negation of an earlier given reality.<sup>212</sup>

But if this is true—if the human being is never anything other than a synthesis—then we can say that a human being is nothing other than *free action*.

For dialectic, and therefore synthesis, exists only insofar as “negativity” exists. And this negativity becomes real only in free, negating, and therefore creative action. The reality of dialectic is therefore the reality of action, in the strongest sense of that word.

But the *reality* of action presupposes three things. First, there must be something given toward which the action is directed: a given reality, or thesis, that is going to be changed—that is, partially negated. Second, there is the action itself, the antithesis. Third, there is the result of the action, the synthesis.

And this three-part structure of action is nothing other than the human being insofar as the human being is dialectical—that is, genuinely human, free, and historical.<sup>213</sup>

To the extent that a human being has not “made” themselves—in the sense that they did not make their own body—they are an animal. And if their “action” consisted in a *pure* and *complete* self-negation, that is, suicide, they would be *nothing*.

So insofar as a human being *exists as a human being*, they have *created themselves*. This should be understood in the same sense in which Christianity could say, for example, that God created the human being “*from nothing*.”

A human being’s *being* is nothing other than their human *existence*, and that existence coincides with human action: action that is negative or free, and conscious. There can therefore be no difference between what a human being *is* and what they *do*.

Once we see this, it becomes clear that human existence is historical and therefore *essentially temporal*.

Action takes *time*. For action to occur, something must have *already* been, and something else must *not yet* be. There must therefore be a *past* and a *future*. Action itself happens in the “present”—that is, *in time*—precisely because the present contains, in some way, and presupposes both past and future.

So if a human being is nothing other than “realized action,” we can also say that the human being is “realized time.”

But why can we not say the same thing about natural “things”? Do they not also endure? Do they not also have a future connected with a past, as well as a present? Why should time *not* be essential to them too?

We can say that time is not essential to natural things because, although they exist in time, time does not exist *in them*—or, which amounts to the same thing, it does not exist *for them*, in their *consciousness*.

In particular, the *future*—the aspect that belongs most essentially to time and distinguishes time from space—does not exist for them.

Strictly speaking, only the present exists. There is therefore neither past nor future in the full sense. Neither is presently real. What “was” has already ceased to exist, while what “will be” has not yet entered existence.

Still, in a certain sense, the past is more real than the future. The past continues to form part of the reality of the present. It is fixed and unchangeable, and therefore “identical,” just as the present is.

The future, by contrast, is not real in this strong sense. What *was*, after all, really did exist. But what *will be* has not yet entered existence at all. It does *not yet actually exist*.

That is why we cannot say that the future is fixed or unchangeable. It cannot be definitively “determined.” In principle, it could be anything. And if the present is going to change, it is only because something new enters it from the future.

The future is therefore what produces change: it negates the present.

It, and it alone, is the “negative.”

In other words, if “negativity” can become real only in time—because to realize negativity is precisely to *change* what is given—then the time in which negativity exists is, above all, the future. The future is the negative moment or aspect of time.

And conversely, any time in which the future rules must itself be “negative,” or dialectical—that is, human and historical.

The future always “negates” the present by turning it into the past. But if the present or the past predominates, then whatever “new” thing comes from the future to replace the “old” present will itself be determined by what already exists. In other words, it will not differ from the old in any essential way. It is as though the present withstands the pressure of the future and remains what it already is and was.

Anything that “endures” in such a time will therefore remain “identical,” eternally equal to itself.

But if time is dominated by the future—by what does *not yet exist*—then the future negates the “old” present and replaces it with something genuinely new, something that was not already contained in the present. What endures in such a time therefore changes in an essential way; it becomes “negative.”

We can therefore say that non-dialectical, natural existence realizes a time dominated by the present or the past, while a time dominated by the future is realized only in dialectical, human, historical existence.

A time determined by the present or the past is therefore *not* dialectical. Its three basic moments or aspects—past, present, and future—do not form the dialectical triad of thesis, antithesis, and synthesis. In a certain sense, they remain “identical,” because the future introduces nothing essentially new into the present, and the present therefore passes into the past without essential change.

*This* kind of time is realized only in natural, spatial-and-material existence, and the natural world exists only in *this* kind of time.

Take “inorganic” nature. It is obviously determined entirely by its present. If we know the present completely, then in principle we know both its entire past and its entire future, because both merely unfold what was already contained in some way in the present.<sup>214</sup>

With “organic” nature, by contrast, knowing the present alone does not seem sufficient.<sup>215</sup> But even if the *present* does not dominate biological time, neither does the future play an essential role. Biological time seems instead to be governed by the past.

Suppose we want fully to understand a chicken’s egg. We have to know that *in the future* it will produce a chicken and not some other kind of bird. But to know this we do not need to know the *future*. It is both sufficient and necessary to know the egg’s *past*: to know that it was laid by a chicken and not by some other animal.<sup>216</sup>

More generally, if anything essentially distinguishes organic nature from inorganic nature, it is precisely this element of *heredity*: the predominance of the *past*.

A time dominated by the *future*, by contrast, is realized only in the non-natural world—that is, in the human or historical world. And historical existence, insofar as it is historical or properly human, exists only in *this* kind of time.

History is nothing other than *real* time in which the future predominates. And conversely, such time does not exist outside human history.

To understand more clearly what this predominance—or “primacy”—of the future means, and more generally to uncover the inner structure of human, historical, dialectical time, let us consider a concrete example and ask why a particular event occurring in the present is called “historical” in the ordinary sense of the word.

In other words: when and why can a particular “present” count as a “*historical event*” rather than simply as the current state of some thing at a particular moment?

Let us take the traditional example of the Rubicon.

Julius Caesar and his troops approach this Italian river. Caesar intends to march on Rome and seize power. Crossing the river will therefore mean revolution, civil war, and the transition to a new “regime”—the “imperial” regime.

On the night before the campaign begins, Caesar walks along the banks of the river. He considers the situation and makes his final decision: early tomorrow morning, his troops will cross the Rubicon.

In a certain sense, we can say that the Roman Empire was born that night. The night is therefore, at any rate, “historical” in the ordinary sense of the word.<sup>217</sup>

But why?

Let us first look at what is happening in the “present”—say, at exactly midnight that night. What actually exists “for the moment,” at the same time as the river and its banks?

All we see is a particular individual walking beside the water.

And there is obviously nothing “historical” about that in itself. Any soldier in Caesar’s army could have been doing the same thing, for all we know. Caesar himself might simply have been walking because he could not sleep. If that had been the case, we would know nothing about it, and there would be nothing historical about it at all.

So if Caesar’s nighttime walk is historical, it is *only* because, while walking, he made the *decision* to march on Rome the next day.

That means he was thinking about the *future*: about something that did *not yet exist*.

It also means that this future was, in a certain way, “present” in his consciousness, and therefore in his “brain”—and *only* in his. It accompanied him, so to speak, as he walked along the banks of the Rubicon.

Although it remained future—that is, although it remained something that did *not yet exist*—it nonetheless had a real presence within the present, within what already actually existed.

And we should notice something else: this future was “revolutionary.” It “negated” the present because it was going to change it *essentially*.

There would have been nothing historical in Caesar imagining some future that followed naturally and necessarily from the existing present.

We can therefore say that it is the real presence of this kind of future within the present that makes the present “historical”—or, if you prefer, human.

And this means that in historical time, the future dominates, prevails, or rules.

But the mere presence of the future is not enough to make the present historical.

After all, anyone can walk beside a river at night dreaming of taking Rome and seizing absolute power: an ambitious young man, a dreamer, a “poet,” a utopian—or even a lunatic.

The presence of the future in such a present is certainly still “human,” because an animal cannot “dream” about the future. But there is nothing “historical” in a future of this kind if it is conditioned only by the present.<sup>218</sup>

The Rubicon is historical only because the march on Rome was conceived by *Caesar*: by an individual who had a genuine “chance of success.”

And that also means bringing the *past* into the present.

Caesar’s “chances” are determined by what he had actually accomplished up to that point—by what he had done in the past. It is only because of his *past* that he is “Caesar” rather than a “dreamer” or a “madman.”

His thought is not a “dream,” and his decision is not a “whim,” only because he himself knows that past and takes it into account—along with everything it implies: his army, the balance of forces, and so on—when thinking about the future and making his decision.

So the past too, although it no longer exists, accompanies him as he walks beside the river. It too is present within the present, within what exists “for the moment.”

The present is therefore historical—genuinely real and, in the strongest sense, human—only when it includes both the future that negates it and the past that conditions it.

In other words, the historical present is “synthetic,” and therefore dialectical.

It is the result of a union, or synthesis, between the thesis on the one hand—that is, its “identity” with the eternally fixed past, or with the determinate character it has received from that past—and the antithesis on the other hand: the future that negates it.

It is now easy to see that in dialectical or historical time, the order of the fundamental “moments” is not the same as it is in natural time.

The order here is:

*f†uture, past, present.*

The historical present is not the source of the past and the future. It does not determine them. It is itself determined.

And it is determined not only by the past, but also—and above all—by the future.

The historical present is therefore synthetic or total: it is “dialectically sublated” and “mediated” by future and past.

It is also easy to see that this dialectical time is nothing other than the time in which human *action* takes place: action in the strong sense of the word, action that revolutionarily negates what is given and builds or creates a new reality.

An action is human—that is, “free” and “conscious,” rather than involuntary, instinctive, or merely reflexive—only insofar as it is “premeditated”: undertaken in order to realize a certain “project.”

It is creative only when this project is new—that is, when it refers to something that does *not yet exist* “in nature.”

And for that very reason it is “negative.” By introducing something *new* into what already exists, it *changes* what exists. It destroys the existing reality insofar as that reality is what it presently is and was.

Yet an action can actually *exist*, and a project can become *real*, only if the project is not “utopian”—that is, only if it takes account of what is and what has been.

So real action—successful action—always enters the present from the future, from a “project” that initially exists only in thought, while at the same time resting on the past: on previously acquired knowledge and experience preserved in memory.

That is why to say that a human being is nothing other than their *free and creative action* is also to say that the human being is the realization of a form of time in which the future enters the present *through the past*.

And conversely, such time becomes real and exists only in the form of human *action*.

So once again we see that dialectic is not a “method”: not a way of looking at reality, understanding it, and talking about it.

Dialectic is itself a particular kind of reality—namely, the human being and human history, and even the time in which that history unfolds.

To accept the idea of “dialectic,” then, is to accept a very specific conception of the human being.

Above all, it means placing human *existence* and human activity on the same level. It means locating a person’s “humanity” not in what *is* but in what *becomes*; not in what is *given* to them but in what they *create*; and so on.

From this we can draw three conclusions.

*First*, the human being is inseparably connected with the body and, through the body, with the whole natural world. The human being is therefore a *finite* or *mortal* being: entirely “of this world,” not a being from “elsewhere,” and certainly not a supernatural and eternal, “immortal” soul temporarily inhabiting a body.

*Second*, the human being is essentially *free*. What a person will become is not completely and permanently determined by what they are or what they have been.

*Third*, the human being is necessarily *historical*: always connected with the past, yet never completely determined by it.

We must therefore say that this “dialectical” definition of the human being as “a free and historical being existing within the natural world”—that is, within *material* space governed by *present* or *past* time—fully corresponds to the picture of the human being held by any citizen of the Soviet state, even one with no special taste for philosophy.

In short, for *us* there is nothing “strange” or “paradoxical” about it.

And this is quite easy to understand, because the life of our country is ultimately shaped by Marx’s theory, which in turn rests on the Hegelian conception whose basic principles I have tried to outline above.

There is, however, another aspect of the Marxist—and “Soviet”—understanding of the human being that I have not yet discussed.

For Marx, and for us, a human being is not only “a worldly, free, and historical being.” A human being is also a “person” or an “individual.”

This means more than saying that every separate human being is, as an animal, a “specimen” or “representative” of the zoological species *Homo sapiens*, just as an individual lion is a specimen of the species *Felis leo*.

It means that every human being is also, *as a human being*, something like a unique “species” in their own right: singular and essentially different from every other person.

Until now, it is true, human “personality” or “individuality” has always been obscured by human “historicity” and pushed, so to speak, into the background.

A human being has primarily been defined by their *sociopolitical position*: by membership in a particular class or state. This has been so because part of human activity—and therefore part of the human being themselves—has had a “sociopolitical,” and therefore “collective,” rather than a “personal and individual” character. Human beings have served not their “private interests,” but those of their class or state.<sup>219</sup>

But once communism has been established—when there are no longer separate classes or states, and when nature has finally been “conquered” by technology—“social” activity will move into the background. Human activity as a whole will then be directed toward what we now rather contemptuously call “private life,” though before communism that contempt is entirely justified.

Only then will human “personality” or “individuality” fully flourish. Only after ceasing to be “historical” in the ordinary sense of the word will the human being become fully an “individual.”

Even so, elements of “individuality” are already present in pre-communist humanity. A person is not only “a representative of their class,” “a citizen of their country,” or “a child of their age.” In a certain sense they are also “one of a kind”: an incomparable “personality.”<sup>220</sup>

We must therefore say that if the dialectical conception of the human being could not account for human beings as “persons,” it would not be fully true. All the more so if it were actually incompatible with the existence of personality.

But that is not the case.

If we recognize the dialectical character of human existence, we must also recognize human “individuality.”

In other words, a human being is an *individual* precisely because they are dialectical—that is, synthetic—and therefore necessarily contain the moments of both thesis *and* antithesis.

We can show this as follows.

Let us first assume, without proof, that every individual being is both *finite and free*, and that conversely every *finite and free* being is individual.

If we grant this, then individuality and dialectical existence turn out to be one and the same thing.

Freedom is nothing other than “negativity,” or the antithetical aspect. Finitude, or mortality, belongs to every living natural being<sup>221</sup> and therefore to the animal that underlies human existence—in other words, to the human “body,” in the broad sense.

But the “body,” as we already know, is the original thesis of the human being. Everything th

etical in human existence is ultimately rooted in the body and inseparably attached to it.

We can therefore say that human finitude or mortality belongs to the human being’s th†etical side, just as freedom belongs to the antithetical side.

And since the simultaneous presence of thesis and antithesis necessarily brings synthesis with it, we can say that every synthetic, and therefore dialectical, being is individual.

Conversely, every individual being is dialectical because it necessarily contains both finitude—that is, thesis—and freedom—that is, antithesis—and therefore forms a synthesis.

In other words, dialectic is realized only in the human being.

So we can say, on the one hand, that only a human being is an individual and, on the other hand, that a human being is always an individual—or, equivalently, that a “person” is always and everywhere a “*human person*.”

But we still have to show that an individual being really must be both finite and free, and that a finite and free being must really be an individual.

First of all, we must emphasize that when we call an “individual” “unique in its *kind*,” this has to be taken literally.

We mean unique in its *kind*: unique in its “nature” or “essence,” in its “essential” qualities—not merely in accidental, external, or secondary details.

For, as Leibniz liked to point out, there are no two completely identical things in nature. We cannot find, for example, two oak leaves that are perfectly identical. Yet no one speaks of the “individuality” or “personality” of these leaves.

If human beings differ—or *can* differ—from one another in an “essential” way, in their essential qualities, then it follows that there is no universal human “essence” or nature.

But human beings remain *human* despite differing essentially from one another. This means that one can possess any number of different essences and still remain human—or, if you prefer, that what is human is precisely what has no fixed “essence,” what is not bound in its future by what it is and what it has been.

This means that a human being can *negate* their “essence”—and therefore, strictly speaking, has no such essence.

So to be a “person” or an “individual” one must contain “negativity” and possess the ability to realize it.

And we already know that negativity is nothing other than freedom, while its realization is free action.

The person is therefore always free.

And once we see this, we can also show that the person is finite.

If the human being has no essence, then human “possibilities” are not limited in advance.

A dog can live only “as a dog,” and a cat only “as a cat.” But a human being can live “as a slave,” “as a master,” “as a bourgeois,” “as a proletarian,” “as a revolutionary,” and so on.

In principle, therefore, a human being can live “however they choose.”

The longer a person lives, the more they will normally change.

If they lived *infinitely* long—that is, if they were immortal—they would eventually realize *all* of their possibilities. For, as Aristotle rightly observed, a possibility that is *never* realized, that remains *eternally* unrealized, is not really a *possibility* at all but an *impossibility*.

And *all* the possibilities of a particular human being are ultimately *all* human possibilities in general.

For if different people possessed fundamentally different sets of possibilities, those possibilities would have to be limited or determined by something eternal and unchanging. In other words, each person would possess a fixed “nature” or “essence,” which, as we already know, is incompatible with freedom.

So if human beings lived *eternally*, every one of them would eventually realize *all* human possibilities. Each would therefore cease not only to differ essentially from the others but would become completely identical with them.<sup>222</sup>

We can therefore say that if a person must necessarily be free, they must also be finite—that is, mortal.

Conversely, an infinite or eternal, immortal being cannot be free, and therefore cannot be a person either.

This is obvious if we imagine eternal beings that differ essentially from one another. For that would mean that the possibilities of each were “determined” or “bounded.” Each would possess an eternal and unchanging “nature” or “essence,” and freedom is incompatible with such an essence.

But the same remains true even if we suppose that all eternal beings are identical.

Insofar as a being is eternal, it has already realized “from all eternity” *all* of its possibilities.

Even if those possibilities were infinite—assuming that such an actual realization of infinity were possible—the totality of its infinite realized possibilities would still constitute an eternal and unchanging, though infinite, “essence” or nature. The being could neither change nor, still less, negate that nature.

So there would once again be no room for negativity, and therefore no room for freedom, in such an infinite or eternal being.

We must therefore say that a person is always finite.

But the converse is clearly not true.

We cannot say that every finite being is an individual or “person.” Animals are unquestionably finite and mortal, yet we do not regard them as persons.

So an individual being must possess something in addition to finitude: namely, as we already know, freedom.

What does this mean?

We can say that an animal dies—comes to an “end”—once it has exhausted or realized *all* of its possibilities. Or, if you prefer, it perishes *because* it has realized them.

Take a female cat. From the embryo onward, she develops continuously until she reaches full sexual maturity. Once she has conceived another embryo and given birth to a kitten, she has, in a sense, “nothing more to say to the world.”

After that she can only repeat what she has already done. She herself no longer changes in any essential way.

Her continued existence therefore has, so to speak, no further “meaning” or “justification,” either for others or for herself. It is as though her death simply belongs “to the order of things.”

And the fact that she really has exhausted all of her “cat possibilities” is revealed and confirmed by the fact that she does not differ essentially from her offspring.

The natural cycle that begins with an embryo and ends with a new embryo remains eternally unchanged, at least as long as we are dealing with *this particular* animal species, and it repeats itself indefinitely.

As Aristotle rightly observed, this cycle is itself nothing other than the realization in time and space of an animal’s “essence” or “nature”—what Plato called its “Idea.”

We can therefore say that animals are not “individuals”: their offspring simply reproduce or repeat their parents. And this is ultimately because animals possess an eternal and unchanging “nature” and are therefore not free.<sup>223</sup>

The human being is different.

Insofar as a person is free—insofar as they possess unlimited or “infinite” *possibilities*—they always die, so to speak, too soon: prematurely, in the middle of the journey, in what we might call an unnatural or “violent” death. Nature *kills* them.

However long a person’s *finite* life may last, they can never realize within it all of their *infinite* possibilities.

They therefore always have, in a sense, the “right” to more life. In principle, if they continued living, they could still bring something new into the world. Additional life would therefore still have a “meaning” and a “justification,” both for the person and for the world around them.

This is why a human being can be an incomparable “person”: an individual who is “one of a kind.”

If human beings can “choose” among unlimited possibilities, each person can choose a possibility that no one else has ever chosen.

They can therefore always differ from every other person.

And this is what it means to be an incomparable person.

For an individual is not someone who tries at all costs to resemble no one else simply for the pleasure of being different. An individual is someone who possesses the *possibility* of being one of a kind, even if in many respects they are in fact like everyone else.

We can therefore say, in general, that “personal” or “individual” existence is existence that is *finite in its actuality* but *unlimited in its possibilities*.

And that, as we already know, means an existence that is simultaneously mortal and free.

We can add one more point.

The unlimited character of human *possibilities*—or, more exactly, the fact that a person dies before having had time to exhaust all their possibilities—is revealed or “proved” by the fact that human existence is not cyclical.

The human body, like the body of any animal, reproduces itself only through descendants. But properly human life does not stand still. In principle, the son does not merely repeat the father; he goes “further” than the father.

And we can say that a person’s “spiritual descendants,” who obviously need not be their biological children, realize possibilities that the person themselves “did not manage” to realize.

But we have already explained that human existence is not “cyclical,” as animal existence is. It is historical.

So any being that is finite “in actuality” but infinite “in potentiality” is nothing other than a “worldly, free, and historical” being.

In a word, it is a human being—and therefore also an “individual” or “person.”

We can therefore say not only that every “person” is necessarily free and finite, and therefore historical, but also that every finite and free—that is, historical—being is necessarily a “person.”

So to say that a human being is an “individual” and to say that a human being is “synthetic,” or dialectical, is to say the same thing in different words.

That is why, once we have said that the human being is dialectical—that is, that human existence simultaneously contains all three dialectical aspects, *thesis*, *antithesis*, and *synthesis*—we can also say that the human being is a “*free and historical person*.”

To summarize, let us repeat the point once more.

In every form of human existence—whether in an individual person, in the human community as a whole, or even in any product of human activity—we can distinguish three aspects at work in the dialectic.

There is the thesis, in which “identity” predominates.

There is the antithesis, in which negativity predominates.

And there is the synthesis, in which “totality” predominates.

In reality, however, these aspects are *inseparable*.

The real human being is always a synthesis in the broad sense of the term. Human existence necessarily contains, alongside synthesis in the narrower sense, thesis and antithesis as well.

But as we have already seen, this real, general “synthesis” can itself function as a “thesis” in relation to another “synthesis” that plays the role of antithesis and, together with the thesis, produces a further synthetic synthesis.

In other words, every synthesis—every human existence or human entity, and everything made by human beings—can serve as the starting point of a dialectical process.

It can become a “thesis” that is abolished by an “antithesis” but preserved within a new “synthesis,” and so on.

When we speak about dialectic and dialectical existence, therefore, we have to approach the question from two different angles.

On the one hand, we can consider one and the same entity, or one and the same stage in its development over time.

From this perspective, the entity or stage is dialectical when it contains all three aspects—thesis, antithesis, and synthesis—*simultaneously* and in practice *inseparably*.

On the other hand, there can also be a dialectical relation between *different* entities, or between *different* stages in the development of one and the same entity. This relation allows us to arrange them in the order thesis, antithesis, synthesis.

In *this* case, the three can exist *separately*. They follow one another *in time*—in the kind of time ruled by the future, that is, by antithesis or “negativity.”

We will therefore call these entities dialectical as well, while calling the relation between them the real dialectic in the proper sense of the term.

We now know, at least to some extent, what the real dialectic described by the philosophical system of Hegelian Marxism—and in particular by Hegelian-Marxist Phenomenology—actually is.

We know that it is not a method but a reality.

And we also know that the philosophical method is nothing other than the method of giving a pure description of actuality.

If this description is “dialectical,” that is only because it reflects the dialectical structure of actuality with photographic precision, like a mirror. That structure exists in reality independently of its philosophical description.

If this is so—if the philosophical description of the real dialectic reflects its actual structure—then the description itself must also be divided along the two lines we have just distinguished.

Philosophy will describe, on the one hand, the dialectical *aspects* of actuality and, on the other hand, its dialectical *stages*: the *dialectic* in the proper sense, the real dialectic itself.

In actuality, as we know, the different *aspects* exist inseparably and simultaneously.

So if philosophy describes them separately, and even one after another, this is only because we cannot speak about everything at once or say everything in a single instant.

In this respect, the philosophical description of dialectical actuality does not, if you like, coincide perfectly with actuality itself.

But it differs from it no more than any description that unfolds in time while describing something whose parts exist simultaneously. It differs no more than a zoological description that talks *first* about a cat’s head, *then* about its torso, and so on.

Indeed, the difference is even smaller here.

For although the aspects of dialectic are simultaneous, they nevertheless possess an objective “logical” order. The “logical” antithesis “presupposes” the thesis, while the synthesis presupposes them both.

So when philosophy describes the different aspects of a phenomenon, it cannot choose an arbitrary order of presentation. It must arrange its descriptions as thesis, antithesis, synthesis.

The dialectical *stages*, by contrast, follow one another in time and can in fact be separated.

The thesis always appears *before* the antithesis, while the synthesis emerges only *after* the antithesis has appeared.

So the structure of the philosophical description of dialectical stages—or of dialectic itself—corresponds to the structure of the reality being described.

Even here, however, the correspondence may not be complete.

First, philosophy may take a thesis realized in the historical development of one entity and pair it with an antithesis taken from the historical development of another entity, even though an antithesis also appears in the first.

Philosophy does this when the second entity turns out to realize the antithesis in question “better”—more distinctly and more completely—than the first.

Second, as I have already noted, philosophy can depart somewhat from strict chronology when describing dialectical stages.

An antithesis is always *generated* after the thesis has *appeared*. But the antithesis often appears before the thesis has reached its *full development*.

And since philosophy naturally aims to describe a thesis in its fullest expression, it may describe a th†etical form that, *in the form being described*, emerges only after the phenomenon it identifies as the corresponding antithesis has already appeared.

And so on.

But it is obvious that this departure from historical chronology is of no real importance and cannot count as a philosophical objection.

What, then, does it actually mean to describe dialectical aspects and stages?

We will understand this fully only when we encounter a concrete philosophical description—that is, the philosophical system as a whole.

But we can already say something about it here.

Suppose philosophy wants to describe the dialectical *aspects* of a particular individual, or a particular society, at a particular moment in its historical existence.

When describing that individual or society as a thesis, philosophy will emphasize everything that was “given” to it: everything it merely “inherited,” rather than what it personally made or created.

It will do this while provisionally acting as though it had forgotten that human beings can negate all of this—or even that they are already negating it in practice.

When speaking of the human being as an antithesis, by contrast, philosophy will notice everything that is new—and only what is new: everything that does not, so to speak, follow automatically from what had already been “given.”

It will instead assume that the human being freely negates this “given” reality, and therefore changes in an essential way—or at least possesses the possibility of such a change.

Finally, when speaking of the human being as a synthesis, philosophy will focus only on what has actually been realized out of this novelty: what has been generated by the negation of the given.

In other words, it will look at what has survived in this person, what has entered into them as a “fact” and has therefore itself become *a new given*.

Philosophy will then try to understand how and why this happened.

In studying the synthesis, therefore, philosophy tries to distinguish, within both thesis and antithesis, what has “stood the test” of actuality from what has “failed” that test.

It will try to identify what was “dead” in the given content of the thesis, and what was false *theoretically* or “utopian”—that is, false *practically*—in the creative project of the antithesis.

When philosophy describes the *dialectic itself*—that is, the dialectical *stages*—it proceeds according to the following principles.

Once it has identified some human-historical phenomenon that can be treated as a thesis, and therefore as the starting point of a historical development, philosophy knows that sooner or later this phenomenon will reach its “logical conclusion.”

That is, it will realize its “meaning” or, if you prefer, its “essence” as modified through time. It will reach what is “essential” within it. In other words, it will realize all the possibilities contained in that essence and compatible with that form of existence.

Philosophy will therefore describe the phenomenon at the moment when it actually reaches this “logical conclusion,” schematizing and “idealizing” it if necessary.<sup>224</sup>

In doing so, philosophy knows that this phenomenon will eventually generate a new phenomenon opposed to it: something incompatible with it, yet related to it as non-A is related to A.

Philosophy will then try to find this opposing phenomenon in the actual world and describe it in its clearest form—again idealizing and schematizing it where necessary.

Finally, once it has established that the second phenomenon has abolished the first, philosophy will look for a third phenomenon that replaces them both, knowing in advance that it will contain traces of both the first and the second.

It will then describe this third phenomenon—again schematizing and idealizing it—precisely as a “third” form that unites the first two.

But in doing so, philosophy will also know that this third form will itself generate a new “negative” phenomenon.

It will therefore describe the third form as the starting point of a new historical process.

And it will continue in this way for as long as there remain phenomena that it has not yet described and that differ essentially from those it has already examined.

This is how philosophy in general proceeds when it describes dialectic. Phenomenology differs from Philosophy in the strict sense only in this: it describes dialectic not as it is “in truth,” but as it “appears” to human beings. In other words, it describes thesis, antithesis, and synthesis—both as aspects and as stages—as **phenomena**.

A phenomenon is reality as it **appears to human beings**. So the phenomenon itself is a **human—or historical—appearance**. For that reason, it too is dialectical. The same dialectical dependence therefore exists between phenomena as between the realities of which they are the phenomena. Thus, by describing the “appearances” of the dialectical stages, Phenomenology also describes the dialectical stages of the appearances themselves.

In other words, phenomenological description is just as “dialectical” as philosophical description, and for exactly the same reason. Why? Because **what it describes is dialectical**. Phenomenology is nothing more than the description of real dialectic considered as a series of “appearances”—that is, considered in its phenomenological aspect. Phenomenology is therefore neither more nor less than a complete phenomenological description of dialectic.

### 2. Phenomenological “*a posteriori* deduction”

We have seen that the method of Phenomenology consists simply in the “pure description” of an object. This method allows us to **choose** the object, but also to **schematize** and **idealize** it. The chosen object is then described as it **ought** to be—that is, as it really would be if it developed and realized itself under conditions perfectly suited to it, conditions ideal for its development, without being distorted by accidental outside influences.

Schematizing and idealizing the chosen object therefore does not alter it in any essential way. In any case, the method adds nothing of its own. Every distinctive feature of the **description** comes entirely from the distinctive features of the **object described**—that is, from the real object of the description. In particular, as we have just seen, the “dialectical” character of the description comes entirely from the dialectical character of the object itself.

The dialectical character of the object described in Phenomenology therefore determines the distinctive character of phenomenological description—or, if one prefers, of the phenomenological “method.” We can define this method briefly by calling it **“*a posteriori* deduction.”**

To explain what this means, I will first describe the distinctive character of real dialectic. This character necessarily turns every description of dialectic into a “deduction” of this kind, without distorting dialectic in the process.

As we know, dialectic necessarily contains the “moment” of **negativity**: creative-and-negating action, or revolutionary action in the broad sense. This action is at the same time the effective expression of **freedom** or, more exactly, its realization.

This means that every dialectical being always appears as the **result** of a certain creative—and temporal—process or development. And precisely because it is dialectical, because it is a result, it can be understood or described only by understanding or describing the process through which it was created.

But this dialectical process is nothing other than the process by which a given being **freely creates itself**. In other words, the being is the **result** of its own negating activity and therefore of its creative, world-making, or **free** (“spontaneous”) activity.

Free activity—or an action whose process of development contains an element of **freedom**—differs from a **necessary** or “determined” process in only one respect: its result cannot be **predicted**.

Even if we knew the entire present and past of a dialectical being perfectly, this would not allow us to know its future. The future is not already “contained” within it. And it is not contained there because, however real the past and present of a given being may be, they do not determine its real future.

Freedom itself is precisely what **is not** in the present and **was not** in the past. It is the new element that seems to come from the future—that is, to come “from nothing.”

Freedom is neither being nor non-being. Yet in a certain sense it is real, because it is present within a real dialectical being. And insofar as it is real, freedom appears as the **presence of nothingness within being and existence**.

This entry of nothingness into what exists is precisely what we call free or creative action.

Clearly, then, freedom cannot be seen in what already **is** or what **was**. For that reason it cannot be foreseen or predicted on the basis of our knowledge of what exists or has existed.

But when freedom **realizes itself** in action—or as action, since outside action it does not exist—it becomes an element, a constituent part, of what is and exists. Once freedom has been realized and has entered existence, its real **result**—the result of a successful or completed action—can be known through knowledge of what exists.

And once we know this **result**, we also know its cause: the free action or “decision” without which the result could not have occurred. Yet before the result existed, this action itself neither **was** nor **existed**. It therefore could not have been an object of knowledge, since we can know only what exists or is.

Because the result of a free action or decision really exists, it has—like every reality—a **concrete and positive content**. So by knowing the result, we know not only that a certain action preceded it, but also **what that action consisted in** and **what it was**: namely, what it had to be in order to produce this particular result.

But every concrete action—that is, every action leading to a concrete result—also necessarily has a concrete starting point. So from our knowledge of the result and of the action that produced it, we can also discover this starting point.

And since everything that exists within a dialectical being is the result of free action, insofar as we are dealing with a dialectical being we must regard the “starting point” as discoverable. The being itself is the **concrete result** from which we can reconstruct the concrete action, the “starting point,” and so on.

Let us return to the example of the **Rubicon**.

On the night when Caesar was walking along the river, at the very moment of that walk, **no one**—neither Caesar himself nor anyone else—could know what decision he was going to make.

If Caesar’s present and past had necessarily determined, or even predetermined, his future—if Caesar had “decided” to cross the Rubicon in the same way that an apple torn from a tree “decides” to fall to the ground—then there would have been no free **decision** at all.

But once the decision had been made, Caesar himself and others could know it, insofar as an action came to realize it. Above all, **we** know it.

And in knowing this decision through its result, we also know who the person was who made it. We know who Caesar himself was.

To know his decision **completely** means knowing that it was not simply an idle fantasy, a bad calculation, and so on, but a decision based on a correct assessment of the forces involved. And to know that means knowing those forces—including Caesar himself, standing at the head of the troops stationed on the banks of the Rubicon.

So in knowing the decision, we know that Caesar had come with his army as far as the river. But if he came there, this means that he had previously decided to do so.

Once again, therefore, we are dealing with the concrete result—realized through action—of a free decision. And knowing this result allows us to know the decision, what the decision presupposed, and so on.

By knowing Caesar’s present—that is, his decision to “cross the Rubicon”—we also know Caesar himself, because Caesar can be defined as **“the man who decided to cross the Rubicon.”**

As a human being, or dialectical being, Caesar walking beside the river is nothing other than the whole chain of free decisions that led him to the Rubicon—or, if one prefers, the result of that **entire** chain.<sup>225</sup>

More generally, the presence of negativity or freedom in a dialectical being prevents us from predicting the future on the basis of the present and the past. But it allows us to **reconstruct the past from the present**.

Formally, we can represent this as follows.

Let **D** stand for the present state of a given being. Dialectical analysis shows that D is the result of a free action—that is, of the effective negation of an earlier state of the being, which we will call **C**.

From the dialectical “equation”

**D = non-C**

we can determine C.

But C in turn appears as the result of a negation, which took place earlier, of a state **B** that preceded it. So the “equation”

**C = non-B**

allows us to determine B.

B in turn is understood as **non-A**, which brings us to the beginning of the whole process—or, if one prefers, to the “genesis” of the being in question.<sup>226</sup>

In other words, once a certain stage of dialectical development has been reached, it may be possible to go in any number of directions from there. But there is only **one path by which that particular stage could have been reached**.

Knowing the present stage therefore does not tell us what stages will follow. But it does allow us to know all the stages that preceded it.

Imagine the existence of a person—or of humanity—from birth up to a given moment **T** as a broken line. Let small circles represent the “free decisions” that fundamentally alter the direction of this existence.

If no free—that is, negating or creative—action occurs at moment T, then the straight segment CD will simply continue. We can therefore predict its course and “deduce” any later point, say D′.

But if a free decision occurs at moment T, then knowledge of the broken line ABCD will not allow us to know what comes next. The line may go toward E, F, G, and so on.

By contrast, knowledge of the point D—or of any point on the segment CD, say C′—allows us to reconstruct the whole broken line ABCD. This means reconstructing not only all the points along the straight segments—A′, A″, B′, C′, and so on—but also the decision points B, C, and A, since nothing beyond T can be known.

If a different decision had been made at B, for example, the line would not have gone toward C. It might instead have gone toward c, and from there no path would have led to D.<sup>227</sup>

> c E **T** D′ B A″ D B′ A′ C′ F A C G

All this is possible because human beings **make history**. They preserve their entire past within their present, even when the present “negates” that past.

Everything that led to the emergence of a given person or historical stage enters into the definition of that person or stage. If historical development had been different, its result would also have been different. Conversely, a different result would presuppose a completely different historical development.

And it is easy to see that historicity does not exclude freedom. In fact, as we already know, it necessarily presupposes it.

A person can take any road and arrive at any result. But once the road has actually been travelled, it remains forever what it was.

There is therefore nothing incompatible with freedom in the fact that the **past is fixed**. Nor is there anything incompatible with freedom in reconstructing that past from the present.

The fact that only one road leads to a particular point means only that, once a person chooses that point as a **goal**, they must necessarily take the road that leads to it.

But the choice remains **free**, since the person may always choose any point or goal at all.<sup>228</sup>

Indeed, ultimately even the choice of road is free. A person may take as their goal precisely the points through which their chosen road passes.

We can therefore say that choosing the goal necessarily determines the road, just as choosing the road necessarily determines the goal. Whichever is chosen—the road or the goal—the choice itself is free. But once the goal has been chosen, the corresponding road must be accepted; and once the road has been chosen, the corresponding goal must also be accepted.<sup>229</sup>

We must not forget, however, that neither “road” nor “goal” exists in advance as something given once and for all to humanity. Roads and goals are **freely chosen**, but they are also **created** through free decisions and actions.

Everything we have said shows that phenomenological description, because it describes dialectic, cannot be what is called an ***a priori* deduction**.

The phenomenologist cannot begin with a few basic propositions about human beings and then “derive” or “deduce” from them everything that can ideally be known about humanity—including everything we know about historical development—without any prior knowledge of that development.

The method of ***a priori* deduction** is found, for example, in geometry. Starting from a small number of Euclidean “axioms,” a geometer can “deduce” everything that can in general be said about geometrical figures that can be constructed with ruler and compass.

For example, without ever having “seen” a parabola, the geometer can construct one and list all its properties. This is what is meant by an ***a priori* deduction**: a deduction carried out before encountering the thing in question.

The phenomenologist proceeds in exactly the opposite direction.

Starting, say, with a parabola already given and fully formed, the phenomenologist would look for the “axioms” that must be accepted in order to determine all its properties and make it possible to construct it.

In this sense, Phenomenology can be regarded as an **“axiomatics” of human existence**, if we understand “axiomatics” in the sense given to the term by the great German mathematician Hilbert and his school.

**Starting from humanity as it presently exists**, Phenomenology searches for the basic, irreducible, and underivable premises without which this present state could not exist.

Once it has found them, it tries to deduce the present state from those premises, just as the geometer derives “theorems” from “axioms.”

The only difference is that the geometer can, in principle, **begin** by laying down the axioms. The phenomenologist must **begin** with a concrete historical situation that is already given.

In other words, Phenomenology deals with the problem that philosophy had been dealing with since Plato and that Kant very accurately defined as the search for the **“conditions of possibility” of experience—or of appearance**.<sup>230</sup>

**Starting from what is given** in the experience of a historical phenomenon, the phenomenologist tries to reconstruct the chain of appearances that led to what is now given.

This is possible precisely because the appearance given to the phenomenologist is **historical**: it contains within itself all the appearances that preceded it.

And precisely for this reason the answer to the problem must be unambiguous. Only one concrete dialectical path can lead to the historical phenomenon that is given.<sup>231</sup>

To discover the “conditions of possibility” of a given appearance is simply to **understand** it.

We can say that we fully understand something only when we know how it was “made”—that is, when we can reproduce it in thought.

We understand a geometrical figure or theorem only when we can “construct” it or “deduce” it from axioms.

Phenomenology similarly allows us to “construct” a given historical appearance in thought, beginning with the same “materials” and using the same “means” as the real history that actually created it.

A method that understands something by mentally reproducing its formation is called the **genetic method**. We can therefore say that the phenomenological method is “genetic.”

But we must be precise about what this means.

Phenomenology can reveal the “genesis”—the origin or development—only of something that already exists and is given to it independently of its knowledge of that genesis.

The genesis described by Phenomenology is therefore the description of the **real development of reality itself**, not merely a description of the way reality is reconstructed in or by thought.<sup>232</sup>

To summarize everything we have said about phenomenological method, we can call it a method of ***a posteriori* deduction**.

It is ***a posteriori*** because Phenomenology can speak only about something that already exists independently of it. What it describes is in some sense **given before** Phenomenology begins to speak about it.<sup>233</sup>

But it is still genuinely a **deduction**, because once Phenomenology knows an existing appearance, it can “deduce” or “construct” it: it can reproduce in thought its “genesis” or development.

Starting from a given historical or human appearance, Phenomenology can determine the number, order, and character of all the free decisions or actions that preceded and created it. It can then work backward until it reaches the first origins of the phenomenon—origins beyond which it cannot go, because they represent the indivisible minimum of humanity, the minimum conditions of historical existence, beyond which lies merely natural existence.

Once Phenomenology has determined these origins, it can then, in its exposition, “derive” or “deduce” the phenomenon from them. This can create the impression that Phenomenology is deducing the phenomenon without having known anything about it beforehand.

But as I have already said, the description of this phenomenological “deduction” is nothing other than the description, in phenomenological form, of the **real historical process** that actually produced the appearance in question.<sup>234</sup>

It follows clearly from all this that the ***a posteriori* deductive** character of Phenomenology comes not from its method, but from the distinctive character of its object.

Phenomenological description can be deductive only because the object it describes is **historical**.

At bottom, Phenomenology describes the real historical process itself, viewed in its phenomenological aspect. Its “method” therefore consists only in **selecting the material** on the basis of a knowledge of the dialectical character of that process.

Phenomenological description takes the form of a “deduction” only because, within real history itself, appearances do not merely follow one another in time. Each appearance is the **result** of all those that came before it, and it could have resulted only from those that actually preceded it, not from some different sequence of appearances.

On this basis, we can say that the phenomenologist proceeds exactly as the author of an autobiography would. In this sense, the phenomenologist uses an **“autobiographical method.”**

When someone sets out to write an autobiography, they are in some sense trying to **understand themselves** and to make themselves **understandable to others**.

To do this, they describe their “genesis.”

They begin with what they are at the moment of writing and try to explain how and why they became what they are.

They know, of course, that if they simply recall their childhood and start only from those memories, they cannot “deduce” their present from them.

But because they **know their present**, they can select from the enormous number of childhood memories those that help them—and others—understand why they became precisely the person they became rather than someone else. In particular, they can understand why they now feel the need to write an autobiography at all.

Yet when they identify the characteristic features of their childhood, they will not feel that the path of their life had already been fixed once and for all at that time.

On the contrary, they will remember moments in adolescence and early adulthood when they freely made one important decision or another—decisions that help explain why they became the person they are.

Their present life will be defined only as the **sum** of all these decisions.

And conversely, to understand their present fully, they must reconstruct **all** those decisions in memory.

But once again, they can select and interpret those decisions correctly only by beginning with an understanding of what they are **now**.

A successful autobiography—that is, a convincing one—must show its author that a person born into the environment described, and who passed through all the stages of development described, could not have become, as an adult, anything other than what the author is.

Conversely, it must convince the author that, in order to become what they are, they **necessarily** had to pass through the stages they actually passed through and had to be born into precisely the environment into which they were born.

Yet none of this should hide the fact that the author could have become completely different if even one of their free decisions had been different from the decision actually made.

And in principle, such a different decision could have been made at any moment of conscious life.

A successful autobiography must therefore reveal clearly the **“unused possibilities”** of the life it describes.

As we already know, Phenomenology can in one sense be regarded as just such an autobiography.

The difference is that its author is not trying to understand himself as a “living” person in the full concreteness of his life. He is trying to understand himself simply and specifically as the **author of this autobiography**.

He wants to grasp and show what had to happen in him and for him so that, at this particular moment, he could write this particular *Phenomenology*, describing precisely what it describes and writing it in precisely the way he writes it.

He therefore writes a *Phenomenology* with philosophy in view. That is, he ultimately wants to understand himself fully as a concrete human being: a person conditioned by a particular historical situation—or, more exactly, by the way that historical situation is given to his consciousness through the knowledge and understanding he has of it.

In other words, he understands himself as conditioned by a situation taken as an **“appearance” or “phenomenon.”**

And since this “phenomenon” also conditions the way he writes his *Phenomenology*, the *Phenomenology* itself is nothing other than a genetic description of that appearance.

After all, the author of a *Phenomenology* is “a child of his time.” We can therefore say that the historical reality which appears to **him** is also what appears, in general, to the **human beings of his age**.

Consequently, although the *Phenomenology* is his autobiography, it is also the autobiography of **humanity as a whole**.

Through the consciousness of the author of a *Phenomenology*, humanity itself is, so to speak, remembering its past and trying to understand how and why it became what it is at this particular historical moment.

Yet the “conception” of the historical present given by a Phenomenology can never be completely exhaustive.

Phenomenology is, if one likes, “autobiographical” and therefore “subjective” in the sense that it does not show what humanity’s past **really was**. It shows only how that past **appeared to humanity** in the course of its history and how it appears to humanity at the historical moment in question.

Phenomenology therefore describes the historical sequence of the ways in which human beings appear to human beings—that is, to themselves.

But because these appearances appear to a human being, and therefore to the very kind of being that carries out the historical process, the sequence of appearances reproduces the sequence of historical events themselves, both chronologically and dialectically.

We can therefore say that a Phenomenology is nothing other than a description of the **autobiographical aspect of the universal history of humanity**.

### 3. The circularity of Phenomenology

If Phenomenology can be defined as a phenomenological autobiography, we must not forget that its main purpose is not simply, or even mainly, to describe its author philosophically.

Its purpose is to **transform** its author, through that very description, from a non-philosopher into a philosopher—that is, into someone capable of writing a complete philosophical system.

Phenomenology must therefore be “true” in more than the ordinary scientific sense, according to which the meaning of its descriptions must correspond exactly to the real content of the object described.

It must also be true in the **strong** sense, because it is the necessary premise of truth in that strong sense: of definitive, complete, and exhaustive knowledge of the most concrete reality—of “perfect” knowledge, or **omniscience**.

As we already know, the philosophical system in the strict sense—that is, Cosmology and Ontology—gives a complete answer to the following question:

**What must the existing world, and the being underlying it, be like for it to be able to “appear” to human beings exactly as it actually does?**

Since the answer must be definitive and therefore exhaustive, it necessarily presupposes complete knowledge of **all appearances or phenomena**.

That is precisely the kind of knowledge Phenomenology is, in principle, supposed to provide.

Phenomenological description must therefore be not only **correct**, but also **complete**.

On the one hand, Phenomenology must give a correct—that is, exact and exhaustive—description of each individual appearance.

On the other hand, it must describe in this way **all appearances that exist**, or more precisely, all essentially distinct **types** of appearance.

In other words, the content of Phenomenology must be **true in the strong, philosophical sense**.

The knowledge of phenomena that it provides must, as people say, be **universal and necessary**.

The **universality** of Phenomenology means that **anyone** capable of understanding its content must find that content convincing. Anyone who understands it must necessarily agree with what its author says and make the author’s discourse their own.

The **necessity** of Phenomenology means that neither its author nor anyone else can alter its content in any way.

Nothing can be added to it.

Nothing can be removed from it.

And everything said in the *Phenomenology* must be said exactly as it is said.

This also means that the knowledge it offers is **definitive or perfect**—true in the strong sense of the word.

It is true both because **each individual description** is correct, exact, and exhaustive, and because it describes **everything that can in principle be described**.

In this sense, phenomenological knowledge has a philosophical character.

And since philosophical knowledge is “perfect” knowledge or **omniscience**, not only because it is knowledge **of everything** but because it includes **all true knowledge whatsoever**, it follows that knowing that philosophical knowledge is true—that it is omniscience—is itself part of philosophical knowledge.

Philosophy must **itself show**, to itself and to others, that its descriptions are “universal and necessary”—that is, true in the strong sense, or more exactly, exhaustive and all-embracing.

And insofar as Phenomenology itself has a philosophical character, it must do the same with its own descriptions.

Admittedly, its descriptions cannot be called fully exhaustive, since Phenomenology describes not the most concrete reality itself but only its **appearances**, its phenomenological aspect.

But **within that aspect**, its descriptions must be just as exact, exhaustive, and complete as a philosophical description of reality itself.

Phenomenology must therefore itself demonstrate both this exactness and completeness and the fact that its description of phenomena must be supplemented by a description of the **reality that appears**.

Only by doing this can it become what it is above all meant to be: a dialectical **introduction to philosophy**.

Once it has described **all phenomena** exactly and exhaustively, it shows, first, why the philosophical question in the strict sense must be asked—the question of the “cause” of those phenomena. And second, it gives the philosopher the means to answer that question **exhaustively**.

How, then—by what “method”—can Phenomenology show, on the one hand, that its descriptions are exact and exhaustive and, on the other, prove that the work itself is genuinely complete, that it describes **all phenomena**?

We know that, for Hegel, philosophy can prove its own truth only because, in being true, it is also **circular**.

And we already know what this circularity means: philosophy returns to its point of departure and repeats what it has already passed through.

In principle, philosophical “circularity” can begin anywhere.

What matters is that, after beginning with the description of some particular appearance—or some “element,” “moment,” or “stage” of reality—philosophy must pass **necessarily and universally** to the description of another.

And this other element is precisely determined. From A, one must necessarily and universally pass to B; one cannot pass directly to C, D, E, and so on, at least not without first passing through B.<sup>235</sup>

By moving from one description to another in this way, philosophy finally returns to the description with which it began.

Its circle then closes.

If we wish to continue, all we can do is trace the same circle again, indefinitely. Having gone from Z to A, we must once again go from A to B, then from B to C, and so on until Z; then begin again.

This circular structure genuinely guarantees the absolute truth of philosophy.

First, it shows that the description has exhausted **all possibilities**. Nothing can be **added** to what has been said, because every possible movement forward or beyond it remains inside the tightly closed circle.

Second, circularity guarantees the validity of each individual description.

To begin with, each description is **exhaustive**. If it were not, there would be no necessity to move on to another description. Only a **complete** description of an appearance can reveal its **incompleteness** and therefore the need to supplement it with a new description. So nothing can be **removed** from any given description.
