And second, the descriptions are exact. If they were not, the movement of description would, so to speak, go astray and fail to return to its starting point. So nothing in them can be **altered**.

A circular philosophy is therefore necessarily true, and a true philosophy is necessarily circular—insofar as it is clear that **only philosophy** can be true in this strong sense.

And it is easy to see that this circularity of true philosophy is nothing other than what we previously called its **dialectical character**.

If the transition from one description to another is neither accidental nor arbitrary, but “necessary and universal,” then this means that the transition is determined by the reality being described.

We must pass from **description A** to **description B** because **A itself passes into B**.

And this necessary real transition is nothing other than real dialectic in the proper sense: the dialectical process through which reality becomes what it becomes.

It is therefore just as inappropriate to speak of a philosophical **“circular method”** as it is to speak of a “dialectical” or ***a posteriori* deductive method**.

The method of philosophy is always and everywhere the same: **pure description**.

If this description takes on a dialectical character, that is only because—as we already know—the reality being described is itself dialectical.

For exactly the same reason, philosophical description also turns out to be ***a posteriori* deductive**.

Dialectical reality itself is necessarily “genetic” and, if one likes, “deductive”: it “constructs” or “deduces” itself from its “initial” state.

And for precisely the same reason, philosophical description is **circular**.

It is circular because dialectical reality itself is necessarily circular.

In one sense, every dialectical triad is circular, since synthesis preserves the thesis and therefore, in a certain way, “returns” to it.

And in the strong sense, the entire real dialectical process is circular.

So the closed circle of philosophy is nothing other than the **pure description of the closed circle of real dialectic**—that is, of the universal history of humanity.<sup>236</sup>

It is true that Phenomenology, in the sense just described, is not **fully** circular.

When it “ends”—when its descriptions reach their conclusion—it does not simply send author and reader back to the beginning. Instead, it carries them **further**, toward becoming philosophers in the strict sense: people whose task is now to describe the “causes” of the phenomena described by Phenomenology, that is, their existing and operative **conditions of possibility**.

Phenomenology examines phenomena and nothing but phenomena: the way the natural and historical world **appears to human beings**.

In other words, it presupposes the existence of human beings and excludes from its description anything that exists, in some sense, **before** humanity.

In this respect, the animal that first gave rise to **human existence**, and the natural world that necessarily provided the conditions for that animal’s life, lie outside the limits of what phenomenological description can reach.

Yet Phenomenology must in one way or another know about this animal.

And this knowledge functions for Phenomenology as an **axiom**: if not something that must be proved, then at least something that cannot be proved from within Phenomenology itself.

So when Phenomenology reaches its end and returns to this “axiomatic” starting point, it directs its author and reader toward philosophy proper, where the axiom itself must be “proved.”

Only the **system of knowledge as a whole**, therefore, is fully circular, because it includes both Phenomenology and Philosophy proper.

The complete system is genuinely closed and self-sufficient.

It contains no “axiom” or premise borrowed from outside itself.

It therefore needs no supplement from some essentially different kind of knowledge.

It derives all its own conclusions and “proves” or “deduces” all its own premises.

If some “given” serves as its starting point—a given that initially appears contingent and unprovable—then because the completed system necessarily **returns** to its starting point, that starting point becomes at the same time the system’s **end**.

The beginning therefore turns out to be the **result** of the system’s own deductions and hence a “necessary” and “demonstrated” effect.

Taken as a whole, the system therefore “proves”—that is, guarantees the truth, necessity, and universality—of **every one of its parts**.

Nothing in it is simply “accepted on faith,” and nothing remains incapable of being completely explained—that is, explained in all its consequences.<sup>237</sup>

In the **strong** sense, the individual parts of the system cannot themselves be called fully circular.

Neither Phenomenology nor Philosophy, nor the two parts of Philosophy—Ontology and Cosmology—are fully circular. Nor are the sections of Cosmology, one of which describes nature and the other humanity.

Ontology has no premises, but it produces deductions or consequences that go beyond its own limits. The other parts of the system have both premises and consequences.

Even so, all the fundamental parts of the system are “circular” in the sense that each returns to **its own starting point**.

And it is only by returning to that starting point that each passes beyond its own limits.

Thus Phenomenology, after making a **complete circuit** of phenomenological description, passes into Philosophy and finally, more specifically, into Ontology.<sup>238</sup>

How does Phenomenology achieve this circularity that guarantees its truth?

As I have already said, it does not achieve it by means of some special “circular method.”

On the contrary, it achieves it almost automatically, through the simple description of the phenomenological aspect of dialectical reality.

If we **begin correctly**, describe that beginning correctly, and then correctly describe each dialectical transformation of what is being described, the description will of itself return to its starting point.

We can even say that the choice of starting point is indifferent.

A phenomenological investigation can begin with **any phenomenon**.

If that phenomenon is not original, an analysis of its dialectical structure will reveal this and force us, before moving “forward,” to search for its dialectical “sources.”

Ultimately this search will lead us to the **true beginning** of Phenomenology.

Indeed, one could say that the phenomenologist begins his **investigation** from the **end** of Phenomenology, since in fact he begins from his own existence as a phenomenologist and searches for its dialectical premises.

But in a systematic **exposition**, Phenomenology must begin “at the beginning.”

Its starting point must therefore be the original “birth” of humanity: the first thesis, still purely natural, in which **negativity** appeared for the first time and thereby transformed that thesis into the first antithesis, which was already human.

And we will see that this “appearance” is indeed the point from which Phenomenology begins.

Viewed from its **theoretical** side, this phenomenon is called **sensation**.

Viewed from its **practical or active** side, it is called **desire**.

Starting from this beginning—from this **“desiring sensation” or “sensing desire”**—and describing all its dialectical transformations correctly, phenomenological description will, so to speak, return to it automatically.

But before explaining how this return occurs, how the description leads us back to the beginning, and what that return means, we must first pause over an essential difference between **Hegel’s Phenomenology and my own**.

For Hegel, his system was true in the strong sense.

He regarded it as the system of definitive or “perfect” knowledge—in other words, as **wisdom**.

His *Phenomenology* therefore appeared to him as definitive.

He could think this only because he believed that the real process of humanity’s historical or dialectical development—the process described in his system—had itself been completed.<sup>239</sup>

If history in the proper sense—understood as humanity’s **creative sociopolitical activity**—has ended, then there really is nothing left to do except describe retrospectively the history that has “appeared” and investigate its cosmological and ontological “causes.”

This is why, once Hegel had reached the description of his own age,<sup>240</sup> he could say that going any “further” could consist only in studying, on the one hand, the “appearances” of past history and, on the other, their “causes”—that is, in writing a *Phenomenology* and an *Encyclopaedia*, or what in my terminology would be Phenomenology and Philosophy.

Consequently, when Hegel reaches the end of the *Phenomenology* and arrives at the description of **himself**, he can show that nothing remains for him to do except write the *Phenomenology*—which he has already written.

So if one wants to move “beyond” the final stage described in the book, one must begin reading the book again from the beginning. The “next” historical or dialectical stage is precisely the writing of the *Phenomenology*, and one can know what this consists in only by reading it.

We, however, as disciples and successors of **Marx-Lenin-Stalin**, cannot regard history as already complete.

Even if we made the assumption—factually false—that socialism had been fully realized throughout the world, communism would still remain to be realized.

Creative-and-revolutionary **activity** is therefore still entirely possible, and the retrospective description of the past is by no means the only thing left to do.

In other words, Phenomenology does not end in the necessary repetition of itself. It ends instead with hypothetical remarks about humanity’s future **historical**, that is, sociopolitical development.<sup>241</sup>

My *Phenomenology*, then, is less circular than Hegel’s.

Even so, in principle, it should be just as circular.

Here is how.

When describing any “appearance” or phenomenon, we must distinguish two things.

First, there is the way the appearing reality **appears to the consciousness to which it appears**—that is, to the consciousness the author of the *Phenomenology* is describing at a particular stage.

Second, there is the way that same reality is **given to the author himself**.

Or, as Hegel puts it, we must distinguish between the way a phenomenon exists **for the consciousness itself** (*für das Bewusstsein selbst*) and the way it exists **for us** (*für uns*)—that is, for the author of the *Phenomenology*, who in Hegel’s view sees the phenomenon as it truly is, or “in itself” (*an sich*).

At the beginning of phenomenological description, the standpoint of the **consciousness being described** and the standpoint of the **consciousness doing the describing** diverge as widely as possible.

A human being reduced to the standpoint of “desiring sensation” or “sensing desire” speaks about—and describes—themselves in a completely different way from the phenomenologist.

And this very divergence shows the phenomenologist that he cannot **stop** at this sensation or desire.

There must be other phenomena—or at the very least, this sensation must appear differently to the phenomenologist himself.

In searching for these other phenomena, the phenomenologist finds one in which the divergence is already somewhat smaller, then another in which it is smaller still, and so on.

As he moves from one phenomenon to another, he observes the gradual disappearance of the difference between the consciousness being described and his own consciousness.

Of course, nothing we have just said is new.

By following the order in which the difference between **“for a consciousness”** and **“for us”** gradually disappears, the phenomenologist is simply following the path of real dialectical development. The order establishes itself.

The reason is—as we saw earlier<sup>242</sup>—that **dialectical overcoming** always involves a certain **understanding** of what has been overcome.

Only by **distinguishing** the thesis from the antithesis does a human being actually **understand** the thesis. They take a critical distance from it, see its “limits,” and therefore grasp its determinations.

And because a thesis exposed to dialectical negation is preserved within the synthesis in an “overcome” or “sublated” form, we can say that synthesis is nothing other than the thesis **made conscious or understood**.

In this sense the thesis has been “raised to a higher level,” since what is conscious in a human being is higher than what remains unconscious or only half-conscious.

This can create the impression that it is precisely the **understanding** of a given appearance that dialectically “sublates” it, raises it to a higher level, and therefore acts as the **driving force** of dialectical development.

But this is only an appearance.

It is actually **negation** that causes the understanding. Negation—negativity, the antithesis—is the true driving force of dialectic.

Still, it remains true that at every dialectical stage the consciousness to which reality appears becomes increasingly developed or complete.

Reality as it appears to that consciousness becomes progressively less different from the reality that is appearing.

And since the phenomenologist’s standpoint is, in principle, philosophical or true—since reality is supposedly **given to him as it truly is**—the dialectical process appears as a gradual convergence between the standpoints being described and the standpoint of the phenomenologist doing the describing.

Eventually, the two standpoints **coincide**.

This means that Phenomenology has reached its “normal” end and can go no further.

For this coincidence shows that, in the course of his descriptions, the phenomenologist has reached **his own standpoint**.

If he wishes to continue, he must therefore describe that standpoint itself.

In other words, he must describe the content of the phenomenologist’s consciousness **as a phenomenologist**.

But the content of that consciousness is nothing other than the **Phenomenology itself**, since the phenomenologist is its author and, as phenomenologist, nothing more than its author.

The “next” stage of Phenomenology therefore consists in repeating its entire content.

Its end thus returns once more to its beginning.

And so on, indefinitely.

Through Phenomenology, then, the phenomenologist **understands, explains, or deduces himself** as the author of the *Phenomenology*. He shows why the content of his consciousness necessarily belongs to the person he is rather than to someone else.

This is precisely what its **circularity** consists in.

Here again, however, we must emphasize the difference between Hegel’s *Phenomenology* and mine.

By understanding himself as a phenomenologist, Hegel found that he could do nothing other than write the *Phenomenology* and then move from it to the *Encyclopaedia*—that is, in our terminology, to Philosophy.

When I understand myself in the same way, by contrast, I find myself to be a **Marxist-Leninist-Stalinist**. For me, alongside the possibility of phenomenological and philosophical knowledge, there still remains the possibility—and indeed the duty—of creative-and-revolutionary sociopolitical activity: the completion of socialism and the laying of the foundations of future communism.

But **insofar as I am a phenomenologist**, I find myself in the same situation as Hegel.

Within that limit, my *Phenomenology* is just as circular as his.

Yet this limitation, without destroying the circularity, changes its meaning and importance.

For Hegel, because history had ended, the standpoint of the phenomenologist was in principle **absolute**.

Reality did not merely “appear” to a consciousness peculiar to **the phenomenologist**—that is, a consciousness characteristic of his historical age—nor was reality mediated by a form of knowledge that existed only **for him**.

Reality was supposedly **given to him as it truly is**.

The Marxist phenomenologist, by contrast, knows that even under fully realized socialism a socialist **ideology** still prevails, whereas the “true” reveals itself completely only under communism.

In other words, he knows that reality appears to **him** only in a specifically socialist form.

This means that the end of **his Phenomenology** is not the end of the **definitive Phenomenology**.

It is not the final end of the dialectical development of phenomena, or of the ways in which world and humanity appear to human beings.

The reason is simply that human beings themselves are still changing as they pass from socialism to communism.

Even so, the end of a “socialist” Phenomenology is just as necessary and just as much “in the nature of things” as the end of a “communist” Phenomenology, or of the genuinely definitive and fully true Phenomenology.

Once the phenomenologist reaches his own standpoint, he obviously cannot **go beyond it**.

He must therefore bring his phenomenological description to an end by describing that standpoint—which means, in effect, repeating **his own Phenomenology**.

In this sense, then, it remains circular.

Phenomenology is circular above all because it eventually reaches the point at which it **describes itself** and therefore begins to **repeat itself**.

In this respect, we can say that it is circular in the same way as every complete autobiography.

A genuinely **complete** autobiography should in principle end with the words:

**“I am now writing my autobiography.”**

And to understand fully what that sentence means, one must read the autobiography again.

Only then will we know exactly what the author is doing “now.”

The difference is that an ordinary, non-philosophical autobiography does not demonstrate the **necessity** of its own being written.

We learn that the author did in fact write it, but we do not see that the author **necessarily had to** write it.

Phenomenology, by contrast, shows that “now” human beings can in principle do nothing other than write a *Phenomenology*—at least if they wish to “do” something essentially **new**, something that did not already exist.

A philosophical or phenomenological autobiography—a *Phenomenology*—therefore differs from a literary autobiography through its **necessity and universality**, and hence through its **truth**.

Yet, as we have seen, all this applies only to the **definitive**, “communist” Phenomenology.

The author of a “socialist” *Phenomenology* could have chosen not to write it and done something else instead—even something essentially new—namely, begun building communism.

But if that is so, if writing a *Phenomenology* is neither “necessary nor universal,” then that *Phenomenology* is not **absolutely true**.

The guarantee provided by **this** kind of circularity is therefore insufficient.

It shows that a *Phenomenology* written by a **particular author** cannot be more complete than it already is.

But it does not guarantee that another author living in the same historical period could not go beyond that completeness.

In other words, nothing guarantees that this circularity is not merely **subjective**.

A particular author may simply have exhausted **his own capacity for understanding**, without thereby exhausting **all the objective possibilities of understanding** available at that historical moment.

So as long as the historical process itself remains unfinished—as the Phenomenology itself shows—this “subjective” circularity cannot serve as a sufficient criterion of its truth.

Fortunately, however, there is also an **objective circularity**. And this is found not only in the definitive Phenomenology, but in ours as well.

As I have already said, “sensation” is the starting point of the phenomenological description. So if the *Phenomenology* is to be circular, it must return to this same sensation when it reaches its end.

And that is exactly what happens.

The phenomenologist begins with a consciousness whose entire content consists in sensation and eventually arrives at his own consciousness. There he discovers his desire to write a *Phenomenology*. But this desire is specifically a desire to *write* it and to *publish* it as a *book* so that other people can read it.

And since a book can be read only through some form of sensation, the *Phenomenology*, at its end, sends us back to its beginning.

To understand what the book called *Phenomenology* is, we must begin by understanding the sensation through which the book “appears” to a consciousness. And that sensation must be understood in exactly the way the *Phenomenology* understands it at the beginning. For the *Phenomenology* shows how, starting from an initial sensation of actual reality, consciousness eventually produces this meaningful book.

So we must understand how sensing the physical appearance of the book leads us to understand its meaning. In other words, how does this sensation lead the reader’s consciousness to reproduce the book in the same way that the author’s consciousness “produced” it?

In both cases we begin with the same content of consciousness—the sensation of material actuality, which may include, for example, the space occupied by this book—and arrive at the same content: the meaning of the *Phenomenology*.

We therefore genuinely repeat the movement of the *Phenomenology*. In that sense, it really is circular.

At first sight, this kind of circularity may seem trivial and unconvincing. After all, almost every philosopher has published books, and that certainly does not prove that those books are true.

But we must not forget that the essential point is not simply that the *Phenomenology* happens to exist as a book. The essential point is that the *Phenomenology itself* shows why it is *necessary* for it to exist in this form.

This kind of “derivation” of the book’s material existence from its meaning appears for the *first time* in Hegel’s *Phenomenology*—and it is repeated in ours.

Earlier philosophers often *wrote* and *published* their works. But they never regarded publication as something required by philosophy itself, or believed that the truth of their philosophy depended on it.

The classical “sage,” on the contrary, is not supposed to concern himself with other people, still less with what they think of him or of his thought. He is “his own judge.” He discovers truth in solitude and knows that the truth does not depend on whether he communicates it to anyone else. If he does share it, he does so only out of compassion for human ignorance or for some other reason external to philosophy.<sup>243</sup>

Hegel, by contrast, was the first to understand that only social recognition can guarantee the “normality” and the historical relevance of thought, including philosophical thought.<sup>244</sup>

I can know that I am not insane, and that my *Phenomenology* is not simply the delirium of a madman, only because other people “recognize” it in one way or another—even if they recognize it only as something “worth discussing.”

Without this guarantee of “normality,” no kind of circularity could guarantee truth. Normality may not be enough for truth, but it remains an absolutely necessary condition of truth and of the search for it.

But circularity also presupposes social recognition in another sense.

The *Phenomenology* is circular only because it describes itself as a certain “manifestation” of its historical period. Yet the phenomenologist can know this only because his period “recognizes” his book. Only that recognition shows him that his *Phenomenology* genuinely belongs to its time, since it reveals the book as a product of “its age.” That is what allows it to count as a particular “dialectical stage.”<sup>245</sup>

So the “circularity” of the *Phenomenology* presupposes—and, so to speak, includes—its being “socially recognized.”

Only the circularity of a book *recognized* by its age guarantees genuine circularity.

But such recognition is obviously impossible unless the book is *written* and *read*. The *Phenomenology* can therefore be circular only if, when it speaks about itself, it also explains how and why it is *read* and *understood*.

And that means precisely that when it reaches its end, it returns to its beginning—to “sensation”—and begins again from there.

In other words, the *Phenomenology* is circular, and therefore true, only because it includes the idea that it *must* be socially recognized.

That is still something genuinely new, and far from trivial.<sup>246</sup>

And it is clear that this kind of circularity is no longer subjective but objective.

The first kind of circularity ultimately takes us only to the author’s *point of view*—the “for us”—from which the book was written from the very beginning and from which all its descriptions of its object are made.

In this sense, we can say that the *beginning* of the *Phenomenology* is also its *end*.

But this shows only that the *author* has exhausted all of *his own* subjective possibilities.

The second kind of circularity, by contrast, takes us back to the *object itself* described at the beginning: sensation.

In this sense, we can say that the *end* of the *Phenomenology* is also its *beginning*.

And this shows that the objective possibilities of the *object itself* have also, so to speak, been exhausted. It means not merely that this particular author can go no further, but that no one else can either.

Put briefly, the second kind of circularity guarantees the universality and necessity of the *Phenomenology*—that is, its truth.

At first sight, this may seem to contradict what I said earlier about the definitive or “communist” *Phenomenology* in relation to our present, “socialist” one.

But there is really no contradiction, for the following reason.

If the communist *Phenomenology* is the last one, then the socialist *Phenomenology* must be the next-to-last.

Admittedly, when I describe *my own Phenomenology* in this way, I am getting somewhat ahead of events. I am treating it as though it were being written *at the end* of the socialist period, when socialism has been completely realized and firmly established throughout the world.

In fact, of course, this is not yet the case.

But by accepting this fiction, we do not violate the basic principles of dialectical thought. Such an “anticipation” is legitimate if the expected development follows “the order of things” and amounts to the completion of something already given and already present in actuality.

And from Stalinist actuality, one can undoubtedly maintain that the further course of history will not consist in the emergence of some *new* social and political system *outside* the USSR. It will consist instead in the spread of the Stalinist-Soviet system across the entire planet.

My anticipation is therefore, if you like, simply an “idealization” of actuality—the kind of idealization that phenomenological description has *always* used.

By “getting ahead of myself,” I nevertheless remain within the same historical age, which already genuinely exists, and therefore within the same dialectical stage.

And understanding this age shows that it can be followed—and *immediately* followed—only by the age called “communist.”

For a dialectical understanding of a given period reveals the dialectical character of the period that must follow it. If, for example, the present stage is an antithesis, the next will be a synthesis, and so on.

As we will see later, our socialist age can be shown to be synthetic—that is, to function as a thesis in relation to the period that follows it. The next period can therefore only be its negation in the sense of a “dialectical overcoming.”

And in Marxism, the “dialectical overcoming” of socialism is called communism.<sup>247</sup>

So we must say that the socialist *Phenomenology* is the next-to-last one.

But from another point of view, we can also say that it is the “last,” and therefore “definitive.”

As we will see, socialism is the final properly *historical* synthesis.

In other words, its “dialectical overcoming” in communism also means the “overcoming” of history as such.

History—that is, the *social and political*, or if you prefer *collective*, process through which humanity develops—ends with socialism.

Society as society and the state as state reach their definitive forms there. The human collective *as such* will no longer change.

In what follows socialism—that is, in communism—*creative* development will no longer be collective but individual.

Why?

Because under socialism the individual will finally and completely become one with society in the widest sense—with humanity as a whole.

In other words, the individual’s “interests” will no longer differ from humanity’s interests.

The collective will cease to suppress the individual personality and will instead give it complete freedom to develop internally.

The dialectic will then take place within the individual person rather than within a *collective* distinct from individuals—society, “class,” or the state—as it did during properly *historical* periods.

And this also changes the character of the *Phenomenology*.

During a *historical* period, the human and natural world did not “appear” to individuals *directly*. It appeared to them primarily insofar as they were representatives of a particular class or society, or representatives of a state.

The world therefore “appeared,” so to speak, to a *collective* through an individual who was essentially the *representative* of that collective.

The phenomena described in a socialist *Phenomenology* can therefore be called *collective* “appearances” or collective phenomena.

Here the dialectical interdependence exists only between *collective* phenomena.

Under communism, by contrast, phenomena will be *individual*.

Dialectical relations will exist between *persons as such*, including between the different ways in which the natural and human worlds “appear” *to those persons*.

The specific content of a communist *Phenomenology* will therefore consist precisely in describing these *individual* phenomena and *their* dialectical development.

In other words, the socialist *Phenomenology* is “definitive” in the sense that it gives an exact and exhaustive description of *all* collective appearances—that is, all properly historical, social, and political appearances.

And it is precisely because of this objective *completeness* that it can be circular in the second sense described above.

It returns to “sensation” because sensation is the first *collective* phenomenon: it belongs to human beings in general, not merely to some single, unique individual.

And the fact that the *Phenomenology* necessarily returns to sensation shows that its “end”—that is, the *Phenomenology itself*—is nothing other than the final collective “appearance.”

It belongs not only to its author but to the whole age—to the entire socialist *collective* whose representative the author is and whose “recognition” he therefore requires.

A genuinely “definitive,” absolutely true, communist *Phenomenology* would therefore divide naturally into two basic parts.

The first would give an exhaustive description of all *collective* phenomena. The second would give an exhaustive description of all individual phenomena.

And the first part would be nothing other than our socialist *Phenomenology*.

So because the socialist *Phenomenology* would survive as a true constituent part of the final *Phenomenology*, it can itself be regarded as definitive or true: the object *proper to it* has been completely exhausted.

Of course, “wisdom” will be reached only under communism.

In other words, it is only for the “communist” author of the *Phenomenology* that actuality will cease to “appear,” from *his own* point of view, and will instead simply be “given” as it truly is.

When he says “for us,” he will genuinely be able to add: “that is, in itself.”

What *he* says about an actuality “appearing” to a consciousness he describes will no longer itself be merely a description of how that actuality “appears” to his own consciousness. It will be a description of *actuality itself*.

And from *his* point of view, the socialist phenomenologist will be seen as occupying the standpoint of a consciousness to which reality still “appears” rather than being directly “given.”

In that sense, he will be able to say that the circle of the socialist *Phenomenology* exhausts only the possibilities of its *author*, not of *actuality itself*.

But the capacities of the author of the socialist *Phenomenology* coincide with the capacities of humanity insofar as humanity belongs to history.

In other words, absolutely everything that can “appear” to human beings during *history* in the strict sense appears to this author.

So if the socialist *Phenomenology* is an “appearance,” or if you prefer an “ideology,” it is the appearance or ideology of the entire history of humanity taken as a whole.

It is an appearance or ideology that cannot be “surpassed”—at least not by continuing in the same direction.

The socialist *Phenomenology* therefore describes how History as a whole “appears” to itself.

It describes the whole of History as a “phenomenon.”

And so we can say that its author exhausts not only *his own* capacity to *understand* the object but also the *object itself* insofar as it is *his* object.

For he gives an exhaustive description of the phenomenological side of the real dialectic insofar as that dialectic is realized—and has been realized—in the completed process of humanity’s *historical*, social, and political development.

That is why this *Phenomenology* can also be circular in the second, objective sense and therefore be *objectively true*.

By exhausting *its own* object, it certainly does not exhaust the phenomenological object in general.

Its object is only the *historical* or *collective* “appearance” of actuality. Actuality can still “appear” to human beings in another way: individually.

But the future dialectic of post-historical phenomena can no longer change the past dialectic of collective historical phenomena.

Their exhaustive description—the objectively circular description found in the socialist *Phenomenology*—can therefore be regarded as unchangeable, and thus as definitive or true.<sup>248</sup>

Our *Phenomenology*, then, can be regarded as true.

And its truth is guaranteed by its circularity, and by nothing else.

What follows from the particular character of this truth?

First of all, this.

If the truth of the *Phenomenology* is guaranteed by its circularity, then only the book *as a whole* can be fully convincing.

Taken in isolation, the description of any individual stage may seem arbitrary. Only when we understand how all the stages depend on one another do we become convinced that each individual description is correct.

That is why passages from the *Phenomenology* cannot properly be criticized when they are removed from the whole.

Strictly speaking, they cannot even be *understood* outside the whole, or if the whole itself is not understood.<sup>249</sup>

For the dialectical character of an isolated element or moment becomes fully intelligible only through the place it occupies within the entire dialectical process.

To know or understand such an element means not only knowing what came before it—its “history,” its “becoming,” or its “origin”—but also knowing what comes after it, what develops out of it: its “goal,” its “tendency,” and its “result.”<sup>250</sup>

But the *whole* does not merely provide the *guarantee* that the descriptions in the *Phenomenology* are true.

The *truth itself* revealed by the *Phenomenology* exists only in this whole.

As we already know, the *Phenomenology* is nothing other than a phenomenological anthropology: a discourse or science whose object is the human being, or more precisely the way human beings “appear” to themselves.

And this discourse claims to be true.

But it is obviously not the only discourse about humanity. Throughout its history, humanity has produced a vast range of theories about itself.

Why, then, should the truth belong only to the theory put forward by the author of the *Phenomenology*?

There can be only one answer.

The theory presented in the phenomenologist’s own name is certainly not an *isolated* theory existing *alongside* or *against* all the others.

The content of the phenomenologist’s theory is nothing other than the content of the *Phenomenology itself*, which consists precisely in describing absolutely *all* the theories about humanity that have appeared throughout the entire historical development of humanity.

There is therefore no need to choose between the phenomenologist’s theory and the theories produced throughout history, because the former *contains* all the others.

And if it is true, it is true precisely because it contains *all* of them—because there is no other possible theory that could be opposed to it, and nothing can be added to it that would change it.

In other words, every theory is true insofar as it “reveals” *one* aspect of actuality.

And every theory is false only insofar as it takes itself to “reveal” actuality *as a whole*.

Actuality *as a whole* is revealed only in the totality of *all* theories.

And since the *Phenomenology* is nothing other than such a totality, it is true in the strongest sense.

Falsity is one-sidedness.

So when an isolated theory is completed by all the other theories—when its one-sidedness is destroyed—its falsity is destroyed as well, and the theory itself ceases to exist as an isolated theory.

The result of integrating all theories is one single, complete theory: an absolutely true theory, which is also the phenomenologist’s own theory.

And this complete, fully true theory is nothing other than the *Phenomenology as a whole*.

The *Phenomenology* is therefore *true* only as a *whole*—that is, as a closed circle.

In one sense, we can say that the phenomenologist “criticizes” isolated theories by completing them.

And if one wishes, one can say that he criticizes them from “his own” point of view.

But “his” point of view is nothing more than the sum of all points of view, including the very point of view he is criticizing.

So the points of view that seem to be criticized by the phenomenologist are in fact criticizing *themselves*.

Or, if you prefer, they criticize one another.

The *Phenomenology* merely records the result of this criticism as a process of self-criticism.

And the final result is the *Phenomenology itself*, in which this criticism or self-criticism is described.

But in saying this, we are clearly saying nothing new.

We are simply repeating that the phenomenologist restricts himself to a “pure description” of the real dialectical or historical process in which phenomena develop, generate their opposites while at the same time forming a unity with them, and in doing so are “dialectically overcome,” passing to an ever higher level.

The final level turns out to be the *Phenomenology itself*: the complete and exact description of the entire process of these dialectical overcomings.

In other words, the *Phenomenology* describes the process through which truth is progressively selected—the process we earlier described as the “technical” or “political” testing of “opinions” and “ideologies.”

And this description *as a whole* contains the *total* result of that testing.

It therefore contains *all* the truth and *nothing but* the truth.

Taken *as a whole*, the *Phenomenology* thus contains everything true, and in that sense it is entirely true.

But because the *Phenomenology* deals only with phenomena, the truth it contains concerns phenomena alone.

It shows only how the natural and human world “*appears*” to the human being who belongs to “history.”

To know what the world must *be* in order to “appear” in this way, we must move beyond the *Phenomenology* to Philosophy in the strict sense.

And this transition is possible only because the world’s “appearances” have been described exactly and exhaustively—that is, because the *Phenomenology* is completely and entirely *true*.

## III. The structure of Phenomenology

We have seen what the *purpose* of the *Phenomenology* is, what *object* it studies, and what *method* it uses to study that object and achieve its purpose.

So before presenting the *Phenomenology itself*, only one thing remains: to say something briefly about its *structure*.

On the one hand, we must explain why it necessarily divides into three basic parts and what is distinctive about each of them (2).

On the other hand, we must say a few words about the distinctive character of the work as a whole (3).

But since the structure of the *Phenomenology* is determined by its object, its method, and its purpose, as well as by the place it occupies within the general system of concrete knowledge, we must begin with this last question (1).

### 1. The place of Phenomenology within the system

In his *investigation*, or search for true knowledge, the philosopher begins with what is given to him “immediately”—that is, with what is given to him not as a “philosopher” but as an “ordinary” human being.

He therefore begins by clarifying and describing for himself how the natural and human world “appears” to humanity, and in particular how it appears to the people of his own age and to himself.

So he *begins* with a *Phenomenology*.

Only after he has taken into himself all these “appearances” of actuality does he move on to explaining their “cause” or their “conditions of possibility.”

Proceeding in this way, he first reaches the really existing natural-and-human world—the cosmos—and describes it in a Cosmology.

Only after completing that description does he arrive, *in the end*, at the ultimate or first “causes” of existence: *being itself*, which he describes in an Ontology.

He therefore moves from what is most “partial” and concrete—himself in his historical reality—to what is most “universal” and abstract: being as such.

But in the “systematic” or “deductive” *presentation* of knowledge that has already been *established*, the philosopher follows the opposite order.

Within the system, the *Phenomenology* should therefore occupy the third and final place, *after* Ontology and Cosmology.

Beginning with the concept of being as such and describing its structure in Ontology, the philosopher must arrive at the concept of the existence of this being in concrete actuality—that is, at the natural and human world, or Nature and Humanity.

He describes these in the two parts of his Cosmology.

He begins with the natural world and then reaches the historical development of the human world, describing the real dialectic in the second part of Cosmology.

In this way he arrives at the historical emergence of the philosophical system that describes all of this—in other words, at his own emergence.

And having reached this absolutely concrete reality, he describes it too.

But because this reality, precisely in its concreteness, “reveals” itself to itself as a “phenomenon,” this final description by the philosopher is phenomenological in character.

The *Phenomenology*, as the third and final part of the system, begins with the *fact* that the Philosopher exists and describes the concrete content of his consciousness.

That consciousness includes the understanding of *all* the ways in which the cosmos “appears” to humanity.

And the *Phenomenology* shows that such an “integral” consciousness makes it possible to give a complete answer to the question of the structure of the being that “appears” to human beings.

For being does in fact “appear” to humanity through the philosopher’s consciousness, and the Ontology with which the system begins provides the answer to that question.

In other words, when the philosopher reaches the *end* of the presentation of his system, he brings the reader back once more to its *beginning*.

In doing so, he shows that his system is true because it is circular.

From a logical point of view, there is no doubt that this third and final place given to the *Phenomenology* within the system is fully justified.

With this structure, the system is logically homogeneous.

Its development begins with what is most abstract—being in general—and moves continuously toward what is most concrete: the content of the real consciousness of a living human being, namely the consciousness of the philosopher himself.

The description of this consciousness concludes the *Phenomenology* and therefore the system as a whole.

This position of the *Phenomenology* within the system would also provide several “technical” advantages for its presentation.

*First*, it would allow us to avoid introducing into the *Phenomenology* the “axioms” we discussed earlier.

The prehuman or natural foundations of human existence—which our present *Phenomenology* can only list without being able to explain their origin or nature—would already have been described and “derived” in natural Cosmology.

A *Phenomenology* placed at the end of the system could therefore refer back to that derivation.

It would not have to ask the reader to accept anything “on faith,” that is, without proof: for example, that human beings possess an animal body inseparable from them, that they live within the natural world and interact with it, that they are finite and mortal, and so on.

*Second*, by starting from the fact—already “derived” in historical Cosmology—that the Philosopher exists, the *Phenomenology* could immediately refer to the *existence* of a distinction between the philosophical and non-philosophical points of view.

That is, it could begin from the distinction between the point of view of the consciousnesses corresponding to the “appearances” being described and the point of view of the philosopher’s or phenomenologist’s consciousness that describes them—the “for us.”

Our present *Phenomenology* uses this distinction from the *beginning* and therefore presupposes it.

But it can prove and explain the *existence* of the distinction only at the very *end*, when it describes for the first time the consciousness that has constantly stood opposite the consciousnesses being described precisely because it is the consciousness *describing* them.

In that sense, everything said in the *Phenomenology* “in the author’s own name” is itself accepted, to some extent, on faith.

It is justified only at the *end* of the *Phenomenology*—or, more exactly, only by the *Phenomenology as a whole*.

Finally, *third*, placing the *Phenomenology* at the *end* of the system would allow us to avoid all the unavoidable repetition that occurs when the system is *presented* by beginning with it.

Since everything needed to describe and understand cosmological and ontological phenomena would already be known to the reader, there would be no need to dwell on those points in the *Phenomenology*, still less to repeat things that had already been said in Ontology and Cosmology.

All of this is certainly correct.

And yet, for what we might call *pedagogical* reasons, the presentation of the system as a whole must nevertheless *begin* with the *Phenomenology*.

As we know, the *Phenomenology* describes the “appearances” of being and therefore serves as the necessary introduction to the description of being itself and of its real existence—that is, as the introduction to Ontology and Cosmology, or to Philosophy and the system in the strict sense.

The philosopher himself was able to arrive at his Cosmology and Ontology only through an investigation of phenomena as such.

The reader likewise cannot fully absorb and master the systematic presentation of Philosophy—which proceeds from Ontology to Cosmology—without first becoming familiar with the *Phenomenology*.

For pedagogical reasons, then, the presentation of the system of concrete knowledge necessarily divides into two basic parts.

The first is the introductory part called the *Phenomenology*.

The second can be called the *System of Philosophy* in the strict sense, beginning with Ontology and ending with Cosmology.

Indeed, after reading the *System of Philosophy*, one may understand perfectly well *what* the “philosophical” point of view—the “for us”—actually is: the point of view from which the *Phenomenology* is written from beginning to end.

But the *origin* of that point of view would remain completely obscure.

The “philosophical” point of view, unlike that of the “scientist” or the “ordinary person,” is characterized by distinguishing the *appearance* from the reality that “appears”—that is, from *existence*—and then distinguishing that existence from *being as such*, the being that underlies it.

But in describing being and existence, *Philosophy* does not explain how or why a human being—and in particular its author—ever arrived at this “counterintuitive” distinction and this “unusual” way of posing the problem.

Only the *Phenomenology* shows how and why a person who begins from an “ordinary” or “natural” consciousness—which does not distinguish an “appearance” from its existence or its being—eventually and necessarily arrives at the purely philosophical question of the “causes” or “conditions of possibility” of appearance *as appearance*.

That is, it shows how one arrives at the cosmological and ontological questions of existence and being as distinct from appearance.

A reader without philosophical training can therefore profitably begin the study of Philosophy proper only by first passing through the phenomenological school—that is, by beginning the study of the system with the *Phenomenology*.

But as I have already said, presenting the *Phenomenology* as the first, introductory part of the system, although pedagogically justified, necessarily creates systematic and structural difficulties and makes the presentation logically imperfect.

*First*, we are forced to begin the presentation of the *Phenomenology* with unproved “cosmological” assertions.

Within the *Phenomenology* they remain unproved all the way to the end.

Obviously, this does not help make the phenomenological presentation itself fully convincing, nor the anthropological conclusions derived from it.

*Second*, as we will see, every properly philosophical description of a given “appearance,” even when it seems to be made from the point of view of the corresponding “consciousness,” is framed by a series of arguments consisting of an introduction and a conclusion.

These arguments are made from the author’s own point of view and explain what the appearance in question is “for us” or “in itself”—that is, what it is “in truth.”

The *Phenomenology as a whole* certainly justifies these arguments, because everything said in such introductions or conclusions eventually appears within one of the consciousnesses being described.

But at first these arguments can seem artificial and unjustified—in other words, arbitrary.

They can therefore put the reader off and lead him to stop reading before reaching the end.

Yet reaching the end means becoming acquainted with the work *as a whole*, and only knowledge of that whole can justify the author’s arguments.

A reader may therefore fail to complete a *first* reading precisely because the *Phenomenology*, although itself an *Introduction* to Philosophy, becomes fully convincing only on a *second* reading.

Finally, *third*, if the system begins with the *Phenomenology*, repetition becomes unavoidable.

The author is forced to say in advance, within the *Phenomenology*, some of what he will later have to repeat in Cosmology and Ontology.

Whenever the author speaks from his own point of view, he cannot speak only about a given phenomenon *as phenomenon* without also touching on the real “existence” that “appears” in this phenomenon to the corresponding consciousness—and sometimes also the being underlying that existence.

Of course, for a reader who does not yet know the Cosmology and Ontology, these cosmological and ontological “digressions” will not feel like *repetitions*.

But the danger is not that they will bore the reader.

The real danger is that they will mislead him and cause him to misunderstand what he is reading.

This form of presentation undoubtedly creates that risk because it cannot clearly separate a properly phenomenological description from a cosmological or ontological analysis of what is being described.

The author must do everything possible to stop the reader from falling into the trap of confusing appearances as such with aspects of existence and being.

Even so, only a reader who pays complete attention to the text will be able to avoid this confusion entirely.

For all these reasons, a *Phenomenology* placed before Ontology and Cosmology almost inevitably has to be read twice.

That is an undeniable disadvantage of this mode of presentation.

Nevertheless, despite this defect, philosophical and pedagogical considerations still require us, first, to treat it as the opening or introductory part of the system as a whole and, second, to read it before studying Philosophy in the strict sense.<sup>251</sup>

### 2. The three fundamental parts of Phenomenology

The *Phenomenology* presented here as an *Introduction to Philosophy* necessarily and naturally divides into two basic parts.

But we will now see that its first part appears only because it comes before Ontology and Cosmology instead of after them.

Its third part, meanwhile, can—and must—exist only within a “socialist” *Phenomenology*. It has no place in a definitive or “communist” *Phenomenology*.

Only the second part of the *Phenomenology*, therefore, is directly and properly “phenomenological.”

That is why, in our work on this philosophical discipline, the second part is both logically central and fundamental, and also much larger than the others.

Let us now examine the distinctive character of these three basic parts of the *Phenomenology*.

I have called the first part “The Prehistorical Foundations of the Appearances of Human Existence.”<sup>252</sup>

This part brings together everything without which it would be impossible either to present or to understand the second, properly phenomenological part.

At a certain level, however, this first part really belongs to Cosmology and, in part, even to Ontology—as do, for example, some of the reflections on negativity, identity, and so on.

Nature and humanity “appear” only to a concrete, living human being.

And every concrete, living human being is in fact always historical: he exists within the general dialectical development of existence that we call the “universal history of humanity.”

“Prehistorical” existence is therefore, in a certain sense, also “prehuman,” and consequently “prephenomenological.”

The prehistorical moments or aspects may in some way be “given” to the author of a *Phenomenology* insofar as he is a philosopher.

But they do not “appear” to the concrete, non-philosophical consciousness being described—that is, to the human being actively creating History and thereby also creating himself.

More than that: the “appearances” described in the first part not only appear to no one; strictly speaking, they have never existed anywhere in the form in which they are described.

And the dialectical process said to connect these appearances has likewise never existed anywhere in this pure form.

The first part discusses desire, struggle, sensation, master, slave, and so on.

Each “appearance” is described in isolation, or as we might say, “in pure form,” as though it existed by itself independently of every other appearance.

But it is perfectly obvious that no real, concrete being has ever been or could ever be the embodiment of *desire alone*, or *perception alone*, and so on.

Likewise, no living human being has ever been or could ever be *only* a master or *only* a slave.

Desire certainly exists in human beings, as do the other elements, and therefore “appears” to them insofar as they are conscious of it and insofar as it forms part of their self-consciousness.

And there is no doubt that living human beings really can be slaves and so on.

But desire is real only in a person in whom many other things are also taking place.

So if desire “appears” to a person, it does not appear to someone who is realizing *nothing but desire*. It appears to a concrete, living human being in whom other aspects and dimensions of human existence are also being realized and to whom they also “appear.”

The same is true, for example, of a real slave.

He is never *only* a slave. He also possesses characteristics belonging to the “human kind,” characteristics found in masters and citizens as well.

If he appears to himself and to others as a slave, he never appears as a slave in “pure form.”

He appears as “above all a slave,” or “primarily a slave,” and so on.

The first part describes six basic aspects or dimensions of human existence, grouped in pairs:

desire and sensation,

struggle and sensory perception,

work and rational reflection.

Every real human being can be said to realize all these aspects or dimensions in himself—or more exactly *through* himself—and to realize them simultaneously.

There are, of course, *moments* when a person is nothing but desire, or nothing but reflection, and so on.

But even then all the other elements remain present “latently.”

In any case, neither in the life of an individual person nor, *a fortiori*, within a given historical *period* can there be even a short stretch of time in which one of the “appearances” described in this first part is entirely absent.

Human beings enter the historical arena—that is, they begin to exist genuinely as human beings—only when they possess *all six* of these fundamental elements of human existence.

That is why the “appearances” described in the first part should be called “*prehistorical*.”

Within History, they are not realized separately, one after another, but all at once.

Historical humanity is therefore always the sum or integration of these appearances, though it is also something more.

Taken together, they form, so to speak, the starting point of the historical process without themselves belonging to that process.

It would actually be more accurate to speak of “pretemporal” elements of human existence, elements which, insofar as they are real, are nevertheless always realized *in time*.

This wording emphasizes two things.

First, the order in which these elements are described does not correspond to a temporal succession, for the simple reason that they scarcely exist separately in reality.

One therefore cannot genuinely *precede* another.

Either they all *coexist* at every moment of time, or they are entirely absent—where human beings do not yet exist.

Second, describing them as pretemporal makes clear that nothing really exists in time that is characterized by desire and sensation *alone*, or by struggle and perception alone, or by work and reflection alone.

What actually exists are concrete people who desire and sense some particular thing, who struggle for particular goals and perceive particular objects, who work at specific tasks and think about definite problems.

There are no really existing “pure forms” of desire and the rest.

There are only particular things that are desired, sensed, and so on: concrete “contents” that make up the whole existence of the historical human being.

But this concrete, living, historical human being—who realizes definite *contents* of desire, sensation, and so on in and through his life—will appear only in the second part of the *Phenomenology*.

We can also say that the elements or foundations of human existence described in the first part are the “conditions of possibility” of that existence.

And because these *conditions* or *premises* lie, so to speak, *outside* human existence or *before* it, we can say that they do *not* exist.

The absence of even one of these six moments would make human existence impossible.

There is no human being, and there can be none, without desire, sensation, and the rest.

But neither desire nor sensation exists “by itself,” whether in a human being or in anything else that really exists.

Even taken together, these elements never exist apart from some concrete content determined—or at least capable of being determined—by a historical situation, meaning one of the dialectical stages described in the second part.

Put briefly, the first part describes “abstractions” which, in the form in which they are described, exist only in the phenomenologist’s consciousness.

Desire really exists in every concrete human being, as do the other elements.

But in no one does desire exist in isolation and without a definite content.

Still, because desire, sensation, and the rest really do exist as *phenomena* within concrete historical human beings, the act of “isolating” and “formalizing” them can itself have a phenomenological character.

So although the “appearances” described in the first part are *abstract*, they are nevertheless abstract *appearances* or abstract phenomena.

They are the constituent elements of every real appearance of human beings to human beings.

They have been artificially isolated and stripped of their concrete content.

As such, they never exist within a concrete consciousness.

But no real “appearance” would be possible as an appearance without them.

And insofar as these abstract “appearances” are still appearances—that is, appearances *to human beings*—their character is not natural but human, and therefore dialectical.

The order in which they are described is therefore not arbitrary.

It is determined by the dialectical relations among them.

But the first part does more than describe these abstract elements or moments of all real human existence—that is, all historical human existence.

It also provides an abstract and formal description of the basic dialectical pattern of that existence.

As we will see, this pattern is defined by three terms:

“master,” “slave,” and “citizen.”

What was said about the six aspects or moments can also be said of these three basic stages.

They too are “prehistorical” in the sense that every real historical human being is already, in one way or another, a “citizen.”

A real slave or master therefore exists only as a citizen considered under the actual aspect of slavery or mastery.

A slave who exists *only* as a slave and appears to himself and others *only* as a slave is just as much an abstraction as “pure” desire.

Every real servile or other form of existence therefore has a concrete *content*, whereas the first part describes only the *pure forms* of master, slave, citizen, and so on.

The master, slave, and citizen described in the first part have never existed anywhere in pure form.

But every real form of existence always appears either as that of a “master,” or a “slave,” or a “citizen,” in the sense that it is dominated and determined primarily by the characteristics of the master, slave, or citizen described in the first part.

We can therefore say that the “abstract” slave, master, and citizen of the first part exist nowhere as such, because no actually existing human being ever embodies only one of these fundamental categories.

Furthermore, as we will see, master, slave, and citizen form a dialectical triad: thesis, antithesis, and synthesis.

Once again, although this triad is nowhere realized in time in “pure form”—so that we cannot say, for example, that the master literally exists *before* the slave—every genuinely historical dialectical process develops according to this pattern.

A stage characterized by the “master” is “negated” in a stage of the “servile” type and is then “dialectically overcome” in a synthetic stage of a “civic” character.

These different formal modes of existence and ways of understanding the world—the master’s, the slave’s, and the citizen’s, as described in the first part—appear again and again throughout humanity’s historical development.

Each time, however, they are filled with new concrete content.

And although we can fully understand what a “master” and so on actually is only from the second part, it would be impossible to identify and understand *all* the concrete realizations of these forms without first knowing the abstract pattern given in the first part.

This dialectical pattern, because it is the pattern of the dialectical development of *phenomena*, is itself dialectical in character.

That is why even the first part of the *Phenomenology* can be called phenomenology: it concerns the “appearances” of nature and humanity to human beings.

But it is almost impossible to speak about these phenomenological *abstractions* without at the same time speaking about their cosmological and sometimes ontological counterparts.

The danger of confusing the phenomenological “level” with the cosmological and ontological levels is therefore especially great in this first part of the *Phenomenology*.

The second part—the properly phenomenological part—will describe the phenomenological side of humanity’s historical existence, so to speak, “from Antiquity to the present.”

Here the phenomenologist is no longer dealing with abstractions but with the most concrete human reality possible: historical actuality—or, more exactly, the history of each way in which the natural and human world “appears” to human beings.

Because of this, we can say that the order of the description generally follows the chronological order in which the “appearances” themselves emerged. But the two do not coincide completely, for a reason we have already mentioned: the “thesis” often takes its final form only after the “antithesis” has already appeared. In other words, the thesis being *described* may actually be later in time than the antithesis being described, and so on. Broadly speaking, everything we have already said about the *Phenomenology* as a whole applies to this second part, because this second part is precisely the *Phenomenology* in the strict sense of the word. We still have to discuss some of its particular structural features.

But first we need to say a few words about the third and final part of the *Phenomenology*, entitled “The Post-Historical Existence of Human Beings.”

This part will deal with communism—that is, with the future. And insofar as it remains phenomenological, it will deal with the way this future *appears* to the human being of the present: namely, to the socialist.

We know, however, that the historical future is “negative,” or free, and therefore unpredictable. This third part will consequently have a “hypothetical” character. The future it describes as an “appearance” may never become present reality—that is, may never become “authentic”—and may remain forever only a “project” for humanity. The most the *Phenomenology* can do here is show that this project is not “utopian”: that it has real roots in an already existing historical reality, or more precisely in the way that reality *appears* to the actually existing human being of the present.

The *Phenomenology* can also show that communism will appear as an antithesis to the entire historical process described in the second part, and that it will therefore be a *non-historical* “appearance” of nature and humanity to human beings. But the phenomenologist can hardly go beyond this purely negative definition. He cannot say anything positive about future “communist” phenomena.

So if this entire third part belongs to the *Phenomenology* in the strict sense, it does so only in order to show that the Phenomenology is not final. In other words, the socialist end of History does not yet mean, strictly speaking, either the end of human existence as such or the completion of the dialectic itself. And since all the phenomena known to us have a historical—that is, sociopolitical or *collective*—character, we can say nothing positive about communist phenomena, which will necessarily have an *individual* character.

We can therefore know that, if a final “communist” *Phenomenology* is ever written, it will contain two main sections. The first will contain our socialist or historical *Phenomenology*—though obviously without its third part. The second will replace that third part with a complete description of all the “appearances” of the communist world.

But we cannot know what that section will contain. That is the “secret of the future.”

### 3. The structural features of Phenomenology

We still have to discuss some of the structural features of the *Phenomenology*, especially those of its second and central part. First, we need to look at the characteristic phenomenological omissions and repetitions. Then we will consider the way the exposition divides into two parallel sections, one describing the “real” and the other the “ideal” aspects of historical “appearances.”

We have already had occasion to discuss the *omissions* and *shortcuts* that are so striking in the *Phenomenology*. Its second part will describe the phenomenological aspect of the dialectical development of humanity as a whole—in short, universal history “from Antiquity to the present day.” Obviously, a relatively short book must leave out the overwhelming majority of historical facts. In this respect, the *Phenomenology* is no different from a good old-fashioned history course. Like the historian, the phenomenologist discusses only what seems especially important and decisive in the *process* of historical development and, in some sense, in the overall picture he forms of that development.

Even so, the *Phenomenology* will seem much more fragmentary to the reader than an ordinary historical account of roughly the same length. More importantly, the phenomenologist selects his historical material in a fundamentally different way from the ordinary historian.

The reason is that the historian and the phenomenologist have different aims—or, if you prefer, different subjects and objects of study. I mean here the non-Marxist historian: the “scholar” who is not also a philosopher.

On the one hand, because the phenomenologist is a philosopher, he deals with *concrete* historical reality and therefore understands it as *dialectical*. On the other hand, because he is a phenomenologist, he is interested exclusively in the *phenomenological* side of that dialectic.

The *Phenomenology* therefore does not describe the *chronological* sequence of historical “events” in general. It describes the *dialectical* sequence of theses, antitheses, and syntheses, selecting only those that seem essential to the movement of dialectical development.

And however long a thesis, antithesis, or synthesis lasts, however many “historical events” it contains, the phenomenologist treats each of them as a single whole, a single “appearance,” and describes its characteristic features *as a whole*.

This is why the chronological “jumps” in the *Phenomenology* are usually much larger than the corresponding gaps in a scholarly history. But the *Phenomenology* does not describe each thesis, antithesis, or synthesis as it really is—that is, as Cosmology or Marxist History would describe it. It describes it only as an *appearance* or *phenomenon*.

In other words, it does not describe the real structure that constitutes the thesis, antithesis, and so on of a particular historical period. It describes the way that period “appears” to the corresponding “consciousness”: the way it is “reflected” in the self-consciousness of the people who live through it.

Naturally, the phenomenologist will choose the fullest and clearest possible “reflection” of a given period. But complete understanding of an age does not necessarily arise at the moment when that age first appears. It may emerge only after the age itself has definitively “died.” As a result, the phenomenologist’s selection can be extremely uneven in chronological terms. Sometimes only a few years separate the “appearances” he describes; sometimes whole centuries or even millennia lie between them.

The phenomenologist therefore seems to “jump” from thesis to antithesis, and then onward again, without describing—as the historian does—the *continuous and unbroken* chain of events that actually connects the phenomena in question.

Indeed, strictly speaking, he does not describe historical “events” at all. What he describes are not events in the proper sense, but only their “reflections”—or, more precisely, the reflections of all the events that together make up a particular dialectical stage.

Reading the *Phenomenology* therefore assumes that the reader already knows the general course of real History and the main “historical events” that compose it.

But the “reflections” of events in consciousness also have a “history” of their own, and anyone reading the *Phenomenology* will find it useful to know at least its broad outlines. For, as I have already said, here too the phenomenologist jumps from one complete and vivid—or, as we say, “adequate”—reflection to another, without describing the historical process through which one reflection developed into the next.

To give a preliminary idea of what the *Phenomenology* “contains,” and of what it selects and describes, I will quote a few pages from the “Preface” to Hegel’s *Phenomenology*.<sup>253</sup>

> It is not difficult to see, Hegel writes (p. 15 ff.), that our time is a time in which a new age is being born. Humanity<sup>254</sup> has broken with the old world in which it has until now existed and imagined itself. It is preparing to consign that world to the past and is transforming it through work.
>
> Human beings, of course, are never at rest but are always moving forward. Yet just as an infant, after a long period of silent nourishment in the womb, suddenly interrupts the gradual and merely quantitative process of growth with its first breath—a qualitative leap that marks its birth—so humanity, as it forms itself,<sup>255</sup> slowly and silently matures toward a new shape [*Gestalt*].
>
> One by one, it loosens the pieces of the structure that made up its previous *world*, so that at first only isolated symptoms reveal that the old world has begun to totter. The frivolity and boredom that spread through what still survives, together with the vague anticipation of something unknown, are the first signs that something different is coming.
>
> This gradual disintegration, which does not yet alter the overall appearance of the whole, is suddenly interrupted by sunrise. Like a flash of lightning, it reveals at once the appearance [*Gebild*] of a new world.
>
> But this new world is no more fully real at first than a child is fully developed at birth. It is essential not to lose sight of this. Its first appearance is only its immediacy, or its abstract and schematic concept.
>
> Just as a building is not finished when only its foundations have been laid, the concept of the whole that has now been reached is not yet the whole itself. If we want to see an oak in the full strength of its trunk, the spread of its branches, and the mass of its leaves, we are not satisfied if we are shown an acorn instead.
>
> The same is true of science—that is, the complete and concrete understanding of a human world. Science is not finished at the moment that world begins.
>
> The beginning of the new human being is the product of a long revolutionary transformation [*Umwälzung*] of many different cultural forms, the result of a winding path repeatedly travelled and of repeated struggle and effort.
>
> This beginning is the whole that has returned into itself from both its succession and its extension. It is the *simple*, that is, abstract, *concept* of the whole that has come into being [*gewordene*].
>
> The real actuality of this simple whole consists in the fact that the old forms [*Gestaltungen*], which have now become superseded moments or elements of a new whole, develop and take shape once again—but now within their new medium [*Elemente*] and within the meaning that has itself come into being.[^E056]

This new “development” of old forms within a new consciousness—forms already superseded or dialectically overcome and preserved—is nothing other than the *understanding* of a particular age, or the understanding of its “appearance”: the understanding of the age itself as a *phenomenon*.

Hegel calls this fully developed self-understanding of an age its “science.” By this he means the knowledge that is “perfect” *for its own time*: the knowledge through which a particular age distinguishes itself from every other age, and through which it finally becomes fully conscious of itself—that is, genuinely human or historical, and therefore dialectical.

We can say that the *Phenomenology* describes only “sciences” of this kind. Or, to put it differently, it describes only the adequate self-understanding of historical ages, each corresponding to one of the fundamental theses, antitheses, or syntheses of the real dialectic.

It says nothing about the collapse of the old world in question, or about the preparation of the new world that follows it. Nor does it discuss the sudden revolutionary “birth” of that new world. It remains silent about the development of the new world itself, just as it remains silent about the different ways in which that world “appears” to the people living within it.

What it describes is only the “science” that this world eventually creates for itself. Such a science usually appears near the end of the world’s development, once that world has taken on its full form and become fully conscious of that form.

Then the *Phenomenology* jumps from one such “science” to another, leaving out everything that “happened” between them as well as everything that “happened” while each of them was coming into being.

But besides this phenomenologically justified fragmentation, there is another kind of omission that may seem even more outrageous to the reader—and to the critic.

The *Phenomenology* confines itself to “European” humanity and simply ignores the history of India, China, America, and so on. Strictly speaking, the phenomenologist studies only one line of historical development: a line traced by a single continuous historical *tradition*, or “memory” of the past. He says nothing about *parallel* processes that have no historical relation to one another—that is, processes that “know nothing” of one another.

This approach is perfectly justified insofar as the *Phenomenology* is the autobiography of its author and of his age. The phenomenologist is looking for his own “ancestors,” for the historical roots of his own age—for everything that is in some way present in himself and in that age, either as consciously remembered history or as an unconscious historical precondition.

From this point of view, a historical phenomenon such as pre-Columbian America naturally cannot concern him.

But insofar as the *Phenomenology* is also an anthropology—that is, a science of human beings in general—this exclusion can be justified only if *all* the possibilities of human existence have in fact been realized within “European” history, so that everything outside it is merely a *repetition* of something already found within it.

The Hegelian-Marxist philosophy of History takes precisely this view.

The dialectic described by Hegel is, in fact, only the dialectic of “European” humanity, and yet it is presented as the dialectic in general.
