Epicurus, for example, accepted a “God” or “gods” of this kind. He was also someone who correctly affirmed and emphasized human finitude, and on that basis denied any interaction between “God” and human beings.

But people with a religious temperament have always understood very clearly that such “theism” is in practice **atheism**.

The only “God” that interests us is one capable of affecting us.

A divinity that takes no interest whatever in us does not exist **for us**.

This “anthropological” or “moral” atheism therefore follows necessarily from the finitude of human existence.

**205)** There are so many different “gods” that it is difficult to find a definition common to all of them.

But all undoubtedly share the character of being **“beyond”** the world—of **transcendence**.

And conversely, the more “transcendent” a divinity is, the more “divine” it is.

Rudolf Otto, in *Das Heilige*, described this “beyond” well as the **“wholly other”** in relation to the world.

**206)** Of course, we can know what dialectic is **only on the basis of these claims about human beings**.

**208)** Spinoza adds that if the falling stone could speak, it would claim that it was falling “freely.”

But he forgets that the stone **does not speak**.

And he never explains why human beings speak whereas stones do not.

Human beings possess self-consciousness and therefore speech only because they are free—that is, **antithetical**—whereas the stone is not.

By denying human freedom, Spinoza is therefore unable, from within his own position, to explain one of the fundamental qualities of humanity: **reason or discourse**, *logos*.

Spinoza failed to recognize negativity in human beings, and this is the fundamental defect of his philosophy.

His criticism of the traditional understanding of freedom as **freedom of choice**, however, is entirely correct.

**209)** As we will see, this does not mean that one should **always negate everything and everyone**.

That is the mistake made by all kinds of “anarchists,” “nihilists,” and “Trotskyists.” They want to stop the dialectic at the antithesis, forgetting that the antithesis does not **exist** without and outside a synthesis.

Such “ultra-revolutionary” behaviour always leads to disaster, because a “pure” antithesis—that is, pure negativity—is equivalent to nothingness.

What one must, and can, negate is a **thesis**: a historical actuality that is already “dead,” an already “old” regime.

But as long as an actuality is still alive—meaning that it is still “making” or “creating” itself, and therefore remains revolutionary—it must be actively affirmed.

To negate it is merely to return to the thesis, which means **counter-revolution**.

That our Soviet actuality is still revolutionary in precisely this sense—that it remains in a period of creative “becoming”—is obvious to everyone, or at least ought to be.

**210)** Hegel plays on the word *Erinnerung*, “memory” or “recollection,” which can also be read, if one wishes, as *Er-innerung*: “internalization” or “bringing inward.”

**211)** In a certain sense, the whole of the *Phenomenology* is nothing other than a “recollection”—*Erinnerung* and *Er-innerung*.

By knowing history in its phenomenological aspect, the author takes it into himself, absorbs it into his consciousness, and thereby makes that consciousness “total,” meaning capable of omniscience.

**212)** In this sense, one could say, for example, that Nicholas II—or Louis XVI—was **thetic**; Lenin—or Robespierre—was **antithetic**; while Stalin—or Napoleon—is **synthetic**.

**213)** Bourgeois and “vulgar” materialism says, in Büchner’s words, that “a human being **is what he eats**.”

Hegel, and after him Marx, instead proclaim, in accordance with their conception, that a human being **is what he does**.

Here “does” must be understood in the strong sense: what a human being **creates** through work and struggle by **negating what already exists**.

**214)** Mathematically, this is explained by the fact that all “laws of nature” are “analytic functions.”

At least, that is the position of classical physics.

It can be shown that the “statistical indeterminism” of quantum mechanics changes nothing essential here.

But this would take us too far.

**215)** Biology has, in any case, so far always dealt with **continuous** phenomena rather than with their “differential rupture.”

And even if we assume that physics can completely explain life, a cat will still remain a **cat** despite the physical explanation.

When we speak of a cat **as a cat**, rather than as a complex of electrons and so on, we are speaking of something that occupies a certain **interval of time**.

That means the cat necessarily includes a **past**. It has to be studied “from birth to death.”

**216)** The egg’s outward appearance—that is, its “present”—will not help us here. Nor will its biological or chemical analysis.

We know that an egg with this biochemical structure came from a **hen** only because we already know that eggs of this kind are laid only by hens.

In other words, we understand both the present and the future from the past, and **only from the past**.

**217)** There were, of course, real or “material” causes—above all economic ones—that brought the Empire into existence.

But we are not now discussing the **real or objective causes** of historical events.

We are discussing why a particular event **is regarded as historical**.

If one prefers, I am speaking about the historical **phenomenon**, not the historical **fact**.

I want to show why the “Rubicon” made such an extraordinary impression on people that they remembered this particular night and still speak today of “crossing the Rubicon.”

Whether Caesar’s night at the Rubicon was itself genuinely “historical” or partly legendary makes no difference to me here.

**218)** The time in which “dreams,” “utopias,” and similar things exist is characterized by the future falling directly into the present **without passing through the past**.

In other words, it ignores the **given circumstances** inherited from the past.

In the dialectical time of real historical action, by contrast, the future enters the present **through the past**, as we will now see.

The past therefore serves as an **intermediary** between future and present.

The present is thus “mediated,” and for that reason dialectical or historical—that is, human in the strong sense of the word.

**219)** It is not only the proletarian who sacrifices private interests for the interests of his **class** and his **class state**.

The bourgeois does the same thing: he pays taxes, takes part in wars, and spends money on propaganda.

The difference is that, within the bourgeois class, private interests are treated as ends in themselves, so long as they do not conflict with the interests of the class as a whole.

The proletarian, by contrast, ultimately sacrifices even his **proletarian** interests in order to establish a **classless society**.

**220)** Bourgeois thinkers love to chatter about “individuality” and “personality.” And because they neither know nor understand Marxism, they very often even try to set their “individualism” against Marx’s doctrine. Yet they fail to understand what Hegel and Marx had already understood: as long as classes and nation-states exist, the “person” will always be degraded, and “individuality” will remain little more than the empty talk of “individualists.” It is therefore absurd to be an “individualist” without also being a Marxist—that is, without striving for a worldwide socialist revolution that will “liberate” individuals by destroying classes and the social barriers between them.

**221)** I take this claim—which is, in any case, absolutely indisputable—“on trust,” without proof. Proving it, if that is even possible, is a task for Cosmology, and perhaps for Ontology. Phenomenology, by contrast, insofar as it is *anthropology*, “proves” only what concerns human beings *as human beings*. The “physical” death of a human being is caused by biological, and therefore natural, processes. Phenomenology does not discuss these. It simply accepts them as “axioms” that do not need to be proved *within* its own field. Phenomenology will, however, discuss “free” death—for example, suicide and the conscious “risk” of one’s life. For our present purposes, though, it is enough to accept that human beings are finite in general: that their *bodies* are mortal and that they cannot free themselves from them.

**222)** In the time of Philo and Plotinus, theologians generally held that *infinite* being (“God”) could not exist in more than one instance. If this is correct, then immortal persons would not merely lack individual differences: there could not even be a plurality of them. There would be only one “human being”—namely, precisely that “God” spoken of by Jewish and Christian theologians. But since I am not certain that this “monophysical” argument is actually sound, I preferred not to use it in the main text.

**223)** From the Hegelian-Marxist point of view, human history comes to an end. In other words, humanity eventually *exhausts* its historical possibilities. At first sight, this seems to imply that a human being can no longer be a person, or be free.

This is precisely what bourgeois “liberals” and “individualists” accuse Hegel and Marx of. They insist that the historical process must be limitless—and therefore that no true knowledge of it can ever be possible, a point that matters greatly to them.

But this argument rests on a misunderstanding.

First, the historical process does not *repeat itself*. It ends, once and for all, with communism. In this sense, historical humanity taken as a whole can itself be called an “individual.”

Second, history does not exhaust *all* human possibilities. On the contrary, Marx speaks of a “leap from the realm of necessity into the realm of freedom,” a leap that occurs at the end of history. Once human beings have exhausted their *historical* possibilities—that is, their social and political possibilities—they still possess infinitely many “personal” or “individual” possibilities, which they will in fact realize under communism.

And if humanity should one day perish—for example, because the Sun dies—it will perish without having exhausted all of its possibilities. This is why some people speak of moving to another planet, and so on.

Third, Marx—and Marx alone—understands that historicity, precisely because its *possibilities are limited*, restricts human freedom and individuality. Bourgeois “individualists” therefore have nothing to teach him on this point.

**224)** See above, pp. 292–309.

**225)** Of course, “free decisions” do not make up the whole of a person’s life. On the contrary, they are extraordinarily rare, and sometimes entirely absent.

But if someone never “makes a decision,” then, if you like, he is not really a “human being” in the relevant sense. In any case, he remains purely “thetic,” and his future can be predicted, because he is nothing more than the result of what is already present in him. Nothing essentially new will then arise.

Conversely, wherever something genuinely new does arise, it cannot be predicted. But once we know what that new thing is, we can deduce *everything* that came before it.

**226)** Since human beings are always historical, A must either be the simple continuation of some state Y—that is, tradition—or its negation. So we have either A = Y or A = non-Y.

In either case, we can go back beyond A. Y was itself once the negation of X, and so on. The chain therefore always leads back to the “first human being,” which means to the first appearance of the dialectical entity as such, and thus ultimately to its non-dialectical origins.

**227)** A circle—and therefore also a break—can occur at any point on the line. In general, it cannot be located chronologically. We can determine how many decisions there were and what they were, but we cannot determine how long the intervals between two decisions lasted, even though there were always such intervals.

In this sense, one might say that human beings are always free, since refusing to change can itself be a free acceptance of what is given.

Strictly speaking, however, this is not correct. Merely continuing what already exists cannot be called “free” in the strongest sense.

If one prefers, we can distinguish two kinds of freedom. The first is the free decision whether or not to be “free”—that is, the choice between negating what is given and accepting it. The second is the actual negation of what is given.

**228)** Except, of course, by choosing points that lie along the path already travelled.

Human historicity rules out literally “repeating the path already travelled.” Even if a human being—or humanity—returned to a state that had existed before, the new state would still differ from the first because it would include the *memory* of the first, and that memory is not identical with the first state itself.

Bergson rightly observed that although the ball on a roulette wheel may keep repeating *one and the same* movement, the same is not true of a person walking around a table. Each circuit places that person in a *new* situation. The first time, he knows he is doing it for the first time. The second time, he knows he has already done it once, and so on.

**229)** To desire an end while rejecting the means—to choose a destination while refusing to travel along the only road that leads to it—is the defining feature of “utopia” and, ultimately, of “madness.”

This will be discussed in the *Phenomenology* itself.[^E065]

**230)** In Plato and Kant, and more generally in philosophy in the strict sense—that is, in Cosmology and Ontology—the question takes the following form:

“How must the existing world, and Being itself, be constituted for the world to be able to ‘appear’ to human beings in experience exactly as it actually appears?”

With regard to humanity and history in particular, philosophy—that is, Cosmology—asks what human beings must be, and what their history must be like, for them to “appear” as they do at a given historical moment.

Phenomenology, by contrast, never goes beyond the limits of these “appearances.” It asks instead:

“How must the world, humanity, and history have appeared to human beings in the past for them finally to ‘appear’ as they do now?”

But these appearances are just as human as human beings themselves. The law governing their relation to one another is therefore the same law that governs actual history: it is dialectical.

**231)** In the natural world—that is, in the non-dialectical and non-historical world—an effect never points uniquely back to one cause. If we know the cause, we know the effect; but the reverse is not true.

For example, if we establish that it is raining, or that it has rained, we know that the road will be wet. But if the road is wet, that does not prove it rained. Someone may have sprayed it with water, and so on.

**232)** Even in geometry, things do not always work in the same way. When we prove that a given figure is a parabola, we also “deduce” it from axioms, since we are, in a sense, describing its genesis. But if we want to “construct” that parabola, we have to proceed in a completely different way.

Its “geometrical genesis” therefore does not coincide with its “logical genesis.”

**233)** The same applies to the communism of the future.

Phenomenology can certainly say certain things about it as a *possible* historical appearance. But it cannot say with certainty that communism will actually be realized. Its realization depends on free action—that is, on a revolutionary struggle that cannot be predicted.

Just as we cannot predict the activity that consciously aims at communism, neither can we predict the exact character of its result: communist society itself.

In this sense Marx speaks of a “*leap* from the realm of necessity into the realm of freedom,” emphasizing that until this leap has actually taken place, there is very little we can say about what lies beyond it.

A “scientific” historical prediction can deal only with the thetic elements of history: the development, “in the normal course of things,” of something that already exists in an embryonic form.

Revolutionary change itself, however, cannot be predicted. Once a revolution has begun, we may be able to predict its course—that is, the way it develops—because this development also proceeds “thetically.” But we cannot predict the original emergence of the revolutionary break itself.

**234)** Here we encounter the “logical circle” once again. See p. 234 ff.

We can fully understand the past only by understanding the present. But we cannot fully understand the present without understanding the past.

The phenomenologist’s method—the method that makes it possible to write a *Phenomenology*—therefore consists, if you like, in moving repeatedly from the present back to the past and from the past forward to the present, gradually clarifying each by interpreting it through the other.

Within the *Phenomenology* itself, however, the method amounts to a straightforward description of the historical process once that process has been understood in a certain way.

As the work proceeds, this “understanding” of the process makes it possible to select the appropriate material, and also to schematize and idealize what has been selected.

**235)** This “deduction” is, of course, *a posteriori*. See above, p. 408 ff.

**236)** What has just been said implies that only true *philosophy* can be circular. Science cannot.

Only *human* existence is dialectical, together with what is contained within it—in particular, the knowledge that *human beings* have of the world.

But science deliberately “abstracts” from the fact that all knowledge is *human*. When science speaks about the world, it excludes the human being to whom that world is “given”—that is, the human being to whom it “appears.”

The object of science is therefore *not* dialectical. And for the same reason, science—even “true” science—is *not* circular.

**237)** This is where the essential difference between philosophy and science lies.

Science always has “axioms,” without which it could not exist. But it cannot “prove” those axioms—that is, it cannot demonstrate their “universality and necessity.”

**238)** We can picture the system as a circle made up of circles.

Ontology completes the full circle of ontological description and returns to its starting point. From there, the next step leads into the cosmological description of nature.

This description is not circular but linear, because nature is not dialectical. It leads instead to the emergence of the human being.

From that point, the cosmological description of humanity traces another complete circle. When it returns to its starting point, it passes into Phenomenology.

Phenomenology then completes its own circle and passes back into Ontology, and so on.

**239)** Hegel’s error cannot be used as an argument against the criterion of circularity.

First, this is because Hegel’s system is not in fact circular; it only *appears* to be. Second, his mistake is less significant than it first seems.

He simply attributed to Napoleon’s Empire what in reality applies only to an International Union of Soviet Republics.

In other words, his mistake was merely chronological—or, put differently, he failed to identify exactly *what* had happened in 1806. In a certain sense, he anticipated the future. But what he anticipated was not itself mistaken.

This is why, in my own presentation of the *Phenomenology*, I pass over the French Revolution and Napoleon. The “appearance” Hegel had in mind exists in a much more complete form and is expressed far more clearly today.

Everything essential that has happened between 1806 and our own time is already present in Hegel’s *Phenomenology*, including, in particular, fascist “racism.” In this sense, Hegel was right to speak of the circularity of his *Phenomenology*.

I too am “anticipating” when I treat the worldwide socialist revolution as though it had already been accomplished. But there is a very good chance that this anticipation will prove correct, whereas the construction of a worldwide classless society by *Napoleon* was *historically* impossible.

**240)** This description did not correspond to actual historical reality—that is, to Napoleon—but it correctly identified the goal toward which that reality was moving as it developed as a thesis.

The reality Hegel had in mind appeared only in Russia in 1917.

But the chronological gap between 1806 and 1917 does not correspond to any gap in the *Phenomenology*. What was essentially new during that period—democratic liberalism—had already been described by Hegel in Chapter V.

**241)** Because historical development contains *freedom*, these considerations do not have the character of “predictions.” They are a “project.” See p. 366 ff.

**242)** See above, p. 224 ff. and note 127; also p. 378 ff.

**243)** This explains the hatred of “censorship” that authors in bourgeois countries still display today, as well as their reluctance to admit that they want their work to be “successful”—that is, that they want “social recognition.”

How many people claim that they “write for themselves” and publish only to earn a living!

**244)** See above, p. 55 ff.

**245)** The “social recognition” of my *Phenomenology* is guaranteed insofar as it is *printed* in the USSR and *accepted* as a doctoral thesis—that is, insofar as it has passed through sociopolitical and cultural “censorship.”

Hegel’s mistake also lies in the fact that the recognition he spoke of in his “Preface” did not actually occur. In *his* time, the book remained unknown and misunderstood. Marx was the first person to understand and recognize it.

As for its “social recognition,” the book is acquiring that only in our own time—or so I hope.

It follows that everything Hegel attributed to *his* time should in fact be transferred to *our* own.

**246)** One could say, if one wished, that the entire difference between bourgeois thinkers and socialist thinkers lies here.

**247)** Because the antithesis contains negation—that is, negativity or *freedom*—it cannot be *predicted*.

The emergence of communism is therefore *not necessary*. It depends on revolutionary struggle, on a free effort that may very well never occur.

And since the concrete content of the antithesis is determined by the unpredictable character of the *negation* of the thesis, we cannot know the concrete content of communism in advance with any precision.

We can nevertheless know that communism “negates” socialism while also “preserving” it and “raising it to a higher level.” And in the present case, as we will now see, that is enough.

It is important to emphasize that the final completion of socialism requires uninterrupted *effort* and *action*. It requires both work and struggle.

Every philosophical stage—every thesis, antithesis, and synthesis—is, so to speak, dialectical “through and through.” Within each stage we must therefore distinguish further sequences of dialectical triads, which means further sequences of antitheses—that is, of creative and revolutionary *actions*.

If even one such action fails, the whole process “comes to a halt.”

In practical terms, this means that the process can move more or less quickly depending on the intensity of the work and struggle devoted to it. But once a stage has already begun, only *chronological* changes of this kind remain possible.

Without the appropriate creative and revolutionary actions, socialism would never have appeared. Indeed, it *might never* have appeared; something entirely different might have arisen in its place.

But since socialism *has* appeared, it will either be brought to completion in a fully determinate way or the historical movement will come to a complete stop.

*Effort* is therefore necessary for one reason only: to prevent this *halt* and to *accelerate* the process.

**248)** But since this *Phenomenology* does not exhaust every possible “appearance” of reality, the Ontology and Cosmology based upon it cannot be regarded as final or absolutely true.

We therefore cannot say everything that can be said about Being and existence if we know only what “appears” of them to human beings.

**249)** Here again we encounter the “logical circle” we have already met many times: the whole cannot be understood without its parts, but neither can a part be understood without the whole.

In practice, this makes a second reading of the *Phenomenology* almost indispensable.

**250)** For example, we understand the Roman Empire fully only when we know not merely that it brings the “ancient” or “pagan” world to an end, but also that it becomes the starting point of Christian and bourgeois history, which ultimately leads to socialism.

**251)** In principle, after reading the *Philosophy* once, one should read the *Phenomenology* again.

This restores the logical structure of the system as a whole. On the one hand, we have the *Phenomenology* as an introduction to the *Philosophy*. On the other, we have the *Philosophy* itself—Ontology, Cosmology, and Phenomenology—as the conclusion of the system, reconnecting it with the contents of the ordinary person’s consciousness.

For this reason, in addition to the “Phenomenology” presented in this book, the author would also like to write another one as the third part of the system.

This second *Phenomenology* would not differ essentially from the first. There would be only two important differences. First, it would follow directly from the Cosmology and would therefore contain no “axioms.” Second, it would contain no cosmological or ontological “digressions.”

**252)** I write “*ante-historical*” rather than “*prehistoric*” because the word “prehistoric” normally refers to the earliest periods of *human history*—the “Stone Age,” and so on.

The first part of the *Phenomenology*, by contrast, deals with appearances that logically “precede” history as such.

**253)** The reader will see that this text, written in 1806, could just as easily have been written today.

It is partly to emphasize this continuing “relevance” of Hegel’s *Phenomenology* that I have allowed myself to quote the passage.

**254)** Hegel writes *Geist*, meaning “Spirit.”

To avoid misunderstanding, I translate this as “humanity”—that is, humanity as it realizes a particular stage of historical development.

This translation is entirely justified by the *meaning* of the term, since Hegel repeatedly insists that there is no “Spirit” outside human beings and their History, and that there could not be one.

He speaks of the “World Spirit” (*Weltgeist*) in the same sense in which we speak of the “spirit of the age,” and so on.

Moreover, in German the human sciences are called the “sciences of spirit” (*Geisteswissenschaften*), while intellectual history is called “spiritual history” (*Geistesgeschichte*).

In Russian, however, the word “Spirit” has a “spiritualist” flavor that is completely foreign to Hegel. I therefore avoid the word in my translations.

**255)** Hegel often plays on the German word *bilden*, which, like the Russian *obrazyvat’* [“to form”], can mean both “to form” or “make” and “to educate.”

**256)** I have already discussed the “repetitions” that occur in the *Phenomenology* and the *Philosophy*.

I will say a few words at the end about the repetitions between this *Phenomenology* and the present introduction.

Here, however, I am concerned only with repetitions within the *Phenomenology* itself.

[^E020]: Kojève habitually writes the same term twice in this text, once according to its Slavic etymology and once according to its Latin or Greek etymology. In most cases we translate only one of the two terms, to avoid unnecessary repetition or possible confusion. *(Translator’s note.)*

[^E021]: Kojève uses the word *soznatel’nost’* (“consciousness” in the sense of the quality or state of being conscious). To avoid an awkward neologism, we have translated it as “conscious awareness.” Kojève himself appears to support this choice: in Russian handwritten notes used in preparing this text, he several times writes the French phrase *prise de conscience*, although that expression does not appear in the Russian itself. It therefore seemed to us that this was how he intended *soznatel’nost’* to be rendered. *(Translator’s note.)*

[^E022]: The term was indeed fashionable, but it could have a sinister side: the “conscious proletarian” often took the form of the informer hunting down “class enemies.” *(Translator’s note.)*

[^E023]: A 1938 manual written by Stalin (1878–1953), the study of which became compulsory in the USSR until the mid-1950s. Particular emphasis was placed on the chapter on “dialectical and historical materialism,” which was sometimes published separately. *(Translator’s note.)*

[^E024]: On this “principal achievement” of Comrade Stalin, see Trotsky’s appendix “Socialism in One Country” in *The Revolution Betrayed*, where Trotsky presents it instead as Stalin’s principal failing. Trotsky wrote that “socialism in one country” belonged to Stalin insofar as Stalin represented the “Russian bureaucracy” and a certain chauvinism that regarded Russia as large enough to live in isolation or surrounded by hostile states. See L. Trotsky, *The Revolution Betrayed* (1936), Paris, Éditions de Minuit, 2022, p. 193. *(Translator’s note.)*

[^E025]: Kojève was more cautious in his revision. His first formulation, “the real work of construction,” was changed to “preparatory work” (the Russian expression carries the sense of preliminary work), which is how we translate it here. *(Translator’s note.)*

[^E026]: Kojève adopts Lenin’s own slogan here and uses the same terms. See Lenin, *The State and Revolution* (1917), Paris, Éditions Science marxiste, 2022, p. 44 and p. 121. *(Translator’s note.)*

[^E027]: There is an allusion here to debates in Russian philosophy and politics concerning sexuality and the family, with Kojève here taking the “Stalinist” side. See L. Trotsky, *The Revolution Betrayed*, *op. cit.*, especially Chapter VII, “The Family, Youth, and Culture,” section “Thermidor in the Family”:

    > “The revolution made a heroic effort to destroy the so-called ‘family hearth’—that archaic, stuffy and stagnant institution in which the woman of the toiling classes performs galley labor from childhood to death. The place of the family as a shut-in petty enterprise was to be occupied, according to the plans, by a finished system of social care and accommodation: maternity houses, crèches, kindergartens […] etc. The complete absorption of the housekeeping functions of the family by institutions of the socialist society, uniting all generations in solidarity and mutual aid, was to bring to woman, and thereby to the loving couple, a real liberation from the thousand-year-old fetters. Until this task is fulfilled forty million Soviet families, in their overwhelming majority, will remain nests of medievalism, female slavery and hysteria.”

    Trotsky adds:

    > “The solemn rehabilitation of the family [by the Stalinist faction, of which Kojève is here a representative] […] is the result of the material and cultural bankruptcy of the state. Instead of openly saying: ‘We have proved still too poor and ignorant for the creation of socialist relations among men, our children and great-grandchildren will realize this aim,’ the leaders are forcing people to glue together again the shell of the broken family, and not only that, but to consider it, under threat of extreme penalties, the sacred nucleus of triumphant socialism. It is difficult to measure with the eye the scope of this retreat!”

    (*ibid.*, pp. 99–100, 104). *(Translator’s note.)*

[^E028]: We should take this opportunity to pay tribute to Nina Ivanoff, Kojève’s companion, who at an already advanced age undertook to transcribe and translate the manuscript that we are translating here. Sadly, her death interrupted the project, and this is the last word she deciphered. *(Translator’s note.)*

[^E029]: A clear allusion to Trotsky and his 1936 book *The Revolution Betrayed*. *(Translator’s note.)*

[^E030]: From a strictly historical point of view, this is a rather questionable claim. Stalin is generally thought to have had little sympathy for Hegel and even to have tried, as far as possible, to suppress the Hegelian inheritance within the thought of Marx and Lenin. In his study *Hegel in Russia*, Guy Planty-Bonjour recalls this political campaign, which went so far as effectively to censor Lenin himself:

    > If one is convinced that Marx owes practically nothing to the German philosopher, one naturally tends to minimize the importance of the *Philosophical Notebooks* [Lenin’s notes from 1914–15 on the *Science of Logic*, the *Lectures on the History of Philosophy*, and the *Lectures on the Philosophy of History*], or even to deny their value altogether: Lenin’s thought would then be contained entirely in *Materialism and Empirio-Criticism*. This was the dominant interpretation in the Soviet Union during the Stalinist period. As M. Garaudy observes, the *Philosophical Notebooks* “were excluded under Stalin from Lenin’s *Collected Works*, just as the *1844 Manuscripts* were excluded from Marx’s *Works*, because they were incompatible with a dogmatic interpretation of Marxism.”

    Planty-Bonjour also writes:

    > Lenin had indeed written his notes on the *Science of Logic*. But Stalin effectively prevented their circulation. Lenin therefore influenced the development of Soviet philosophy through the anti-Hegelian book *Materialism and Empirio-Criticism*.

    See G. Planty-Bonjour, *Hegel et la pensée philosophique en Russie, 1830–1917*, The Hague: Martinus Nijhoff, 1974, pp. 281 and 332. *(Translator’s note.)*

[^E031]: This is a quotation from Lenin’s 1908 article “Leo Tolstoy as the Mirror of the Russian Revolution.” Tolstoy (1828–1910) is presented there as a mirror of the 1905 Revolution. As Lenin emphasizes, however, if Tolstoy is a mirror of the revolution, this also means that the revolution was not a clear or homogeneous movement. Religious philosophy itself, especially in the form of Tolstoyanism, took part in it in its own way, without understanding what it was doing—that is, unconsciously. *(Translator’s note.)*

[^E032]: Kojève wrote in the margin: “cf. 26: *Weg des Zweifels; Weg der Verzweiflung*.” He is referring to Hegel’s famous formulation in the “Introduction” to the *Phenomenology of Spirit*. See G. W. F. Hegel, *The Phenomenology of Spirit*, trans. B. Bourgeois, Paris, Vrin, 2019, p. 122. *(Translator’s note.)*

[^E033]: Kojève originally wrote “in every philosophy,” then changed this to “in true philosophy.” It is not certain, however, whether the phrase “in true philosophy” was itself later crossed out. *(Translator’s note.)*

[^E034]: Kojève writes: “*Erscheinung*. Phenomenon. *Erscheinen*. Appearing [*javlenie*] (from the phenomenon [*fenomen*] to the human being → to a consciousness through a cognition).” *(Translator’s note.)*

[^E035]: In Russian, Kojève uses *javlenie* (“appearance” or “appearing”) and *fenomen* (“phenomenon”). We have tried to preserve this distinction as far as possible because Kojève himself writes in the margin of the manuscript: “‘Appearing’ = ‘phenomenon’ + how + to whom.” We have therefore translated *javlenie* sometimes as “appearance” and sometimes as “appearing.” In a note to this book dated 15 February 1941 (folio 939), Kojève supports the translation of *javlenie* as “appearing,” although in French it has occasionally seemed necessary to translate it as “apparition” in order to preserve natural usage.

[^E036]: Kojève underlined these words—the Russian *poznanie*—and placed a question mark in the margin. It should also be noted that *Erfahrung* is normally translated as “experience.” *(Translator’s note.)*

[^E037]: For the sake of clarity, the French editors chose at this point to translate *poznanie* as “experience” or “cognitive experience,” following the usual French translation of Hegel’s *Erfahrung*. Kojève eventually placed *Erfahrung* alongside *poznanie* himself, though with a question mark.

    Earlier in the text, *poznanie* had generally been rendered as “cognition,” which is closer to its primary meaning, though “experience” was sometimes used for *samo-poznanie* in order to distinguish it from “self-knowledge” (*znanie sebja*).

    In general, however, cognition can be understood as an experience through which knowledge advances. This also brings us close to the original sense of the German *Erfahrung*, which is related to *fahren*, “to travel” or “to go”: experience understood as a kind of movement or progression.

    In any case, when Kojève speaks of a “cognition of oneself,” the editors judged “experience” to be the more natural term. In French, as in English, we would normally speak of the **experience one has of oneself** rather than one’s “cognition of oneself.”

    That is what is at issue here: knowing oneself by **experiencing oneself**—even if, in the end, that experience expands to the dimensions of the entire world.

[^E038]: Kojève wrote in the margin: “cf. *Encyclo.*, §79.” See G. W. F. Hegel, *Encyclopedia of the Philosophical Sciences. I. The Science of Logic* (1817), French trans. B. Bourgeois, Paris: Vrin, 2019, pp. 342–343. *(Translator’s note.)*

[^E039]: Kojève uses the rather dismissive Russian term *intelligenty*—literally, “intellectuals” or “clever people.” The French editors chose *intelligentsia*, since the word is itself borrowed from Russian and preserves something of the cultural background of Kojève’s expression. *(Translator’s note.)*

[^E040]: Kojève wrote in pencil in the margin: “‘Appearance’ = ‘phenomenon’ + how + to whom.” *(Translator’s note.)*

[^E041]: It is very difficult to reproduce in French Kojève’s use of the Russian word *nečto*, which the French editors render, for lack of anything better, as “something.” This should not be taken to mean that the human being is a “thing” in the Russian sense of *vešč’*. Kojève’s point is precisely that the human being is not a “thing” but “something” other than a thing. He also plays on the Russian words when he writes that this *nečto samo po sebe — ničto*: this “something, in itself, is nothing.” The wordplay cannot be reproduced exactly in French. *(Translator’s note.)*

[^E042]: The distinction is subtle in French but important. Kojève distinguishes *nečto drugoe*, “something different” or “another thing,” from *nečto inoe*, “something other.” The distinction becomes clearer in light of one of his earliest important texts, *Atheism* (1931). There Kojève tries to understand the status of God as the radically Other—something transcending both world and human beings. God, in this sense, is not merely “something different,” *nečto drugoe*: one other thing among others, and therefore something that could still be encountered within the world. God is instead the radically “other,” *inoe*: the Other par excellence, the other of all other things, something that cannot be reduced to an object within the world. Kojève later associates this radical Other with “nothingness,” the “other” of being. The French editors therefore render *nečto inoe* as “quelque chose autre,” “something other,” rather than allowing it to collapse into the ordinary “something different.” *(Translator’s note.)*

[^E043]: Kojève writes *čelovečnost’*, which can mean “humanity” in the sense of the quality or character of being human. Russian has another word, *čelovečestvo*, for “humanity” in the sense of humankind as a whole, and Kojève deliberately plays on the distinction. Later in the book, for example, he can speak of “the degree of humanity (*čelovečnost’*) attained by humanity (*čelovečestvo*).” In English, the first sense could also be rendered as **“humanness”** to make the distinction explicit.

[^E044]: Kojève uses the word *čelovečestvo*, meaning humanity in the collective sense: all human beings taken together. *(Translator’s note.)*

[^E045]: Kojève notes in the margin that the preceding three paragraphs, beginning with “Since, as we will see” and ending with “in the natural sense of the word,” should be “deleted or moved to a footnote.” *(Translator’s note.)*

[^E047]: The “disaster” of Trotskyism lies precisely in its slogan of “permanent revolution.” It functions as a utopia gone wrong. Why? Because it is too *impatient* to “realize all the possibilities of the Revolution.” It fails to take account of the “real” dimension—namely, the obstacle of time, something Stalin, according to Kojève, understood well. This does not mean that Trotsky is *wrong forever*; it means that he is wrong for the time being. See A. Kojève, *Introduction to the Reading of Hegel*, *op. cit.*, p. 591. *(Editor’s note.)*

[^E053]: Kojève wrote a “?” in the margin beside Bakunin’s name. *(Translator’s note.)* Kojève is referring to a Soviet political poster displayed in the streets of Saint Petersburg between 1917 and 1920. The poster adapted a famous quotation from Bakunin. Bakunin had written in German that “the joy of destruction is at the same time a creative joy” (see M. Bakunin, “The Reaction in Germany” [1842], in *The Young Hegelians*, trans. F. Fischbach, Paris, Gallimard, 2022, p. 75). In Russian the quotation was translated, repeated, and altered many times, until it became almost proverbial in roughly the form Kojève gives here: “The spirit that destroys is the spirit that creates; the passion for destruction is the passion for creation.” It is also possible that this quotation became mixed with another famous line, this time from Pushkin: “The spirit of negation is a spirit of doubt,” from the poem “The Angel,” written in 1827. That would explain the use of the word “spirit,” which does not occur in Bakunin’s original formulation. Finally, if Kojève seems uncertain whether Bakunin was the author, this may be because Bakunin published the article under the pseudonym Jules Elysard. *(Translator’s note.)*

[^E054]: “Ivan the Amnesiac” is a Russian proverbial expression (*krylatoe vyraženie*). In his large dictionary of *Popular Expressions* (*Krylatye slova*), Nikolai Sergeevich Ashukin (1890–1972) explains: “In Tsarist Russia, escaped convicts who were recaptured in Siberia and wanted to conceal their real identity would ask to be registered as people who no longer remembered their family background. This gave rise to the nickname ‘Ivan the Amnesiac.’” See N. Ashukin, *Popular Expressions* [*Krylatye slova*], Moscow, State Publishing House, 1955, p. 227. *(Translator’s note.)*
